Possession: Ipswich 45%-55% LiverpoolShots: 14-10Shots on target: 5-7Corners: 4-3Touches in opposition box: 16-21

The Swede’s two early goals have earned Liverpool all three points at Portman Road and the travelling Liverpool fans are singing his name. Isak’s fellow teammates are pushing him towards the travelling fans to take their adulation as they belt out his name.

The final whistle goes at Portman Road and Andoni Iraola picks up his first win as Liverpool boss with a 2-0 victory thanks to Isak’s quickfire double inside the opening 10 minutes. Like they did two seasons ago, Liverpool win 2-0 at Portman Road.

Enciso has a late shot from the edge of the box but it goes wide of the far post.

McAteer shoots from range but there is not enough power to trouble Alisson, who makes the save down to his right.

A late change from Liverpool as Koumas replaces Wirtz.

Due to that VAR review for the Liverpool penalty that was not, there will probably be five or six added minutes.

Clarke’s shot from just outside the Liverpool penalty area takes a deflection off his teammate Diop and goes wide.

Davis is getting a fair bit of joy down Ipswich’s left and the ball has been on to him quite a few times. He is being afforded too much space by Liverpool to get crosses in.

Andoni Iraola is bringing on Nyoni for Mac Allister, who was on a booking.

Davis is found making a run in behind and his cross from the left side of the box is blocked by Araujo and goes behind for a corner. Lukic’s delivery is headed away at the front post by Gravenberch.

Double change for Ipswich as McAteer and Ouattara replace Fatawau and Palacios.

Barcola drives down Liverpool’s left and, as he approaches the Ipswich box, cuts onto his right and feeds it across to Gakpo, whose shot misses the target.

The ball comes to Flemming on the edge of the box and he tries to curl one into the far corner but it is an easy save for Alisson.

Barcola is nearly played in behind but Scherpen does really to get out of his goal quickly and gets to the ball first, just ahead of Barcola.

Davis and Ipswich can count themselves very, very lucky. It would have been a penalty but Szoboszlai was offside when the original ball was played. For the second time tonight, an offside call massively goes in Ipswich’s favour; one to deny Isak a hat-trick and now to deny Liverpool a penalty. A massive let-off for Ipswich.

#IPSLIV – 68'VAR recommended an on-field review for a potential penalty, but determined that Szoboszlai was in an offside position in the build-up.REF: "After review, there's a penalty shout on Szoboszlai. However, in the build-up to the penalty shout, Szoboszlai is in an… pic.twitter.com/DN4i8rj5fg

Liverpool are demanding a penalty. Szoboszlai is played in behind and is constantly having his shirt pulled by Davis. Davis then appears to bring Szoboszlai down inside the box but the referee waves it away. Davis gets none of the ball and the referee is being sent to the screen...

Barcola’s first few touches in a Liverpool shirt are pretty good down the left. He is playing in his most natural position of wide left, with Gakpo now down the middle and Szoboszlai on the right.

Gary O’Neil is going to make a double change as Clarke and Flemming come on, with the latter making his debut. Maeda and Emersonn come off.

So, here comes from the £123m Frenchman as Barcola enters the fray for his Liverpool debut. Gravenberch also comes on. There will be no first Liverpool hat-trick for Isak as he heads off, as does Munoz.

Bradley Barcola comes on to make his Liverpool debut! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/PjO78nlcqj

Andoni Iraola must be ripping his air out with the lack of composure and control from his side since half-time. It is no wonder he is about to turn to his bench and a certain Frenchman.

Enciso is given far too much space to drive towards the Liverpool box before shooting but Alisson makes the save. Liverpool, despite being 2-0 up, have showed a real lack of composure since the break.

If trends are anything to go by, Bradley Barcola will be introduced in the next three or four minutes. Andoni Iraola likes to change things around the hour mark and if the Frenchman warms up anymore, he will nearly overheat.

Kerkez is the latest player into the book for a foul on Fatawu.

Fatawu receives it out on the right for Ipswich and cuts inside onto his preferred left foot before curling an effort towards the far post but it goes wide.

Jacquet takes a heavy touch from a high ball and ends up taking out Emersonn, which earns the Frenchman a booking.

Liverpool work it well down their left as Isak plays it into Gakpo, who drives towards the Ipswich box. He plays it across the face of the penalty area to Szboszblai, who flicks it first time into the path of Wirtz. The German’s effort takes a deflection and goes behind for a corner.

Szoboszlai’s outswinger finds a free Mac Allister at the front post but the Argentine’s header is straight at Scherpen. That was a good chance for Mac Allister.

We are back under way at Portman Road. No changes for either side at the break.

We have just seen replays of a possible penalty shout for Liverpool right at the end of the first half for a foul on Gakpo by Fatawu and it looked a decent shout.

Possession: Ipswich 41%-59% LiverpoolShots: 8-7Shots on target: 2-6Corners: 3-2Touches in opposition box: 7-12

Perhaps if Liverpool were playing a team with a bit more savvy, the 2-0 scoreline they currently protect would have been in jeopardy. Ipswich have put some nice moves together and had half chances but not enough to really turn the screw. Andoni Iraola, certainly, has been unhappy at times and it is becoming a trademark to see him spin around from the technical area in disgust when a ball has been squandered. In the main, though, he can be satisfied with this opening 45 minutes. Liverpool should be winning from here.

The first half is brought to an end at Portman Road and Isak’s quickfire double early in the half gives Liverpool a 2-0 lead at the break.

Wirtz feeds a lovely pass into the left channel to pick out the run of Isak into the Ipswich box but Diop comes in with a crucial challenge.

Two added minutes at the end of this first half.

Araujo slices a clearance out of play for an Ipswich corner. A real gift for the home side as Araujo was not under any real pressure.

Isak should head away at the near post but it comes to Mac Allister to clear away.

A chance for Wirtz as the ball falls to the German on the edge of the Ipswich box but his shot is saved by Scherpen down to his left.

Enciso is the first Ipswich player into the book tonight for delaying a restart.

Szoboszlai, for the third time in the half, shoots from range. Again, the Hungarian gets plenty of power on it but fortunately for Scherpen it is straight at him.

Enciso turns neatly not far outside the Liverpool box and then shoots but slices the shot a fair way wide.

Tommy Elphick, a member of Andoni Iraola’s coaching staff, is booked for his protestations. Liverpool are not happy with some of the fouls being given against them and then some that are not given for them, including a clear foul from Emersonn on Van Dijk that was not penalised.

Isak has the ball in the Ipswich net for the third time tonight and thinks he has his hat-trick but the offside flag goes up. It comes from a stunning piece of play from Wirtz down Liverpool’s left, taking up a pocket of space and taking the ball on the turn beautifully. He then spots Isak in space at the far post and picks him out perfectly, with Isak slotting home. However, the offside flag is up and replays prove he was just offside. Could Isak have timed his run just fractionally better and still reached the cross? Probably but it was very close.

Mac Allister receives a pass from Wirtz and, from just outside the box, decides to shoot but his effort goes just over. Scherpen did appear to have it covered anyway.

A crucial intervention from Araujo. Enciso drives down Ipswich’s right after Fatawu’s header, with Mac Allister tracking back. From the right side of the Liverpool box, Enciso’s deflected cross comes towards Maeda at the far post but Araujo makes an important clearance.

Moments later, Davis again meets a Fatawu cross at the far post but his header is off target.

Fatawu’s dangerous cross from the right all the way to the back post finds Davis, who heads back across goal. Emersonn takes a touch with his chest on the edge of the six-yard box before shooting but Jacquet is on hand to make a crucial block. Ipswich though do have their first corner of the game.

Lukic clips it in and Alisson should punch away with ease. However, the ball comes off Gakpo and, very fortunately for Alisson, the ball gets trapped between his own legs and he can gather. Alisson will be a relieved man.

Szoboszlai sends another powerful shot from range towards the goal and forces Scherpen into another decent save. Ipswich are not helping themselves at times by just giving the ball away inside their own half.

Szoboszlai comes close to adding a third for Liverpool. Fatawu inexplicably gives the ball away inside his own half before Mac Allister plays it forward to Szoboszlai, who takes just one touch before firing towards goal. Scherpen gets down well to his right to make the save.

And there he is. You have been waiting 12 months to see the Alexander Isak of Newcastle play for Liverpool but here he is, a confident, instinctive-finishing menace. His first goal was marvellous, his second was a work of art, given the pass from Cody Gakpo, and what a position Liverpool have put themselves in to get their first win under Andoni Iraola. And, while we are at it, Gakpo has made both Liverpool’s goals: what on earth were they doing thinking of selling him to Manchester City?

Isak, on his last trip to Portman Road, scored a hat-trick for Newcastle here in a 4-0 win back in December 2024. He already has two goals to his name tonight inside the opening quarter of an hour.

Emersonn misses from close range for Ipswich but the offside flag goes up against Greaves. It was a bad miss from Emersonn but Greaves, who had delivered the cross for Emersonn, was offside.

The first booking of the game goes the way of Mac Allister, who is booked slightly harshly for a foul on Enciso.

Moments later, Ipswich have their first effort of the game but Fatawu curls over from the edge of the box.

Another fine goal from Isak and Liverpool lead 2-0 not even 10 minutes into this game. It is Gakpo who assists again with a superb pass with the outside of his right foot from halfway into the left channel to pick out the run in behind of Isak. The Swede cuts inside Greaves onto his right before then chopping back onto his left. He then coolly slots home past Scherpen and Liverpool have the dream start.

Inside NINE minutes Alexander Isak has two goals! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/3UGq0bwqRm

Liverpool take a deserved lead at Portman Road. Kerkez wins the ball back for Liverpool on halfway and the ball comes to Gakpo. The Dutchman drives forward and spots Isak in space to his right. Isak’s movement is very clever as he drifts off the defender into space. He takes a touch before smashing the ball past Scherpen at his near post. Should Scherpen have saved that? Possibly but Isak did hit that very hard. For the first time this season, Liverpool lead in a Premier League match.

A blistering finish from Alexander Isak! 💥 pic.twitter.com/jSGlIZsQtA

Wirtz is penalised for a very soft foul on Enciso, who just threw his hands in the air after the slightest bits of contact. The referee Darren England was not initially going to give it but eventually does, giving Ipswich the chance to swing it in from the left into the Liverpool penalty area.

Fatawu swings it in with his left but Alisson punches away.

It has been all Liverpool in these early stages but have yet to have a shot. Ipswich have barely touched the ball thus far.

Liverpool win the first corner of the game as Davis is forced to put it behind after good work from Munoz down Liverpool’s right.

Szoboszlai’s outswinger is headed away from danger.

Both sides emerge from the tunnel at Portman Road and we are moments away from kick-off. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

Ipswich: Scherpen, O’Shea, Diop, Greaves, Davis, Palacios, Lukic, Fatawu, Enciso, Maeda, Emersonn.Substitutes: Walton, Furlong, Kipre, Ouattara, Florentino, Nunez, McAteer, Clarke, Flemming.

We do not focus on the outcome or results, we just commit to being the best version of ourselves. We cannot go toe-to-toe with everyone. We have to be sensible and smart.”

Here was one of the world’s best wingers, with his 13 major honours, 28 international caps and £123m price tag – a combination that could easily lead a man to view himself through the prism of a superstar: never mind what I can do for you, what can you do for me?

Liverpool’s due diligence on Barcola had all been positive – not least from the currently injured Hugo Ekitike, who had been a vocal advocate of his compatriot’s capabilities to the recruitment team – but Iraola wanted to gauge for himself exactly what the 24-year-old was going to offer.

We are about to find out the two starting XIs at Portman Road. Will Bradley Barcola start for Liverpool on his debut?

The third matchday of the new Premier League season kicks off at Portman Road as newly-promoted Ipswich host Liverpool.

Andoni Iraola has drawn his first two games in charge of Liverpool, both 2-2 stalemates against Newcastle and Nottingham Forest respectively. Liverpool secured a move for forward Bradley Barcola from PSG in the final few days on the window for a fee that could rise to £123m and the Frenchman is set to make his Liverpool debut tonight.

“We are very happy with Bradley,” Iraola said. “He was our priority; to sign a very good player in that position. He has come with the right mentality. I like that he wanted Liverpool a lot, he just wanted to come here. That is a good first sign. Being the player he is and the things he has won recently, he has come with the willingness to help us. I am very happy with him.

“He trained well with us, and if everything goes well in today’s [Thursday] training, he will definitely be available for tomorrow [tonight]. He has trained with us three times. He has not had minutes in pre-season but he has been training normally with the group. It is a decision we have to make. We have to consider that he has not had minutes in pre-season.”

Liverpool won both fixtures when Ipswich were last in the Premier League two seasons ago, including a 2-0 win on the opening weekend in Arne Slot’s first game in charge of Liverpool as they went on to win the Premier League that season.

Ipswich won their first home game on their return to the Premier League, beating Sunderland 2-1 on the opening weekend. However, they fell to a 5-2 defeat in their first away game at Manchester United. Over the course of the summer transfer window, Ipswich made a total of 14 signings and spent over £200m.

“What we can do is perform in a way that always gives us a real chance, which we have done so far,” Ipswich boss Gary O’Neil said. “We were in that game at Manchester United until a couple of moments took it away from us. We were in it, so that is what we need to do, we need to make sure that no matter who it is, whether it is Liverpool, Manchester United, Manchester City, when they come to Portman Road, we need to make sure we are right in the game to give ourselves opportunities. We will always be a threat; we have scored four goals in two games. That is really good for a promoted side. We look a goal threat, and we need to keep that going and that will be tested.”

Team news from Portman Road to follow shortly.

#1469. Newcastle star Amar Dedic sparks six-car police swoop after being spotted with a BOW AND ARROWS in Northumberland beauty spot before weapon is seized

Published: 13:29 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 17:28 EDT, 5 November 2026

Newcastle United star Amar Dedic was at the centre of a major police operation after he was spotted carrying a bow and arrows at a Northumberland beauty spot – with at least SIX patrol cars involved in the search for the £30million defender.

The Bosnia international sparked alarm when a concerned member of the public reported seeing him and a friend walking with the weapon near a reservoir in the countryside outside Newcastle.

Police dispatched marked and unmarked vehicles to the area in Harlow Hill, with some understood to have been armed response units, before Dedic and his companion were finally intercepted around seven miles away in the exclusive Darras Hall estate.

Sources have described the dramatic swoop on Dedic's vehicle before officers searched the car and seized a bow and arrows, with the 24-year-old questioned about his activities.

In a bizarre twist, Newcastle goalkeeper Mark Gillespie and former defender Paul Dummett arrived at the scene while police were speaking to Dedic. It is understood the pair were in the area by chance and stopped to offer assistance.

After speaking to the two men, officers were satisfied there was no threat to the public, with police subsequently stating that the equipment was believed to have been intended for recreational use.

Amar Dedic played in Newcastle's 1-0 defeat by Everton on Monday evening

Dedic was spotted with a crossbow off Military Road, the 61-mile B6318 in Northumberland

However, enquiries remain ongoing into the incident, which happened on Wednesday afternoon. It is understood that Dedic and his friend had fired some arrows while in the countryside, although it remains unclear what they were aiming at. Hunting any animal or bird with a bow and arrow or crossbow is illegal in the UK.

Dedic joined Newcastle from Benfica during the summer and has impressed at right back despite the club's difficult start to the season.

Daily Mail Sport understands he will not face disciplinary action from Newcastle over the incident, although there is a feeling that the player was naive to believe he could walk around the countryside carrying such weaponry.

A Northumbria Police spokesperson said: 'Shortly after 1.55pm on Wednesday, we received a report of two men carrying a bow and arrows while walking along a track by the reservoir on Military Road in the Harlow Hill area.

'Officers attended and subsequently stopped a vehicle in the Darras Hall area and seized a bow and arrows. At this stage, it is understood they were for recreational use and there was no threat to the public. Enquiries are ongoing.'

Dedic is expected to be available for Saturday's Premier League trip to Fulham, where Newcastle will attempt to halt a run of four defeats in five matches across all competitions.

#1468. Gasly takes shock Italian GP pole and denies Russell

Sometimes inspiration can come from the unlikeliest of sources. After claiming the first pole of his Formula One career, an absolutely stunning effort in his 192nd attempt – edging out Mercedes’ George Russell right at the death – Alpine’s Pierre Gasly revealed that a harmless jibe from his performance coach Ben Thorpe just before the session started had riled him up.

It turned out Gasly and Russell had been playing online chess until about 15 minutes before qualifying.

“Since the [drivers’] briefing last night, I figured out that he [Russell] is obsessed with chess, and so am I,” Gasly explained later in his press conference. “There are a few of us in the paddock who are. So we have exchanged our IDs on Chess.com and we have had a little game going on.

“I won yesterday, and another one that carried on into today,” the Frenchman added. “I was feeling confident and I was picking [taking] piece after piece. Then Ben told me: ‘You are getting George here but he is going to get you in a few minutes!’. And I thought ‘F--- off!’.”

What a way to break your duck. And what a day on which to do it. On Friday, Gasly lost his only podium of the season when the International Court of Appeal reinstated two five-second penalties he received in Monaco, dropping him from third to seventh in that race. The ruling produced fireworks when Flavio Briatore, Alpine’s executive adviser, then accused one of the judges on the ICA panel of being biased towards McLaren, one of two teams who had brought the appeal.

Another 24 hours later, the fireworks were for all the right reasons. And there was no appealing the result; the start of Russell’s final lap in Q3 was slightly compromised by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, but the Englishman could have no real complaints, losing out by 0.060secs in the end, prompting wild celebrations in the Alpine garage.

To say the result was a surprise would be an understatement. This was the Enstone team’s first pole in 17 years, since Fernando Alonso took P1 Renault at the 2009 Hungarian Grand Prix.

The warning signs were there. Alpine had been quick all weekend. But the Tifosi packing Monza’s grandstands fully expected it to be a battle between Mercedes and their beloved Ferrari for pole.

The Scuderia’s performance was underwhelming. Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were only ninth and 10th quickest in Q2, the latter squeaking into Q3 by one thousandth of a second from Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto. “F--- me,” Hamilton said after dodging that bullet.

And although they improved a bit in Q3, Hamilton managing to claim P5, just behind Leclerc in P4, they never threatened the front row. In fact, they later got lucky as McLaren’s Oscar Piastri, who took P3, was later hit with a three-place grid drop post-qualifying for impeding Liam Lawson, meaning both Ferrari drivers rose one place.

It could prove significant. Hamilton, like Russell, knows this weekend represents a golden opportunity to close the gap to Kimi Antonelli in the title race. The two Britons are tied second in the championship heading into the weekend, 59 points behind the Italian. But Antonelli, who sacrificed his qualifying to help Russell, must start from the back of the grid on Sunday due to exceeding the permitted number of engines in a season.

It promises to be a fascinating race, with Antonelli fighting his way through the pack and Russell and Hamilton trying to make hay while they can. Russell sounded confident. “I think they [Alpine] have got a car that’s got some good straight-line speed, which will be nice for them in the race. But, yeah, confident I’ve got the pace to go for the win.”

Could he be underestimating Gasly again? The Frenchman, who lives locally in Milan and speaks fluent Italian, has won here before. He claimed the only victory of his F1 career at Monza for AlphaTauri in 2020.

“Anything is possible tomorrow,” insisted Steve Nielsen, Alpine’s managing director. “We didn’t expect to be in pole position, we are. Tomorrow, good starts, good strategy, good pit stops – who knows? Let’s try to win it.”

Gasly himself said he had no idea what he was capable of. “My plan is to stay first as long as I can. How long is that going to be? I have no idea. My focus is going to be on my driving and making no mistakes and making the best out of what I have.” Perhaps that will be enough for another checkmate.

Antonelli acknowledged that his engine-parts grid penalty meant he had no reason not to assist his teamate Russell by offering towing assistance.

He seemed a little peeved at times on the radio, but he did his job. With Russell likely to need to return the favour for him later this season, there is no point causing bother.

He told Sky Sports: “It’s what I have to do. The team asked me and of course I did what I had to do, I tried to help as much as possible. It’s a bit weird going in two, even the lap I did alone was a bit of a weird feeling. Overall with the penalty today I had to be a good teammate and I had to help as much as I could. I think I did a good job with that and happy it worked out.”

Here’s Oscar Piastri, asked if a pole had been possible: “I don’t think so, no. I think the first lap felt good and I tried to see if anyone wanted to go in front out of the pit lane but no one did and I knew it was always going to be difficult and misjudged the braking a little bit and locked up. That was the session but good to have a decent result, it has been a while. I’ll take it.”

Alpine managing director Steve Nielsen said to Sky Sports that they were aiming high: “Pierre is a class act, as you say, if you give him the machine, he will deliver. We failed to do that a few times last year. We haven’t always given him the most competitive machinery this year, but when we have he has delivered. Particularly earlier in the season so to see the team bounce back, to see him deliver on the track he knows well, he lives locally, he lives in Milan. It was wonderful.

“We mustn’t forget Franco either, he’s done a great job today. I really feel we have given them a good car, and who knows? Anything is possible tomorrow.”

Here’s what he said immediately after the session: “Massive congrats to Pierre because that’s an incredible performance. We were actually playing a game of chess about 15 minutes before qualifying and he beat me there and I thought ‘well I think I’ll beat you in qualifying’ and here we are - he’s ahead of me again! I was disappointed not to get pole. It was a bit messy with Verstappen opening the lap. But Pierre and Alpine have been super fast, even from Q1. Happy to see them get a good result.”

Gasly’s advantage, it appears, seems to be over Russell’s car understeering and lacking grip in turbulent air.

P1 ☝️#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/U0hebWsjWY

He says: “It was amazing, thank you everyone. It was an incredible qualy. I felt very good in the car. I was trying to chip away in evert session. I’m so happy, it’s been nine years trying to get a pole. First win [was] in Monza, to get pole is very special.”

He then pays credit to his team and the fans in Italian, and I am leaning on my Latin to get the gist of it.

“I was disappointed not to get the pole,” admits Russell who said he had been playing chess with Gasly before the game and the Frenchman won that, with Russell confident he was going to beat him in qualifying.

Alpine been in the news all weekend. Fair to say that pole lap from Gasly is better PR for the team than Flavio Briatore’s bizarre outburst in the FIA press conference yesterday. Well done that man.

His tone is evidently disappointed. In truth, given Hamilton is fifth, he is in a strong position to have the best of the weekend.

Gasly, yes, was fastest, but Russell has been the most consistent.

Piastri could be in trouble, too, for impeding earlier in the day’s sesion. Ferrari, in fourth and fifth, do not look entirely competitive.

Russell is second, Piastri third, Leclerc fourth, Hamilton fifth, Verstappen sixth, Antonelli seventh, Colapinto eighth, Norris ninth and Lindblad 10th.

He starts his flying lap, and locks up at turn 1 and exceeds track limits. That means Norris will be unable to get a tow from him too.

After being the quickest at FP2 and FP3, he is top of the pack once more with a bit over five minutes left.

Antonelli has done him a favour there, but Russell may need to return the favour in similar circumstances down the line.

Hamilton is now down in ninth, and struggling, about 0.8s off the pace.

Hamilton needs to catch Leclerc to get a tow. It failed to happen last time out.

Piastri finished Q2 in P2 but it looks likely he'll be penalised for this incident involving Lawson#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/RGzzEeqyql

Lawson, Hulkenberg, Sainz, Ocon, Bearman and Bortoleto are all out.

Hamilton is 10th, one-thousandth of a second quick enough to scrape through, and Leclrec ninth.

“**** me” exclaims Hamilton, without saying, ‘Asterisk’ once.

Antonelli asks for the chance to go out with another team ahead so he can get a tow of his own.

Norris now second quickest, so perhaps those brakes are up to speed.

There is some suggestion that Hamilton might need a front wing change.

The Silver Arrows working in tandem Kimi in front, George slipstreaming behind #F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/H476E91GJs

But Gasly is going fastest in his out lap.

Verstappen now goes fastest. Lawson is in behind, with Carlos Sainz making a surprise appearance up top.

Hamilton and Russell are yet to lay down times.

Norris is uncomfortable with his brakes at Monza.

Given he’s well outside of the fastest for now, the pressure is on him to make Q3.

The two Aston Martins are out, along with Yuki Tsunoda, Alex Albon, Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez.

Q2 awaits, with Gasly fastest - aiming for what would be his first pole.

Alonso, meanwhile, has wirthdrawn from the session. Things going wrong for the veteran, who must have no other hobbies.

FOUR MINUTES TO GO IN Q1TOP 6 ⬆️Gasly VerstappenColapintoAntonelliRussellHamiltonBOTTOM 6 ⬇️Hulkenberg AlbonBottasAlonsoStrollPerez#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/BYdYjrjtnu

Pierre Gasly takes his Alpine for a spin. He is now fastest, with Verstappen second, and Colapinto bookending the Dutchman.

Antonelli and then Russell next, with the stricken Antonelli likely to give his colleague a tow.

The Red Bull man is 0.216s clear of Hamilton, with Piastri just behind.

No surprising stragglers just yet, but 11 minutes to go of this section.

We’ve 16 minutes left, and some cars are finally coming out to do battle.

18 minutes ahead before the final two rounds. Nobody is doing anything. As they say in football: tactically fascinating.

Monza paddock is absolutely sweltering. 33.8C out here. I just passed Fabio Capello on my way back to the media centre. He was speaking to Sky Sports Italia so I wasn’t able to give him my thoughts on where he went wrong at the 2010 World Cup.

Decent ding dong between Hamilton and Verstappen in practice earlier. Hopefully Hamilton is fired up for this. With Antonelli taking his grid drop at his home race, there’s a big opportunity for both Hamilton and Russell to close the gap this weekend.

The tifosi are ready 🙌It's time for qualifying at the Temple of Speed 👊#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/jeiTcb8Ij2

The cars will soon be out on the track, and we’ll have reports of their progress.

There are actually times when affection for a car company makes sense, despite what I said earlier.

Sound on... listen to the reception for Charles and Lewis ❤️#F1 #ItalianGP @ScuderiaFerrari pic.twitter.com/kk6BvA1UdC

As touched on earlier, Lewis Hamilton has to hope Charles Leclerc will work with him.

The Monegasque (look it up) is the junior partner at this point, whether he wants to be or not. That might not make him entirely delighted, but he can tow the British driver around and give him a launch for fast laps, if he’s feeling helpful.

Everyone now has access to PowerPoint, which means we all now have to have, “learnings.”

Imagine if someone you met in real life said that to you.

3 hours of laps and learnings done.#ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/GTvOvL5L5M

Given Antonelli is still one of the quickest on the track, it would be no surprise if he can at least make the top 10.

Favourable accidents and yellow flags might offer up more opportunities, too, but both Hamilton and Russell need to strike while they have such a clear advantage.

George Russell tops Lewis Hamilton in final practice in Monza 🇮🇹💪 pic.twitter.com/jxIO13aRX6

I’m as big a fan of F1 as the next man, assuming the next man quite likes F1, but there is something strange about supporting a car company, isn’t there?

🇮🇹 Sentendo il calore dell'Italia! 🥰🇬🇧 Feeling the warmth of Italy! 🥰 pic.twitter.com/ze6Ww1Z0zx

The session starts in around 40 minutes, so drivers are on their Gameboys and Instagram, and reading the weekend edition of The Telegraph.

Words we live by, this weekend and always ❤️ pic.twitter.com/0QoGlpzOHI

Here’s our interview with Alex Albon about a grim weekend at Monza.

“Alex Albon remembers the 2022 Italian Grand Prix well. He had been looking forward to it. ‘We had a car which was good down the straights that year so I was quite excited to be going to Monza,” the Williams driver recalls, a little wistfully.

‘We did FP1 and FP2 and sure enough we were quick so I was like: ‘This is going to be a good weekend.’

“Albon could not have been more wrong. He remembers waking at around 1am that night and being unable to get back to sleep.

“What happened next was the stuff of nightmares. Albon called the doctor, was diagnosed with appendicitis, sent to San Gerardo Hospital in Monza for surgery, only to suffer an unexpected complication during the procedure, which resulted in acute respiratory failure.”

He shares the joint record with Michael Schumacher for most wins at Monza.

Schumacher, a Ferrari legend, ended his career with five. Hamilton has the same.

Sport loves an emotional link to records, so be prepared for this to become a big moment.

Five wins apiece for Michael and Lewis 🖐#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/j10lMygYft

The Italian team are bringing an upgrade engine to Monza for the weekend.

Hamilton would desperately love to go out at the top after what is a remarkable return to decent form after some years of desperate struggle.

With Antonelli possibly out of the running this weekend, this is the chance to change the - *spits in self-scorn* - narrative.

Russell might have incurred a penalty if he had done this in qualifying.

The Mercedes man blocked Oscar Piastri’s run at a corner, forcing some heavy braking from his rival.

Thankfully, Piastri ducked out, and thankfully for Russell, he’s not facing censure.

A near miss for Oscar Piastri! 😬 pic.twitter.com/y6UMu8wIDM

Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton go racing! 🍿 pic.twitter.com/Zs8u8h4XoT

The former world champion is still looking for more from his car.

“Just looking at the deltas there, I was losing something like 0.6secs to George on the straights, which is something we need to look into,” Hamilton said yesterday, before explaining his conundrum for qualifying, suggesting he may go out after Leclerc.

“The tow is everything here so [I’m] likely to be looking for the tow.”

Because Antonelli exceeded the limit of parts used for his engine, he is taking a grid penalty at Monza.

Few would entirely rule out a storming ride for him on Sunday to end up top of the pack, but is is clearly a huge task for him to score points of any kind with that disadvantage.

They are now likely both past their peaks, but Hamilton and Verstappen recalled their battles of 2021 when they clashed in practice earlier.

Verstappen was already hacked off with Hamilton for seemingly obstructing his path earlier in the session, and they almost came together in the dying moments of the session.

Hamilton needed to take the escape road at the first chicane, where the pair made contact in 2021, as Verstappen looked to slip around his occasional rival. The two of them scarcely avoided another contact.

On the radios, Verstappen claimed, “He caused that,” while Hamilton reported to Ferrari that he was, “Blocked by Max.” Perhaps there will be more aggro later.

The full list of times from earlier today.

FP3 CLASSIFICATIONRussell in the box seat heading into qualifying#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/BUrCsv92dT

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of and qualifying for the Monza Grand Prix.

Before the weekend’s racing, George Russell was, at least publicly, less than bullish about his chances in Italy.

He did, though, believe he would deliver a better showing than he had in recent weeks.

“I don’t know if we can say we’re favourites this weekend, but we probably have a greater opportunity than we’ve had in the last two races where it’s been less about the power unit and more about the chassis,” he said.

“It’s so close right now, that last tenth in qualifying can be the difference of a couple of positions, which can change the podium. Right now, I don’t know who is going to be the team to beat.”

Russell was almost a minute off winner Lando Norris of McLaren in Hungary, finishing seventh in his Mercedes. Two weeks ago, in the Netherlands, he took the last spot on the podium, with Norris winning again.

However, in the second practice session on Friday and FP3 today, Russell was quickest. He led his former colleague, Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, who was second fastest.

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen hinted at a rare good weekend as he was third fastest, about a third of a second behind Russell.

Russell, of course, needs a win soon, or he is in danger of seeing the championship run away from him entirely, as Kimi Antonelli already leads him by 59 points in the world title chase.

Perhaps psychologically just as pressing is that erstwhile teammate Hamilton is tied with Russell on 183 points, in third because he has one victory compared to Russell’s two. Slipping down the rankings could knock his confidence.

Russell has not secured pole for the last four races, so a strong showing in qualifying might be the boost he needs ahead of Sunday’s race, while Norris is looking for a pole position hat-trick.

#1467. Crisis-hit FIFA chief Gianni Infantino 'requested VIP treatment for his daughters and their dogs at Miami airport'

By DANIEL MATTHEWS, US SENIOR SPORTS WRITER

Published: 09:47 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 17:30 EDT, 5 November 2026

FIFA president Gianni Infantino is facing more uncomfortable questions after it emerged that his office asked for 'VIP treatment' for his daughters and their pet dogs on a trip from Miami to Qatar.

Infantino's future has been under the microscope after a scandal-laden few months, with honorary Japanese FA president Kohzo Tashima announcing on Thursday that he will stand against Infantino in next year's presidential election.

On Thursday, The Times revealed that back in May, Infantino's presidential office wrote to Miami airport officials asking for someone to 'assist' three of his daughters - and their pets - through security for a personal trip to Qatar.

Miami airport's VIP protocol reportedly allows diplomats and other special guests to be escorted through security checkpoints up to the door of the plane. Officers can also request early boarding.

These privileges are not automatically laid on for loved ones traveling separately, with protocol stating that 'courtesies... will not be extended' to family members of VIPs 'when the families are traveling on their own.'

But according to documents reviewed by the Daily Mail, members of Infantino's family enjoyed the airport's services dozens of times while traveling without the FIFA president between 2024 and 2026.

Gianni Infantino's office reportedly requested 'VIP treatment' for his daughters and their dogs

The FIFA president's future has been under the microscope after a scandal-laden few months

In a statement to The Times, Miami airport insisted these requests are dealt with 'on a case-by-case basis.' The Daily Mail has contacted FIFA for comment but a spokesperson told The Times: 'Port courtesy requests were made to Miami international airport (MIA), on the advice of a former adviser to the Fifa president.

'Port courtesies are provided at no charge to the president of Fifa given his position as the head of an association or NGO. Mr Infantino’s family members are also entitled to request these services under MIA’s own Courtesies of Port Handbook and these are also provided free of any charge, on a case-by-case basis, at the discretion of MIA.'

Infantino's position is already under threat heading into FIFA's presidential election next March, when he is hoping to be elected to a fourth term. Back in December, Infantino awarded Trump the inaugural FIFA Peace Prize – to widespread ridicule.

During the World Cup, the Balogun affair saw Infantino accused of favoritism and caving to the White House, while the FIFA president and Trump were mocked for handing over the trophy to Spain together.

Before long, Infantino faced a mutiny over his secret plans – later scrapped – to sell a stake in the World Cup to private equity investors including Joshua Kushner, the brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

Then earlier this week, FIFA strongly denied allegations that Infantino influenced Trump administration officials to fast-track a work permit for his undocumented Nicaraguan housekeeper after she lost her legal status, according to bombshell documents.

The global soccer chief is alleged to have turned to politically-connected contacts to secure a new work permit for Yajarlin del Socorro Fernandez after the White House revoked her legal permission to work in the United States, according to documents reviewed by the Daily Mail.

#1466. Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD1,2,3. Understanding how disruptions to these functionally diverse genes lead to the core features of ASD remains a major challenge4. Moreover, ASD is three- to four-fold more common in male than in female individuals5, and female autistic people tend to carry more autosomal risk alleles for ASD compared with their male counterparts6,7; however, the biological basis of this ‘female protective effect’ (FPE) has remained unknown8,9. Here we show that individual perturbations of 18 ASD genes in human neural progenitor cells converge on shared effects on gene expression, including widespread downregulation of other ASD genes. De novo reconstruction of a gene regulatory network enabled identification of central transcriptional regulators that drive this transcriptomic convergence, including prominent ASD gene CHD8 and candidates including REST. Furthermore, X-linked transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and the inactive X chromosomes in female individuals10, emerged as a key activator of many ASD genes: we propose that the higher ZFX expression level observed in the female brain can buffer damaging mutations in diverse ASD genes, contributing to the female protective effect. Together, these results show how key gene regulatory networks can become broadly and similarly dysregulated upon disruption of individual ASD genes and provide molecular insight into the female protective effect in ASD.

Large-scale genetic studies have implicated hundreds of genes in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), with many identified through rare mutations that result in loss of function of one allele1,2,3. This suggests that gene dosage plays an important part in ASD11 and makes it critical to determine how appropriate expression levels of ASD genes are maintained. Characterization of gene regulatory networks (GRNs) could provide important insights into mechanisms mediating the proper transcriptional dosage of these ASD genes. In addition, ASD is significantly male-biased in prevalence, and although some ASD genes have been identified on the X chromosome12, X-linked mutations alone cannot fully explain this sex bias8,13. Moreover, it has been consistently demonstrated that female individuals require greater autosomal genetic risk to manifest ASD compared with male individuals6,7, but the genetic mechanisms of this female protective effect (FPE) are unknown8,9.

Here we use GRN reconstruction to identify key drivers of expression of ASD genes, including CHD8 and REST. These analyses also identify female-biased transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and inactive X chromosome in female individuals10, as a key regulator of ASD genes, suggesting a direct transcriptional mechanism that could contribute to the FPE. This study provides a crucial framework for determining how variants in diverse genes can cause convergent molecular effects that ultimately result in ASD.

Functional interrogation of ASD genes revealed strongly overlapping effects on downstream targets in human neural progenitor cells (NPCs). Knockdown (KD) studies were performed for 20 ASD genes, including 18 genes from the Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative (SFARI) gene database14 and two long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) previously implicated in ASD (NR2F1-AS1 (ref. 15) and SOX2-OT16). RNA-degrading CRISPR enzyme CasRx17 and an array of three guide RNAs (gRNAs) per target (Supplementary Table 1) were used to induce individual KD of each target gene relative to non-targeting controls (NTCs) in NPC cultures from a control human male (XY) induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell line (Fig. 1a,b and Extended Data Fig. 1). RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis after 24 h of KD demonstrated that nearly all perturbations led to substantial numbers of significantly differentially expressed genes (DEGs; adjusted P (Padj) < 0.05), with a median of 920 DEGs per perturbation (25th percentile: 644, 75th percentile: 1,485) (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 2). To ensure sufficient statistical power for downstream analyses of these DEGs, we focused on the 18 perturbations (18 of 20, 90%) that resulted in more than 20 DEGs, excluding the ARHGAP5 and ARID2 KD samples from further analysis. The remaining perturbations each led to a minimum of 287 DEGs, which enabled robust characterization of these samples.

a, Experimental design schematic showing CasRx-based KD in NPCs. b, Immunocytochemistry of iPS cell-derived human NPC cultures, representative of three independent analyses with similar results. c, Bar plot depicting enrichment of SFARI genes or intellectual-disability-only genes among the DEGs for each KD condition, excluding the targeted gene itself. Bars indicate the OR from a one-sided Fisher’s exact test; error bars indicate the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval on the OR. P values were adjusted using Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing. d, Circos plot depicting transcriptomic convergence of HC-SFARI DEGs shared between different KD conditions (Extended Data Fig. 3a). e, Heatmap showing the relative expression of HC-SFARI genes that were DEGs in at least ten KD conditions (recurrent dysregulation) (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). Statistically significant DEGs were identified using DESeq2 (Wald test) with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing and are indicated by an asterisk. Top ASD risk genes from ref. 1 are shown in bold. f, Relative CytoTrack dye intensity (−log2) over time. Transcriptome-wide analyses showed that ASD gene KDs caused remarkably widespread disruption of other ASD genes. Most sets of DEGs exhibited significant enrichment for known ASD genes in the SFARI Gene database (15 of 18, 83.3%) (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 3). By contrast, there was no significant enrichment for genes implicated in intellectual disability but not ASD (intellectual-disability-only genes) (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 3) (Methods), despite their comparable expression in NPCs (intellectual-disability-only genes: 1,062 of 1,242, 85.5% expressed; SFARI genes: 797 of 1230, 64.8% expressed). This suggests that perturbation of ASD genes particularly affects other ASD genes, as opposed to neurodevelopmental genes more broadly.

We observed a striking pattern of transcriptomic convergence across perturbations, which we defined as statistically significant overlap of the same DEGs (Extended Data Fig. 3). This was particularly evident for high-confidence SFARI (HC-SFARI) genes, the SFARI genes in the highest evidentiary tier for association with ASD (Fig. 1d). Moreover, HC-SFARI genes tended to shift in a concordant direction as a result of different perturbations even when they were not significant DEGs within a particular KD sample (Extended Data Fig. 3c). Such genes included prominent ASD risk gene CHD8 (ref. 18), which was significantly downregulated by most (11 of 18, 61.1%) of the KDs. Notably, 27 HC-SFARI genes were DEGs in at least 10 of the KDs (27 of 183, 14.8%, P = 4.1 × 10−9), and all were consistently downregulated (Fig. 1e), indicating convergent dysregulation of many of the strongest risk genes for ASD.

High levels of CasRx have been reported to cause non-specific RNA degradation of a magnitude that is correlated with the expression level of the KD target, whereas use of lower CasRx levels avoids this problem19. In our NPC transcriptomic studies, CasRx was expressed from only a single safe-harbour locus (AAVS1), which limited its expression. We also performed several further experiments to confirm that non-specific RNA degradation did not affect our results. First, we found no relationship between expression levels of KD targets and numbers of resulting DEGs when considering either the whole transcriptome (P = 0.990, R2 = 8 × 10−6, linear regression) or SFARI genes specifically (P = 0.784, R2 = 0.0043, linear regression) (Extended Data Fig. 4a). We next generated NPCs expressing fluorophores mKO2, mScarlet and iRFP670 and targeted each individually with CasRx (Supplementary Table 4); flow cytometry showed no collateral effects on the fluorescence intensity of non-targeted fluorophores (Extended Data Fig. 4b and Supplementary Table 5). Finally, we confirmed strong transcriptomic convergence on shared downregulated DEGs by performing further KD studies of a subset of our target genes using short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) in NPCs (Extended Data Figs. 4c,d and 5 and Supplementary Table 6). Re-analysis of data from a study that used Cas9 to knock out ASD genes in iPS cells and iPS cell-derived excitatory neurons (ExNs)20 similarly demonstrated strong transcriptomic convergence on shared downregulated DEGs both within each cell type and between cell types (Extended Data Fig. 5 and Supplementary Table 6). Recent studies published since our work was submitted have also noted convergence across diverse ASD models21,22. Together, these data confirm that disruption of ASD genes results in transcriptomic convergence across various cell types and experimental contexts.

The marked transcriptomic convergence we observed in our KD studies suggested that candidate ASD risk genes could be nominated by the following features: (1) consistent downregulation following ASD gene KDs; and (2) dosage sensitivity, as indicated by high genic constraint scores (Supplementary Table 7 and Methods). This approach yielded 397 genes (Supplementary Table 8), including 113 SFARI genes (odds ratio (OR) = 5.87, Padj = 1.85 × 10−39) and 49 HC-SFARI genes (OR = 11.17, Padj = 1.11 × 10−29), demonstrating that these criteria effectively prioritize known ASD genes. Notably, this set of genes showed no enrichment for intellectual-disability-only genes (OR = 1.01, Padj = 0.509). All of the remaining 284 non-SFARI genes exhibited significant co-expression with SFARI genes (all Padj < 0.05), which has previously been shown to help prioritize novel ASD risk genes4, further supporting their relevance to ASD. Moreover, at least 40 of these genes showed some association with ASD in at least 1 major sequencing study (Supplementary Table 9). For example, mutations in AKT3, although classically associated with brain overgrowth disorders such as megalencephaly, have recently been associated with ASD; other genes including KIF11, KIF2A and SOS1 have also been associated with ASD in multiple studies (see references in Supplementary Table 9). Therefore, the remaining genes merit consideration as candidate ASD risk genes.

Many ASD gene perturbations also caused similar phenotypic effects in NPCs. Proliferation analysis using heritable dye (CytoTrack) showed that 9 of 18 (50%) of the KDs led to a statistically significant decrease in proliferation (Fig. 1f, Extended Data Fig. 6a, Supplementary Table 10 and Supplementary Fig. 1), including several genes that have been implicated in microcephaly (SETD1B23, SETD2 (ref. 24), SETD5 (ref. 25), KMT2E26 and WAC27). By contrast, only 1 of 18 (5.6%) of the KDs led to a significant increase in NPC proliferation rate. This suggests that reduced NPC proliferation is a common phenotype that results from disruption of several different ASD genes, consistent with previous findings28. Deciphering the specific relationships between these molecular phenotypes and abnormal head size in ASD is complex, as reports implicate increased rates of both microcephaly and macrocephaly across individuals with autism29,30. Indeed, two KD targets that we found to decrease proliferation in NPCs, SETD2 (ref. 24) and KMT2E26, have been reported to be associated with either microcephaly or macrocephaly depending on the specific variants studied in these genes. Thus, although disruption of NPC proliferation is a convergent phenotype observed across many of our perturbations, how this relates to downstream changes in head size remains to be determined.

Inducible KD in cerebral organoids also revealed shared neurodevelopmental phenotypes. For these organoid studies, we created the FLEx-based inducible CRISPR knockdown (FLICK) construct. FLICK enables control over the timing of KD through doxycycline-inducible genetic recombination that results in constitutive expression of CasRx and an EGFP reporter (Fig. 2a), providing robust KD (Extended Data Fig. 7a). The FLICK constructs also contain identifying sequences that can be captured during single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) and used to determine the KD target in a given cell; this enables analysis of mosaic cerebral organoids.

Avg., average; Dox., doxycycline; ExN-Early, early ExN; ExN-Imm, immature ExN; ExN-Mat; mature ExN; IPC, intermediate progenitor cell; IPC-Div, dividing IPC; IN, inhibitory neuron; RG, radial glia; RG-Div, dividing RG.

For long-term studies, we targeted ASD genes whose KDs were not found to impair NPC proliferation in our CytoTrack experiments (Supplementary Table 10). FLICK constructs targeting these genes or expressing NTC gRNAs were each separately transposed into iPS cells. We then used fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) to isolate cells that had integrated the FLICK constructs on the basis of their expression of fluorescent reporter TagBFP. Following FACS, we pooled an equal number of FLICK+ iPS cells for each KD target and for the NTCs, and cultured this mixed iPS cell population for 4 days to allow the cells to recover before generating mosaic organoids (day 0). Recombination of the FLICK construct, which leads to constitutive expression of CasRx and an EGFP reporter, was induced in a subset of the cells (approximately 10%) by treatment with doxycycline from days 14–15, when the organoids predominantly consisted of PAX6+ NPCs (Extended Data Fig. 7b). These organoids were subsequently grown until either 1 or 2 months of development (Fig. 2b) and analysed by scRNA-seq; this analysis identified all expected cell types (Fig. 2c,d and Extended Data Fig. 7c,d) including radial glia, intermediate progenitor cells, inhibitory neurons and ExNs. Further scRNA-seq analysis confirmed that the FLICK construct could produce efficient KD (Extended Data Fig. 7e).

Long-term organoid KDs revealed shared phenotypes across several perturbations. Several KDs, particularly those targeting BAZ2B, CLASP1 and EHMT1, were depleted from the organoids compared with NTCs (Fig. 2e), even though these KDs did not impair proliferation in NPC cultures (Extended Data Fig. 6a and Supplementary Table 10). This discrepancy between our NPC cultures and organoids suggests that long-term organoids, which support progenitor proliferation as well as differentiation, can be used to identify neurodevelopmental phenotypes that are not apparent in short-term NPC cultures. Notably, microcephaly has been associated with pathogenic variants in these genes31,32,33, consistent with the organoid phenotypes. Furthermore, these KDs also altered cell type proportions in organoids, producing relatively greater numbers of ExNs and fewer radial glia (Padj = 0.021 for BAZ2B, 0.018 for CLASP1 and 0.012 for EHMT1; ordinary one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test) (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 7f). Together, these results indicate that disruption of these genes may result in increased ExN differentiation at the expense of self-renewal of radial glial progenitors. Most of the other KDs also resulted in a trend towards an increased proportion of ExNs by the 2-month time point, suggesting that this is a convergent neurodevelopmental phenotype, in line with previous observations34,35.

Depletion of ASD genes also resulted in prominent transcriptomic convergence in cerebral organoids (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 7g). Radial glia with different KDs exhibited highly overlapping DEGs, further supporting our findings from NPC cultures. Indeed, the DEGs identified in organoid radial glial progenitors strongly overlapped with the DEGs identified from KD of the same target in NPC cultures (Extended Data Fig. 7h), suggesting that these effects on gene expression are not specific to a particular experimental context. Transcriptomic convergence was also observed in other cell types, including intermediate progenitor cells and ExNs (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 7g), demonstrating that the convergence of ASD genes on shared downstream effects is not unique to neural progenitors. This was consistent with findings of studies that identified shared ASD DEGs in postmortem brain tissue from individuals with distinct causes of ASD36,37,38, as well as with widespread observations of convergent ExN phenotypes such as disordered synaptic structure or activity upon disruption of distinct ASD genes20, suggesting that convergence does not reflect merely a shared alteration of cell type or fate of progenitor cells. Furthermore, we found that detection of overlapping DEGs using scRNA-seq was heavily dependent on the number of cells sequenced for each perturbation, as demonstrated by downsampling analysis (Fig. 3b). This sample-size dependence may partially explain the lack of robust transcriptomic convergence observed at the individual gene level in some previous studies with smaller sample sizes34,39. Our use of an isogenic background is also likely to have contributed to our detection of transcriptomic convergence, as different genetic backgrounds have been found to significantly affect neurodevelopmental phenotypes resulting from the disruption of ASD genes in organoids34. Finally, although some convergently disrupted genes were cell-type specific, many genes were consistently disrupted across several cell types, including SFARI DEGs (Fig. 3c). This suggests that although cell-type-specific features affect the transcriptomic consequences of ASD gene perturbations, certain effects could be broadly shared by diverse cell types.

a, Heatmap of cross-enrichment of DEGs for radial glia and ExNs showing convergence in long-term organoids. b, Pie charts denoting proportions of pairwise sets of DEGs that showed significant cross-enrichment (transcriptomic convergence). Downsampling of the number of cells per condition to the number indicated above each pie chart decreased the transcriptomic convergence observed. c, Network visualization of SFARI DEGs in long-term organoids shared among different KDs conditions and cell types. The thickness of edges represents the number of shared DEGs. Nodes were plotted on the basis of clustering with the Fruchterman–Reingold algorithm (igraph). Nodes that are closer together had more shared DEGs on average. d, Proportions of cells with each KD target from scRNA-seq of mosaic organoids with acute KD. e, UMAP showing clustering of cells from acute KD mosaic organoids from scRNA-seq. f, Heatmap of cross-enrichment between different KD samples showing transcriptomic convergence in acute KD organoids.

Acute disruption of ASD genes in 2-month organoids revealed even greater convergence on shared DEGs. A further set of mosaic FLICK organoids was grown for 2 months before induction of KD with doxycycline treatment from days 61–62; this was followed by scRNA-seq 2 days later, to determine the acute effects of disruption of these genes in organoids that had developed normally. This approach resulted in similar numbers of cells per KD (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 7i), enabling deeper analysis of the KDs that had been depleted from the organoids with long-term KD (Fig. 2e). As expected, these organoids contained a mixture of cell types (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 7j), with ExNs by far the most abundant cell type at this developmental time point (Extended Data Fig. 7k). Many KDs resulted in ExN DEGs that were enriched for the DEGs identified from NPC cultures (Extended Data Fig. 7l), again suggesting shared changes in gene expression across cell types upon KD of ASD genes. Furthermore, acute KD of the target genes that had been depleted from organoids over the course of long-term KD (Fig. 2e) allowed us to obtain much greater cell numbers for these perturbations, which showed that these KDs also resulted in strong transcriptomic convergence (Fig. 3f).

Transcriptional regulators that could mediate transcriptomic convergence in ASD were identified through MAGIC analysis (Methods), which uses chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP–seq) data from ENCODE to identify transcription factors and cofactors whose binding targets are enriched within a gene set of interest. This identified transcriptional regulators whose target genes were recurrently differentially expressed across many of the ASD gene KDs in NPCs (Extended Data Fig. 8a and Supplementary Table 11), including HC-SFARI genes such as CHD2 and SIN3A. Of the recurrent MAGIC regulators not previously implicated in ASD, several were both highly constrained (Supplementary Table 7) and co-expressed with known ASD genes (Extended Data Fig. 8a), features that have been demonstrated to be predictive of novel ASD risk genes4.

MAGIC analysis also identified consistent drivers of convergence in organoids (Extended Data Fig. 8a and Supplementary Table 11). Of the top recurrent transcriptional regulators identified in NPCs, half (13 of 26, 50%) were also identified in organoid radial glial progenitors (Extended Data Fig. 8b). MAGIC also identified recurrent ExN regulators shared across developmental stages and across long-term versus acute KD timescales, including many SFARI genes. Nine of these genes were also identified as top transcriptional regulators in neural progenitors, indicating that they may be key drivers of convergence in various cellular contexts.

Of particular interest, the RE1 silencing transcription factor (REST) was significant according to MAGIC analysis in 17 of 18 (94.4%) NPC perturbations (Extended Data Fig. 8a) and consistently emerged as a top MAGIC regulator across all tested conditions (Extended Data Fig. 8b). Although direct mutations in REST have not previously been associated with ASD, REST has critical neurodevelopmental roles and functions as a master negative regulator of neurogenesis40,41. Dysregulation of REST has also been reported following disruption of ASD genes including CHD8 (ref. 42) and Rett syndrome gene MECP2 (refs. 43,44). Re-analysis of human and mouse REST ChIP–seq binding sites (Methods) identified strong enrichment of SFARI genes (Padj = 3.6 × 10−67 and 7.7 × 10−50, respectively), including HC-SFARI genes (Padj = 2.2 × 10−13 and 3.7 × 10−8, respectively), among REST targets (Extended Data Fig. 8c), supporting a key role for REST in regulation of ASD-relevant gene expression.

De novo GRN reconstruction from our NPC RNA-seq data using ARACNe enabled association of further transcription factors and chromatin modifiers (together referred to as ‘regulators’) with their downstream targets (regulons) (Methods). We validated this approach by separately constructing ‘held-out’ GRNs that excluded data from samples in which the KD target itself was a potential regulator, thereby preventing circularity in regulon inference. Regulons predicted from these held-out GRNs strongly overlapped with the DEGs observed following KD of the corresponding target genes in NPCs (Padj < 3.98 × 10−116 for each, combined P = 4.08 × 10−937) (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 9a). Thus, ARACNe effectively captures bona fide regulatory relationships.

Statistically significant DEGs were identified using DESeq2 (Wald test) with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing. Statistically significant enrichment of second-degree (2°) regulon genes among the downregulated DEGs is indicated by the Padj value (one-sided Fisher’s exact tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing). b, Depiction of a subset of the NPC GRN constructed using ARACNe. All regulators are shown along with first-degree (1°) target genes that are SFARI genes. c, Gene set enrichment analysis (weighted Kolmogorov–Smirnov running-sum statistic, permutation test, with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing) demonstrating enrichment of genes with high PageRank scores within the gene sets shown. d, Bar graph depicting mean normalized (norm.) degree, a measure of interconnectedness, across regulators from different gene sets. e, Depiction of modules of top regulators identified through iterative walktrap clustering. The full NPC GRN revealed a high degree of interconnection between ASD genes and their upstream regulators (Fig. 4b). Indeed, ASD genes were strongly enriched among central genes of the NPC GRN (Padj = 9.81 × 10−6 for SFARI genes, 1.99 × 10−4 for HC-SFARI genes, centrality assessed using the PageRank algorithm, Methods) (Fig. 4c). By contrast, intellectual-disability-only genes did not exhibit enrichment among the central genes of the GRN (Padj = 0.19), consistent with the lack of enrichment that we observed among the DEGs resulting from ASD gene KDs (Fig. 1c). In addition, central GRN genes were enriched for pathways associated with the G2M checkpoint (Padj = 6.0 × 10−4) and mitotic spindle (Padj = 3.6 × 10−5), consistent with the NPC proliferation phenotypes we observed (Fig. 1f and Supplementary Table 10).

We next identified GRN regulators that acted as key drivers of ASD-associated transcriptomic convergence. This analysis revealed 70 top drivers of convergence whose activity was consistently altered by ASD gene KD (Methods) and whose targets were both enriched for SFARI genes and central to the GRN (Supplementary Table 12). Nearly half of these top drivers of convergence were SFARI genes (31 of 70, OR = 6.35, Padj = 3.9 × 10−11), and nearly one-third were HC-SFARI genes (22 of 70, OR = 10.61, Padj = 6.7 × 10−12). By contrast, only 7 of these top drivers of convergence were intellectual-disability-only genes (7 of 70, OR = 2.06, Padj = 0.078). Moreover, the top drivers of convergence were consistently downregulated across nearly all ASD gene KDs (Extended Data Fig. 9b). They were also highly interconnected in the GRN (P < 1 × 10−6) (Fig. 4d), as well as in the STRING database of protein–protein interactions (P = 2.0 × 10−9) (Methods). Taken together, these findings suggest that these genes both act as central regulators of many ASD genes and cross-regulate each other, driving transcriptomic convergence in ASD.

Iterative walktrap clustering identified 4 gene modules among the 70 top drivers of convergence (Fig. 4e), one of which (the blue module) was especially strongly interconnected. This module exhibited very high cross-interaction through STRING analysis (P < 1 × 10−16) and included REST (Extended Data Fig. 8) and several notable ASD genes including CHD8, one of the strongest known risk genes for ASD18. Notably, the inferred CHD8 regulon from the GRN was strongly enriched (first-degree regulon Padj = 4.6 × 10−7; second-degree regulon Padj = 3.9 × 10−20) for direct CHD8 target genes previously identified through ChIP–seq from NPCs45 (Fig. 4f), further supporting the validity of ARACNe-predicted regulatory relationships. Moreover, consistent with previous reports45,46, CHD8 ChIP–seq targets were also highly enriched for NPC-expressed SFARI genes (Padj = 2.6 × 10−8) and HC-SFARI genes (Padj = 8.5 × 10−8). The CHD8-containing module also included three transcriptional regulators (SETD2, SETD5 and KMT2E) that we had directly perturbed, and DEGs from these KDs exhibited significant enrichment for CHD8 ChIP–seq targets (Padj = 1.2 × 10−5, 7.8 × 10−8 and 2.6 × 10−4, respectively) (Fig. 4f), further demonstrating convergent regulation of shared targets by critical ASD genes. This analysis highlights CHD8, a high-confidence ASD risk gene, as a key driver of transcriptomic convergence in ASD.

Previous studies have found that genes downregulated in ASD tend to be more highly expressed in the neurotypical female versus male brain47,48, raising the possibility that this baseline female-biased expression may contribute to the FPE8,47,48. We identified 82 genes that were consistently downregulated by ASD gene KD and exhibited female-biased expression in the brain (Methods); 28 of these were highly constrained (Extended Data Fig. 10a), including 12 highly constrained SFARI genes (OR = 2.79, P = 8.65 × 10−3) (Fig. 5a). Re-analysis of single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq) data (Methods) from the frontal cortex of neurotypical male controls and autistic male participants—including individuals with 15q duplication syndrome and genetically idiopathic ASD—revealed that many of these highly constrained genes were significantly downregulated in ExNs from autistic male individuals, further supporting their relevance to ASD (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Fig. 10a).
