Bars indicate the OR from a one-sided Fisher’s exact test; error bars indicate the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval on the OR. P values were adjusted using Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing. e, Schematic depicting a model of the contribution of ZFX to the FPE in ASD. expr., expression.

ZFX is of particular interest because it is expressed from both the active and inactive X chromosome in female individuals10, making it one of the most highly and consistently female-biased genes across diverse tissues49, including the developing cerebral cortex (Extended Data Fig. 10b,c). Moreover, a recent report has implicated pathogenic ZFX variants in ASD50, and other coding variants in the ZFX gene have been identified in ASD probands3,51,52. ZFX encodes a potent transcriptional activator of genome-wide targets53, and we identified many regulatory relationships between ZFX and ASD-relevant gene sets in our GRN (Fig. 5b), including the top drivers of transcriptomic convergence in ASD that we had previously identified (OR = 9.8, Padj = 2.2 × 10−6). We also found that ZFX was a downstream target of many of these top drivers, with several reciprocal regulatory relationships (Fig. 5c). The strong enrichment of ZFX targets for ASD-relevant genes was further confirmed by re-analysis of ZFX ChIP–seq data (Fig. 5d). As ZFX is recurrently downregulated upon disruption of ASD genes, its female-biased expression, in combination with its role as a regulator of ASD-relevant genes, could result in cascading and broad sex-differential impacts on ASD gene expression, potentially contributing to the FPE in ASD (Fig. 5e).

Here we have shown widespread transcriptomic convergence following depletion of ASD genes and identified key chromatin modifiers and transcription factors, including CHD8 and REST, as critical drivers of this convergence. These drivers were highly interconnected with each other, often through mutual regulatory relationships; these findings demonstrate how disruption of a single regulator can lead to changes that propagate throughout a GRN. We also identified the transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and inactive X chromosome in female individuals, as a key transcriptional regulator of ASD genes; the female-biased expression of ZFX could thus buffer the effects of ASD gene disruptions in female individuals, contributing to the FPE in ASD. Taken together, these findings provide a model for how diverse genes can converge on core transcriptomic changes and generate shared ASD phenotypes, as well as how sex-differential activity of these genes can lead to male-biased risk for ASD.

Our detection of widespread transcriptomic convergence probably benefited from several experimental design choices that were intended to minimize variability. For instance, to avoid confounding effects of different genomic backgrounds, we perturbed the ASD genes in an isogenic background. In addition, we performed these perturbations by introducing KD constructs in a polyclonal manner instead of creating different cell lines for each ASD target gene, as the process of clonal selection can introduce line-to-line variability54. For our cerebral organoid studies, we created the FLICK KD construct so that we could generate mosaic organoids containing all KD conditions as well as the NTCs, minimizing any effects from organoid-to-organoid variability. By reducing variability across our experimental designs, we probably enhanced our sensitivity to detect convergence.

We also optimized our RNA-seq approaches for the different experimental contexts. Initially, we used highly homogeneous NPC cultures, enabling us to perform bulk RNA-seq on this single cell type. This allowed deep transcriptomic profiling, avoiding the problems of ‘dropout’ that affect scRNA-seq55. However, for samples that contained a heterogeneous mix of different cell types, such as cerebral organoids, bulk RNA-seq results could reflect differences in relative cell type abundance as well as changes in gene expression. Thus, we used scRNA-seq to analyse our organoids and sought to compensate for the decreased sensitivity of this approach by sequencing a large number of cells for each KD condition. As our downsampling analysis demonstrated (Fig. 3b), these large cell numbers were critical for detection of transcriptomic convergence through scRNA-seq. Furthermore, for our NPC experiments, we performed RNA-seq 24 h after introducing the KD constructs. We selected this short timeframe to focus our analysis on the initial effects of each KD, rather than long-term consequences that could be more strongly influenced by compensatory responses and stochastic effects. This short timeframe may have been particularly well suited for detection of transcriptomic convergence, which would have further benefited our GRN reconstruction.

Building an understanding of the complex relationships in GRNs is critical for identification of key ‘rate-limiting’ genes that affect the GRN as a whole and lead to particular biological outcomes. Previous studies of Hirschsprung disease have identified an analogous GRN centred on rate-limiting gene RET, which can be affected by direct mutations in RET itself or disruptions to upstream regulators of RET56. Here we similarly identified critical genes, including CHD8 and REST, the effects of which can propagate throughout the GRN and drive transcriptomic convergence in ASD. Our findings are consistent with those of previous studies identifying CHD8 as an important regulator of ASD gene expression45,46,57. Moreover, haploinsufficiency of CHD8 has been found to result in dysregulation of REST in the mouse brain42, consistent with the highly interconnected relationships we found in our GRN. In addition, disruption of Rett syndrome gene MECP2 affects REST43,44, and REST is dysregulated in ASD brain tissue relative to neurotypical controls42, further supporting its relevance to ASD. Given that REST is a master negative regulator of neuronal genes40,41 and that CHD8 affects proliferation and neurogenesis58, it is plausible that the convergent dysregulation of CHD8/REST targets could directly underlie the altered proliferation we found in NPCs (Fig. 1f), as well as the increased relative abundance of ExNs that we observed following some of the ASD gene KDs in organoids (Fig. 2f). Several previous studies have also identified imbalances in neural proliferation versus differentiation following ASD-relevant perturbations28,58,59; thus, future work is needed to further characterize the molecular mechanisms linking our observed convergent changes in gene expression to these shared neurodevelopmental phenotypes.

Our results also provide insight into the male bias of ASD. Downregulation of ZFX by KD of many different ASD genes in NPCs and lower ZFX levels in ExNs from individuals with ASD (Fig. 5a) suggest that decreased ZFX expression may be a recurrent transcriptional feature of ASD. The higher baseline level of ZFX in the female brain due to its expression from both X chromosomes could thus buffer against this ASD-associated downregulation. Consistent with this, a recent study of sex-biased gene expression across cell types in the cortex found that promoters of autosomal genes exhibiting female-biased expression were enriched for ZFX transcription factor motifs, whereas promoters of male-biased genes were not60. Male individuals have a Y-linked homologue of ZFX called ZFY; however, this encodes a weaker transcriptional activator than ZFX53, and the GRN regulon of ZFY showed no enrichment for SFARI genes (OR = 1.1, Padj = 0.36), suggesting divergent roles with respect to ASD. Further functional characterization of ZFX and other genes expressed from the inactive X chromosome may provide critical insights into how female-biased expression affects ASD risk13. Moreover, it will be valuable to directly compare the transcriptional effects of ASD gene perturbations between male cell lines, as used in this study, and female cell lines. Indeed, our use of a male rather than female founder cell line may have contributed to the striking changes in gene expression we observed, as female cells may be able to better tolerate the same ASD gene KDs owing to higher baseline expression of ZFX and/or other factors that contribute to the FPE.

As many genes that have been implicated in ASD show rare heterozygous loss-of-function mutations1, we prioritized ASD genes with a high probability of loss-of-function intolerance in our study. We also focused on genes that exhibited a ‘head-to-head’ configuration with an adjacent lncRNA; several lncRNAs in such a configuration have been found to fine-tune the expression of their neighbours61, meaning that this configuration could be used to putatively identify particularly dosage-sensitive genes. We further included two lncRNAs that had been implicated in ASD through heterozygous loss-of-function mutations15,16. Our Cas13-based KDs on average produced a 48.2% decrease in expression of the target genes (Supplementary Table 2); thus, this experimental approach seems to be suitable for study of how heterozygous loss of function of haploinsufficient genes can contribute to ASD.

Although our perturbations were focused on genes associated with ASD through rare single-gene mutations, it is likely that other classes of ASD-associated variants disrupt the same convergent network. Supporting this, studies of postmortem brain tissue have demonstrated that idiopathic ASD cases share core transcriptomic changes38 and have overlapping DNA methylation signatures62 with cases of ASD caused by rare mutations of large effect size, such as chromosome 15q11–13 duplication. Moreover, reports suggest that common alleles of smaller effect size that have been implicated in ASD can also drive changes that converge with those caused by rare ASD variants63. This raises the possibility that distinct causes of ASD, including rare single-gene mutations, large copy number variants and common genetic variation, could result in similar phenotypes by converging on disruption of shared ASD-relevant GRNs. Further characterization of these GRNs has broad potential to clarify our understanding of the genetic architecture of ASD across a wide variety of genetic variant classes and to identify potential therapeutic targets that could benefit individuals with diverse causes of ASD. More broadly, although this work was focused on ASD, the approaches used here are widely applicable to different cell types and conditions. Thus, this study provides a framework for identification of critical transcriptional regulators across diverse contexts, from development through disease.

CasRx17, specifically NLS-RfxCas13d-NLS (Addgene, 109049), was used in combination with target-specific gRNAs for KD of targeted transcripts. A deep-learning-based tool66 was used to design gRNA spacer sequences targeting the genes of interest. These spacer sequences were filtered to exclude homopolymers (more than four As, more than three Cs, Gs or Ts). Spacer sequences with potential off-target interactions were identified using BLAST67 and excluded. For each target gene, three separate spacer sequences were selected and combined into a tandem pre-gRNA array, with each spacer sequence preceded by the CasRx direct repeat (DR36) sequence66: CAAGTAAACCCCTACCAACTGGTCGGGGTTTGAAAC. Tandem pre-gRNA arrays were processed by CasRx into individual gRNAs for KD17. See Supplementary Table 1 for full sequences.

To create constructs for the initial NPC KD experiments, we used the lentiviral pSicoR plasmid68 (Addgene, 11579) as the backbone. The mouse U6 promoter was replaced with the human U6 promoter, which was used to drive expression of the CasRx gRNA arrays. These constructs were used in combination with a CasRx knock-in cell line (described below).

To obtain enough NPCs for CasRx KD validation by auto-western blot (described below), an all-in-one construct was created that contained CasRx and EGFP expressed from the CAG promoter element and gRNA arrays expressed from the human U6 promoter. The backbone also contained inverted terminal repeats, which allowed the construct to be integrated into the genome by piggyBac transposase69. These constructs were based on the LiOn design70 (Addgene, 154019), such that expression of CasRx and EGFP was dependent on recombination of the construct by piggyBac transposase, preventing expression from the episomal plasmid. This all-in-one construct was also used for the fluorophore KD assays and NPC proliferation assays. For expression of fluorophores in NPCs, iOn-based constructs were created with mKO2, mScarlet or iRFP670 driven by the CAG promoter element.

For shRNA-based KD, shRNAs were designed using the Horizon siDesign Center tool (https://horizondiscovery.com/en/ordering-and-calculation-tools/sidesign-center). Predicted shRNAs starting with G were selected, and those with potential off-target interactions were identified using BLAST67 and excluded. The selected shRNAs (Supplementary Table 13) were cloned into the pSicoR plasmid68 (Addgene, 11579).

For organoid experiments, we created the FLICK construct by engineering several features into a backbone incorporating the FLEx design71. In particular, we included a modified Cre recombinase that included an intron, which prevented recombination of the plasmid during cloning72. We also included CasRx17 as well as all necessary components of the Tet-On 3G system73 to enable doxycycline-inducible recombination. Furthermore, we included identifying barcode sequences a short distance upstream of the polyA sites for the fluorescent reporters, which enabled us to determine which KD construct was incorporated in each cell through scRNA-seq. Finally, we incorporated inverted terminal repeats, allowing the construct to be integrated into the genome by piggyBac transposase69. The sequences of all constructs were verified by whole-plasmid sequencing (Plasmidsaurus).

All human cell culture work was performed under protocols approved by Boston Children’s Hospital IRB (S07-02-0087). The control male human iPS cell line 280 was previously generated and fully characterized74. Human iPS cells and iPS cell-derived NPCs were grown on tissue culture plates precoated with Matrigel (Corning, 354277) or Geltrex (Thermo Fisher, A1413302). The cells were passaged as needed using Accutase (Millipore Sigma, SCR005) or ReleSR (STEMCELL Technologies, 100-0483). Human iPS cells were cultured in mTeSR Plus medium (STEMCELL Technologies, 100-0276). Human NPCs75 were generated from iPS cells using a STEMdiff SMADi Neural Induction Kit (STEMCELL Technologies, 08582) by following the monolayer culture protocol for at least 3 weeks. NPCs were continuously grown in neural induction medium plus SMADi and were not switched to neural progenitor medium. The medium was supplemented with 10 μM Y-27632 (STEMCELL Technologies, 72304) for approximately 1 day following passaging of iPS cells or NPCs.

Cerebral organoids were generated from 280-iPS cells using a STEMdiff Cerebral Organoid Kit (STEMCELL Technologies, 08570), following some recommendations from Giandomenico et al.76 with further modifications. In particular, the organoids were embedded in Matrigel (Corning, 354277) at day 7 and grown in expansion medium until day 14, at which point they were removed from Matrigel and switched to maturation medium on an orbital shaker. Full details are available at protocols.io (https://doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.x54v95p5ql3e/v1).

None of the cell lines was authenticated. All cell lines routinely tested negative for mycoplasma contamination.

CasRx17 was knocked into the AAVS1 safe-harbour locus of 280-iPS cells using targeting constructs that have been previously described73. Individual iPS cell colonies were picked and expanded. Southern blot analysis was performed by Celplor to confirm correct targeting of the AAVS1 locus. Karyotype analysis was performed using KaryoStat (Thermo Fisher); this revealed a 2.4-Mb gain on chromosome 1, described in microarray nomenclature as arr[GRCh37] 1q32.1(204108163_206539638)x3. This region did not contain any of the target genes.

Lentiviruses were generated using standard protocols that have previously been described77. Lentiviruses were applied at a multiplicity of infection of 4.0, as this value yields more than 98% transduced cells. RNA was extracted 24 h later.

Bulk RNA was extracted using a Direct-zol RNA Microprep Kit (Zymo Research, R2062), and 3′ RNA-seq libraries were prepared following a modified version of the TagSeq protocol78, incorporating recommendations and pooling strategies from the CheapSeq protocol79. Briefly, 200 ng of total RNA from each sample was combined with an indexed oligo(dT) primer and buffer (NEB, M0466L) as described for CheapSeq. RNA was fragmented in a preheated thermocycler at 94 °C for 2.5 min without the lid, after which the samples were moved immediately to ice. Each sample was then mixed with a template-switching oligo that contained an index and a unique molecular identifier (UMI), as well as other reagents required for reverse transcription, as described for CheapSeq. The reverse transcription reaction was performed at 42 °C for 90 min, without heat inactivation. Remaining single-stranded RNA and oligos were then digested by addition of 0.5 μl of buffer EB (Qiagen, 19086), 0.5 μl of thermolabile ExoI (NEB, M0568S) and 0.25 μl of RNase A (Thermo Fisher, EN0531) and incubation of the samples at 37 °C for 30 min, followed by heat inactivation at 85 °C for 5 min and a hold step at 4 °C.

Up to 8 samples with different index sequences were then pooled, and cDNA was purified by performing a 1.4× left-sided solid-phase reversible immobilization (SPRI) selection (Beckman Coulter, B23317). Q5 UltraII Mastermix (NEB, M0544L) was then used, with partial read 1 and partial read 2 primers, to amplify the cDNA for 7 cycles on a C1000 Touch Thermal Cycler (Bio-Rad, 1851197), following the CheapSeq PCR parameters. Amplified cDNA was purified through a 0.7× left-sided SPRI selection (Beckman Coulter, B23317). Final library construction was performed using Q5 UltraII Mastermix (NEB, M0544L) with standard TruSeq indexing primers (NEB, E6440S), with amplification for eight cycles following the CheapSeq PCR parameters. Libraries were purified by 0.4× to 0.65× double-sided SPRI selection (Beckman Coulter, B23317). Purified libraries were assessed using a TapeStation HSD1000 (Agilent, 5067-5584 and 5067-5585). For oligo sequences, see Supplementary Table 14.

The CheapSeq PCR parameters were as follows: 98 °C for 30 s; X cycles (see above) of 98 °C for 10 s, 65 °C for 75 s; 65 °C for 5 min; and 4 °C hold.

Three distinct NPC samples were analysed per condition. Individual KD conditions were compared with three NTC conditions, which were considered together as a set of nine control samples. Gene expression was quantified using alevin-fry with UMI deduplication (salmon-v1.9). A salmon index and transcript-to-gene map were built using GENCODE v.45. Counts from distinct transcripts that mapped to the same gene were summed. Only genes with a baseMean expression greater than 10 in NTC samples were considered for further analyses. Differential expression analysis was performed using DESeq2 (v.1.42.0), with the model ~Batch + sgRNA.

For KD confirmation, P values were adjusted using Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing for the set of 20 directly targeted genes. The raw P value for SRCAP was derived from droplet digital PCR (ddPCR), as SRCAP was filtered from the RNA-seq analysis owing to low expression. See Supplementary Table 2 for details. For transcriptome-wide analyses, P values were adjusted using Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing for the set of 11,168 analysed genes (baseMean > 10 in NTCs).

To confirm KD of SRCAP, the RNA samples that had been used for RNA-seq (above) were assessed by ddPCR. RNA was first converted to cDNA using SuperScript IV VILO Master Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 11756050). Next, we performed ddPCR by combining cDNA at an RNA-equivalent concentration of 0.25 ng μl−1 (5 ng per 20-μl reaction), primers at a final concentration of 0.1 μM and QX200 ddPCR EvaGreen Supermix (Bio-Rad, 1864033). The ddPCR reactions were performed using a QX200 AutoDG Droplet Digital PCR System (Bio-Rad). Expression levels were normalized using the expression of housekeeping gene HPRT1. The results were analysed using the model Expr ~ Batch + type, where type was either NTC or the targeted gene (SRCAP). The resulting raw P value was adjusted with those for the other KD targets (from RNA-seq) using Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing for the set of 20 directly targeted genes. See Supplementary Table 2 for details.

Primers (Supplementary Table 15) were designed with Primer-BLAST80, which assesses potential off-target interactions using BLAST67. Oligos were ordered through Azenta or IDT. Primer specificity was confirmed by Sanger sequencing of PCR products (Azenta).

For analysis of protein expression levels following CasRx KD, LiOn-based KD constructs (‘Molecular cloning’) were nucleofected into 280-NPCs with a piggyBac-transposase-expressing plasmid (see ‘Nucleofection’ for details). Four days later, EGFP+ cells expressing the KD constructs were collected by FACS (BD FACSymphony S6). The cells were pelleted and flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen. Protein extraction and auto-western blot were performed by RayBiotech using antibodies against vinculin (R&D systems, MAB6896, clone 728526; diluted 1:25) and WAC (Abcam, AB109486; diluted 1:50).

SFARI genes: all genes included in the SFARI gene database14 (3 April 2025 release).

HC-SFARI genes: SFARI genes with a score of 1.

Intellectual disability genes: genes from the SysNDD database81 (accessed 23 August 2025) that were: (i) associated with an intellectual disability term (HP:0001249, HP:0001256, HP:0002342, HP:0010864, HP:0002187); (ii) in the ‘definitive’ category; (iii) not SFARI genes.

Enrichment analyses were performed using one-sided Fisher’s exact tests (fisher.test, base R v.4.3.1), and P values were adjusted using Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing (p.adjust, method = “BH”, base R v.4.3.1). In bar plots, main bars indicate the OR from a one-sided Fisher’s exact test; error bars indicate the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval on the OR (no upper bound is defined for a one-sided test).

Fluorophore-expressing constructs (‘Molecular cloning’) were nucleofected into 280-iPS cells with a piggyBac-transposase-expressing plasmid (see ‘Nucleofection’ for details). iPS cells were expanded, and cells expressing all three fluorophores were isolated by FACS using a Cytek Aurora CS spectral cell sorter. The sorted iPS cells were further expanded and induced into NPCs (‘Cell culture’). LiOn-based CasRx KD constructs were then nucleofected into these NPCs with a piggyBac-transposase-expressing plasmid. Four days later, cells expressing all four fluorophores (with EGFP indicating expression of the KD constructs) were analysed for fluorescence intensity of the reporters using a Cytek Aurora CS spectral cell sorter. Ordinary two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni’s multiple comparisons test was used to test for significant differences in the geometric mean fluorescence intensity (log2) across samples and reporters.

For each target, pSicoR-based constructs with three different shRNAs were pooled and then nucleofected into 280-NPCs (see ‘Nucleofection’ for details, with modifications as described here). As these constructs are not transposable, the plasmid expressing piggyBac transposase69 was omitted, and the amount of pSicoR-based plasmid was increased to a total of 15 μg. The day after nucleofection, EGFP+ cells expressing the constructs were isolated by FACS (BD FACSymphony S6) and replated to allow recovery overnight. The following day, RNA was collected using Zymo DNA/RNA Shield. Finally, 3′ RNA-seq was performed by Plasmidsaurus (DGE RNA-Seq service).

We performed differential expression analysis using the same analytical pipeline as for our CasRx KD experiments: DESeq2 (v.1.42.0) was used with the model ~targetGene to calculate differential expression relative to NTC shRNAs (designed to target non-expressed transcripts luciferase and lacZ). For transcriptome-wide analyses, P values were adjusted using Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing for the set of 14,601 genes with baseMean > 10 in NTC cells. DEGs were defined as genes that were differentially expressed with adjusted P < 0.05.

Gene expression counts from ref. 20 were downloaded from GEO (GSE107878), and differential expression analysis was performed with the same analytical pipeline as for our CasRx KD experiments: DESeq2 (v.1.42.0) was used with the model expression ~ targeted gene. DEGs were identified relative to control cells for both neurons and iPS cells. Only genes with mean expression greater than 10 in control samples were considered to be potential DEGs, and P values were adjusted accordingly using Benjamini–Hochberg correction. DEGs were defined as genes that were differentially expressed with adjusted P < 0.05.

We quantified the overlap between DEGs identified from: (1) our CasRx KD experiments in NPCs, (2) our shRNA KD experiments in NPCs, (3) knockout iPS cells from ref. 20 and (4) knockout ExNs from ref. 20. For each pairwise comparison of DEGs, enrichment analyses were performed using one-sided Fisher’s exact tests with a universe of genes that were expressed by both sample types. P values were adjusted using Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing.

To determine whether a gene of interest was significantly co-expressed with SFARI genes in our NPC RNA-seq data, we calculated the median Pearson correlation between the expression of the gene of interest and that of each SFARI gene. To assess whether the degree of correlation was significant, we created an empirical null distribution by calculating the median correlation between the gene of interest and 1,000 randomly selected gene sets of the same size as the SFARI gene set, using the universe of NPC-expressed genes (baseMean > 10 in NTCs). A one-sided empirical P value was then calculated as the proportion of null values greater than or equal to the observed median correlation. Regulators with P < 0.05 were considered to be significantly correlated with SFARI genes.

Consistently downregulated DEGs were defined as genes that exhibited: (1) statistically significant downregulation by at least three of the KDs, and (2) at least 80% concordance in the direction of significant differential expression across all KDs.

LOEUF scores (oe_lof_upper) were obtained from gnomad v.2 (ref. 82) for evaluation of genic constraint. For each gene, we calculated a per-gene LOEUF score by calculating the median of the LOEUF values of each gene’s associated transcripts. Although LOEUF is a continuous metric, we used LOEUF < 0.35 as recommended to identify highly constrained genes.

Candidate ASD risk genes (Supplementary Table 8) that were identified in any of the following major sequencing studies are included in Supplementary Table 9: refs. 2,52,83,84,85,86.

Further references provide additional support for some of these candidate ASD risk genes: refs. 87,88,89,90.

Nucleofections were performed using a Neon Transfection System (Thermo Fisher Scientific). For NPCs, 2 million cells were nucleofected with 10 μg of transposable plasmid and 2 μg of a plasmid expressing piggyBac transposase69 using 100-μl tips. For iPS cells, 1 million cells were nucleofected with 5 μg of transposable plasmid and 1 μg of a plasmid expressing piggyBac transposase69 using 100-μl tips. For small-scale nucleofections, 10-μl tips were used, and cell numbers and plasmid amounts were reduced proportionally. Nucleofection of NPCs was performed using the following settings: voltage = 1,600 V, width = 10, pulses = 3. Nucleofection of iPS cells was performed with voltage = 950 V, width = 30, pulses = 2.

LiOn-based KD constructs (‘Molecular cloning’) were nucleofected into 280-NPCs with a piggyBac-transposase-expressing plasmid (see ‘Nucleofection’ for details). Four days later, the cells were treated for 20 min with dye from a CYTOTRACK Red 628/643 Cell Proliferation Assay Kit (Bio-Rad, 1351205) diluted 1:500 in medium. The cells were then rinsed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS; Thermo Fisher Scientific, 10010031) and passaged, with one-fifth of each sample plated into a well of each of four separate plates to be used for the subsequent four time points. The remaining cells were analysed by flow cytometry (BD FACSDiva software v.8.0.3) for assessment of the initial CytoTrack intensity on day 0. For the next 4 days, one well of each sample was dissociated each day and analysed by flow cytometry. The CytoTrack intensity values (negative log2) from the EGFP+ cells expressing the KD construct were normalized to those of the EGFP− cells from the same well to control for well-to-well variability in proliferation rates. They were further normalized to their initial CytoTrack intensity from day 0 to control for variability in dye incorporation. The results for each KD are displayed relative to the mean value from the NTC samples, plotted as the mean ± s.e.m. Statistical analysis was performed using ordinary two-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test (GraphPad Prism). Full details of sample numbers and statistical results are available in Supplementary Table 10.

To induce expression of Cre and initiate recombination of the FLICK construct, cells or organoids were treated with 2 μg ml−1 doxycycline (Sigma, D9891-1G) for 24 h.

To determine KD efficiency using FLICK constructs, we analysed three distinct samples per condition. Control 280-iPS cells were nucleofected with constructs encoding the NTC1 control gRNA array or a gRNA array targeting the gene ENSG00000261840, with a plasmid expressing piggyBac transposase69 to genomically integrate the FLICK constructs. For induction of KD, the cells were treated with 2 μg ml−1 doxycycline (Sigma, D9891-1G) for 24 h. Cells that had recombined the FLICK construct were then isolated through FACS (BD FACSymphony S6) for EGFP+ cells, which were replated in triplicate and grown for a further 2 days. RNA was then isolated using a Direct-zol RNA Microprep Kit (Zymo Research, R2062). To generate cDNA, we reverse transcribed 500 ng of RNA using SuperScript IV VILO Master Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 11756050). We then performed quantitative PCR (qPCR) by combining cDNA at an RNA-equivalent concentration of 1 ng μl−1 (10 ng per 10-μl reaction), primers at a final concentration of 0.5 μM and PowerUp SYBR Green Master Mix for qPCR (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A25742). The qPCR reactions were run in technical triplicate for each sample on a CFX384 Touch Real-Time PCR Detection System (Bio-Rad, 1855484) using the ‘fast cycling mode’ conditions described in the Master Mix protocol. Expression of the KD target gene (ENSG00000261840) was assessed using the ΔΔCt method, with expression first normalized to that of housekeeping gene HPRT1 for each sample and then displayed relative to the average of the NTC control samples, plotted as mean ± s.e.m. Statistical significance was assessed using a two-tailed t-test (GraphPad Prism).

Cerebral organoids were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, diluted in PBS from 16% paraformaldehyde (Electron Microscopy Sciences, 15710), at 4 °C overnight. Following fixation, cerebral organoids were rinsed with PBS and then equilibrated in 30% sucrose (w/v in PBS) at least overnight at 4 °C. For large organoids, the 30% sucrose solution was replaced at least once following overnight incubation to ensure complete cryoprotection. For cryosectioning, cerebral organoids were frozen in Tissue-Tek O.C.T. Compound (Sakura, 4583) on dry ice. A Leica CM3050 S cryostat was used to obtain 30-μm sections, which were collected on Fisherbrand Superfrost Plus Microscope Slides (Fisher Scientific, 12-550-15) and stored at −80 °C.

For immunohistochemical analysis, we prepared a blocking buffer by combining 0.3 M glycine (Sigma, G7403-1KG), 1% bovine serum albumin (Sigma, A4503-50G), 0.3% Triton X-100 (Sigma, T8787-50ML), 10% normal goat serum (Fisher Scientific, NC9660079) and PBS. Slides were rinsed in PBS to remove O.C.T. and then incubated in blocking buffer for 1 h at room temperature. Blocking buffer was removed and replaced with fresh blocking buffer containing the primary antibodies of interest, and the slides were incubated in a slide moisture chamber (Avantor, 76278-848) at 4 °C overnight. Slides were then rinsed with PBS three times for 5 mins each time. Secondary antibodies and nuclear stain DAPI (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 62248) were diluted in blocking buffer (1:500 and 1:1,000, respectively) and added to the slides for 30 min at room temperature; the slides were protected from light from this point forward. The slides were then rinsed in PBS three times for 5 min each time. Cover slips (Epredia, 152455) were mounted using Fluoromount-G (Fisher Scientific, OB100-01), which was allowed to dry at least overnight at room temperature. After drying, slides were stored at 4 °C.

The following antibodies were used: PAX6 (BD Pharmingen, 561462, clone O18-1330), diluted 1:300; Nestin (Millipore Sigma, HPA026111-25UL), diluted 1:500; TBR2 (Millipore Sigma, HPA028896-100UL), diluted 1:300; CTIP2 (Abcam, ab18465, clone 25B6), diluted 1:300; EGFP (Aves, GFP-1010), diluted 1:1,000; Goat anti-chicken IgY, Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermo Fisher, A-11039), diluted 1:500; Goat anti-rabbit IgG, Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermo Fisher, A-11008), diluted 1:500; Goat anti-rat IgG, Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermo Fisher, A-11006), diluted 1:500; Goat anti-mouse IgG, Alexa Fluor 555 (Thermo Fisher, A-21424), diluted 1:500; Goat anti-rat IgG, Alexa Fluor 647 (Thermo Fisher, A-21247), diluted 1:500; Goat anti-rabbit IgG, Alexa Fluor 647 (Thermo Fisher, A-21245), diluted 1:500; Goat anti-rabbit IgG, Alexa Fluor 750 (Thermo Fisher, A-21039), diluted 1:500.

Cerebral organoid sections were imaged using a Zeiss LSM 980 confocal microscope. Standard image processing was performed using Adobe Photoshop.

For scRNA-seq, cells were collected from:

1 month: 10 organoids, pooled together and collected as a single batch;

2 months: 14 organoids collected in 2 batches, with 7 organoids collected together on day 60 and a further 7 organoids collected together on day 61;

acute KD: 8 organoids, pooled together and collected as a single batch.

For collection of cells, mosaic cerebral organoids were cut into pieces using spring scissors, rinsed twice with PBS to remove debris, and then dissociated using a Neural Tissue Dissociation Kit – Postnatal Neurons (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-094-802) with the enzyme mixes described for brain tissue. Gentle dissociation was performed by trituration with pipette tips of decreasing diameter, starting with wide-orifice tips (Rainin, 30389218) and progressing to standard tips. Cells with recombined FLICK constructs were isolated through FACS (BD FACSymphony S6) for EGFP+ cells. Transcriptome-wide scRNA-seq libraries were prepared using Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3′ Reagent Kits v.3.1 (Dual Index) from 10x Genomics, following user guide CG000316 Rev. A.

Full details of protocols are available from protocols.io (https://doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.5qpvoj5pzg4o/v1). Briefly, for quantification of FLICK constructs from the initial pool of iPS cells used to generate mosaic organoids (day 0), RNA was extracted from triplicate samples of 42,000 cells using a Direct-zol RNA Microprep Kit (Zymo Research, R2062). For generation of cDNA, 50–250 ng of RNA was reverse transcribed using a SuperScript IV First-Strand Synthesis System (Invitrogen, 18091050) with an oligo(dT)VN primer containing UMIs. Sequencing libraries were then generated using Q5 Hot Start High-Fidelity 2X Master Mix (NEB, M0494L) and custom primers.

To generate FLICK barcode libraries from scRNA-seq libraries, we used 5 μl of amplified and cleaned cDNA (produced by following the 10x User Guide CG000316 Rev. A to the end of step 2). Barcode-containing cDNA was amplified for sequencing using Q5 Hot Start High-Fidelity 2X Master Mix (NEB, M0494L) and custom primers. Libraries were cleaned using SPRIselect DNA Size Selection Reagent (Beckman Coulter, B23317) and assessed using TapeStation High Sensitivity D1000 reagents (Agilent, 5067-5603 and 5067-5584).

We aligned the scRNA-seq data to the prebuilt Cell Ranger (v.9.0.0) hg38 reference using cellranger-count in feature-barcode mode to perform simultaneous gene expression and guide abundance quantification. Introns were not included in gene expression quantification (--include-introns=false) to avoid quantification of partially degraded transcripts that had been targeted by CRISPR–CasRx. CRISPR guide sequencing library FASTQs for 2-month samples were downsampled to 1.25% of reads using seqtk (v.1.4) to match CRISPR library sequencing depth for 1-month samples and to minimize background for guide assignment using the cellranger-CRISPR guide quantification pipeline. All other parameters were set to default values. Cell Ranger guide assignments were used to filter to only cells with exactly one assigned guide.

Long-term and acute KD samples were processed separately but equivalently. CellBender (v.0.3.2) was used for detection and filtering of ambient RNA contamination, whereas scrublet (v.0.2.3) was used for automatic doublet detection and filtering. All other downstream analysis was performed with Seurat (v.5.0.0). High-quality cells were retained according to the following quality control metrics: (1) percent mitochondrial (percent.mt) gene expression < 20% and (2) 500 < number of expressed genes (nFeature_RNA) < 6,000.

Cell type annotation was first performed on only NTC cells. NTC cells were extracted to create a control-only Seurat object. This object subsequently underwent normalization (NormalizeData), variable feature identification (FindVariableFeatures), scaling (ScaleData; regressed covariates of percent.mt, percent_ribo, nCount_RNA and nFeature_RNA) and dimensionality reduction (RunPCA and RunUMAP). Integration was performed using harmony (v.1.2.0) across organoid batches, and the integrated object was used for unsupervised clustering (FindNeighbors and FindClusters, resolution values of 0.6 and 1.2). A small number of unsupervised clusters (fewer than 1,000 cells) were filtered owing to low cluster-wide quality control metrics (exceptionally high or low nCount_RNA, high percent.mt). All subsequent two-dimensional visualization of this control-only Seurat object was performed using a UMAP representation of the integrated data. Cell type annotation was performed using canonical brain marker genes. A Seurat object was next constructed for all cells, following the processing pipeline (for instance, normalization, scaling, dimensionality reduction and integration) described above. For cell type annotation, label transfer was performed from the control-only Seurat object (TransferData) to the full Seurat object. Expression patterns of canonical brain marker genes were then used to refine and finalize these cell type annotations.

The relative abundance of cells for each KD target was determined for each time point (day 0, day 30, day 60 and day 61). For day 0, relative abundance was determined from bulk RNA-seq libraries (‘Construction of FLICK barcode sequencing libraries’) using a custom pipeline (‘Code availability’). For days 30, 60 and 61, relative abundance was determined from scRNA-seq data using the CRISPR guide assignments generated by Cell Ranger (‘Alignment and quantification of organoid scRNA-seq data’). For each sample, results were normalized to the starting proportion at day 0 and displayed relative to NTCs from the same time point. Results were plotted as the mean ± s.e.m. Statistical analysis was performed using repeated measures one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test (GraphPad Prism), considering all long-term samples (days 30, 60 and 61).

The relative ExN/RG proportion was determined for each KD target at day 30, day 60 and day 61. Results were normalized to the NTC sample from the same time point. Statistical analysis was performed using ordinary one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test (GraphPad Prism), considering all long-term samples (days 30, 60 and 61).

Differential expression analysis was performed between perturbed cells per guide and cells that received NTCs, stratified by main cell types (radial glia, intermediate progenitor cells, ExNs and inhibitory neurons). Seurat FindMarkers was used to perform differential expression with logfc.threshold = 0, min.pct = 0.10, min.cells.group = 3 and all other parameters set to default values. Enrichment analyses of DEGs were performed using one-sided Fisher’s exact tests, and P values were adjusted using Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing. The universe was defined as all genes expressed in both comparisons of interest.

We visualized shared DEGs between organoid cell types (Fig. 3c) using R package igraph (v.2.1.4). The Fruchterman–Reingold layout algorithm (layout_with_fr) was used to determine final node placement.

MAGIC91 (v.1.1) was used to identify transcription factors and cofactors whose targets were enriched in the DEGs from individual perturbations. The strategy of ‘gene body (promoter to the end of the last exon) plus 1Kb flanking sequence either side of the gene body’ was used. For NPC analyses, the universe was set as all genes with baseMean > 10 in NTC samples. For organoid analyses, the universe was set as all genes expressed in at least 10% of cells of that cell type (Seurat min.pct = 0.10; no log2 fold-change cutoff), as these were the genes assessed for differential expression.

Data was extracted from Table S2 from ref. 92. Mouse genes were mapped to human genes using Orthology.eg.db (v.3.20.0), org.Mm.eg.db (v.3.20.0) and org.Hs.eg.db (v.3.20.0). Enrichment analysis was performed using a one-sided Fisher’s exact test with all BrainSpan genes with normalized expression ≥ 1 as the universe (version ‘RNA-Seq Gencode v10 summarized to genes’; https://brainspan.org; accessed 6 January 2024). P values were adjusted using Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing. Results are displayed as bar plots, with main bars indicating the OR from a one-sided Fisher’s exact test and error bars indicating the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval on the OR.

A GRN was constructed using bioinformatic tool ARACNe-AP93. The input comprised the RNA-seq data from our 3 NTCs and the successful KD samples with at least 50 DEGs. We used curated lists of transcription factors94 and epigenetic regulators95 and selected genes expressed in NPCs (baseMean > 10 in NTC samples) as the candidate genetic regulators. To create the GRN, we used default parameters and 100 bootstraps that were then aggregated to form the final network. We then used VIPER96 (v.1.36.0) to identify differentially active regulons following standard operating procedures. In brief, we identified regulons with significant differential expression between NTCs and KDs using a t-test, with a null distribution defined by sample permutations.

To benchmark the predictive power of the ARACNe-derived GRNs, we generated further ARACNe networks after individually holding out perturbation samples for 5 target genes that were identified as regulators of at least 250 genes (range: 478–1,219 genes) in their second-degree regulons (that is, their direct targets, which constituted their first-degree regulon, as well as the direct targets of those genes). For each held-out regulator, we assessed the overlap between the predicted positively regulated genes within its second-degree regulon and the set of downregulated DEGs resulting from perturbation of the same regulator, using a one-sided Fisher’s exact test. P values were adjusted using Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing. P values across the five held-out perturbations were combined using Fisher’s method.

To identify central regulators in our GRN, we converted the GRN to a graph using R package igraph (v.2.1.4) and ran the PageRank algorithm97 using igraph method page_rank. We then ordered genes by their PageRank score and ran gene set enrichment analysis98 using R package fgsea (v.1.32.4), testing the following ontologies: SFARI genes, HC-SFARI genes, intellectual disability genes (exclusive of SFARI genes) and the 50 Molecular Signature Database Hallmark Pathways99 (obtained from https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/msigdb).

VIPER96 (v.1.36.0) was used to identify GRN regulators whose regulons were significantly differentially active across the KDs compared with NTC controls. From these, we prioritized 70 regulators whose regulons were significantly enriched for both SFARI genes (one-sided Fisher’s exact test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing) and high PageRank scores (gene set enrichment analysis with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing).

We calculated the mean normalized degree for the indicated set of regulators and their first-degree regulons (Fig. 4d) using R package igraph (v.2.1.4) by running the function mean(degree(graph, normalized = TRUE)). We then created an empirical null distribution of mean normalized degrees for each indicated set of regulators by creating 1 million subnetworks of the same set size of randomly selected GRN regulators. The relative mean normalized degree was calculated as the observed mean normalized degree for a given set of regulators divided by the mean of the values for the corresponding empirical null distribution. A one-sided empirical P value was then calculated as the proportion of null values greater than or equal to the observed mean normalized degree, with a detection limit of P = 1 × 10−6.

To evaluate known or predicted protein–protein interactions between the top 70 regulators, we used the STRING database GUI100. For the universe, we used the full set of genes that were considered as candidate genetic regulators in the GRN: transcription factors94 and epigenetic regulators95 that were expressed in NPCs (baseMean > 10 in NTC samples). All other parameters were set to default values. For clustering of our 70 regulators into modules, we performed iterative walktrap clustering using R package igraph (v.2.1.4) by running the function cluster_walktrap with default parameters.

For enrichment analysis of CHD8 targets, we used Supplementary Data 1 from ref. 45. Enrichment of the indicated gene sets was tested using one-sided Fisher’s exact tests, with the universe set to NPC-expressed genes (baseMean > 10 in NTCs). P values were adjusted using Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing. Results were displayed using bar plots, with main bars indicating the OR from a one-sided Fisher’s exact test and error bars indicating the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval on the OR.

To identify genes that exhibited female-biased expression in the neurotypical brain, we combined DEG call sets from the following work: Table S4 from ref. 101 (identified as significantly female-biased in either the UCLA cohort, BrainVar cohort or through meta-analysis); ref. 102 (https://storage.cloud.google.com/adult-gtex/bulk-qtl/v8/sb-eqtl/GTEx_Analysis_v8_sbgenes.tar.gz, identified as significantly female-biased in either BRNCTXA or BRNCTXB); Table S4 from ref. 103 (identified as significantly female-biased in the brains of all assessed species (human, mice, rats, dogs, and macaques)); and Table S13 from ref. 60 (identified as ubiquitously female-biased).

Processed snRNA-seq data from the human frontal cortex was obtained from ref. 64. The sex of individual samples was verified on the basis of expression of XIST and Y-linked genes. Only a small number of female samples (one female control sample, one sample from a female participant with idiopathic autism and one sample from a female participant with 15q-duplication-associated autism) were included in this cohort owing to the known male bias of autism. Thus, all downstream analyses focused on the 17 male samples included in this cohort. Differential expression analysis was performed using Seurat function FindMarkers on a cell-type-specific basis between (1) male controls and samples only from male individuals with idiopathic autism; (2) male controls and samples only from male individuals with 15q-duplication-associated autism; and (3) male controls and all samples from male individuals with autism, either idiopathic or 15q-duplication-associated. To control for donor effects, we ran FindMarkers using MAST104. Significant genes were defined as those with absolute log2[fold change] > 0.1 and transcriptome-wide Padj < 0.05.

Data were used from refs. 60,101,105,106.

ZFX ChIP–seq targets were obtained from Table S3E of ref. 65. ZFX targets were also obtained from Table S10 of ref. 53, by San Roman et al., who previously performed integrative analysis of ZFX ChIP–seq data (ENCODE), and ZFX KD RNA-seq data from ref. 65. Enrichment was analysed using one-sided Fisher’s exact tests, and P values were adjusted using Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing. For analysis of common ZFX targets from ref. 65, the universe was defined as genes expressed in both of the cell lines used for ChIP–seq for which RNA-seq data were also available (C4-2B and MCF-7). For analysis of ZFX targets from ref. 53, the universe was defined as genes expressed in the corresponding cell type from ref. 65. Results are displayed using bar plots, with main bars indicating the OR from a one-sided Fisher’s exact test and error bars indicating the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval on the OR.

Software used in this work included R (v.4.3.1) and R packages DESeq2 (v.1.42.0), Seurat (v.5.0.0), igraph (v.2.1.4), scrublet (v.0.2.3), harmony (v.1.2.0), Orthology.eg.db (v.3.20.0), org.Mm.eg.db (v.3.20.0), org.Hs.eg.db (v.3.20.0), VIPER (v.1.36.0) and fgsea (v.1.32.4), as well as Cell Ranger (v.9.0.0), CellBender (v.0.3.2), MAGIC (v.1.1), salmon (v.1.9), seqtk (v.1.4) and BD FACSDiva v.8.0.3.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

All raw data and processed count matrices are available at GEO under accession GSE332574. Differential gene expression results can also be found in Supplementary Tables 16–65. This study also used the following publicly available datasets and websites (copies of these datasets are also available at GitHub (https://github.com/MayaTalukdar/convergence_in_autism_ms)): GENCODE v.45 (reference transcriptome annotation; https://www.gencodegenes.org); SFARI Gene database (3 April 2025 release; https://gene.sfari.org); SysNDD database (accessed 23 August 2025; https://sysndd.dbmr.unibe.ch); RNA-seq expression data from CRISPR-edited iPS cell-derived neurons and iPS cells (ref. 20; GEO accession GSE107878); gnomAD v.2 (LOEUF/oe_lof_upper constraint scores), Table S11 (ref. 82); ASD sequencing study, Table S5G (ref. 2); ASD sequencing study, Tables S2 and S9 (ref. 52); ASD sequencing study, Table S6 (ref. 83); ASD sequencing study, Table S9 (ref. 84); ASD sequencing study, Table S6 (ref. 85); ASD sequencing study, Table S5 (ref. 86); ENCODE ChIP–seq compendium, accessed through MAGIC (ref. 91); https://www.encodeproject.org); human and mouse REST/NRSF ChIP–seq binding sites, Table S2 (ref. 92); BrainSpan RNA-Seq data, ‘Gencode v10 summarized to genes’ (https://www.brainspan.org; accessed 6 January 2024); MSigDB Hallmark gene set collection (https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/msigdb); STRING protein–protein interaction database: https://string-db.org; CHD8 ChIP–seq target genes, Table S1 (ref. 45); sex-biased expression data, Table S4 (ref. 101); sex-biased expression data (ref. 102; https://storage.cloud.google.com/adult-gtex/bulk-qtl/v8/sb-eqtl/GTEx_Analysis_v8_sbgenes.tar.gz); sex-biased expression data, Table S4 (ref. 103); sex-biased expression data, Table S13 (ref. 60); sex-biased expression data, Table S2 (ref. 105); sex-biased expression data, Tables S1 and S2 (ref. 106); snRNA-seq data from frontal cortex of autistic and control male participants (ref. 64); ZFX ChIP–seq target genes, Table S3E (ref. 65); and integrated ZFX target gene analysis, Table S10 (ref. 53). Source data are provided with this paper.

#1465. Newcastle’s limitations exposed by Bournemouth before hosts fight back for draw

This was the definition of a hard-earned point. Newcastle United came back from two goals down to rescue a point against Bournemouth, but this was not a convincing performance from Matthias Jaissle’s side.

Newcastle were abject for the first half an hour and the visitors could have been out of sight. It was disjointed and lacklustre as Bournemouth dominated before the break and regularly threatened Lukasz Hornicek in goal.

Even during the fightback, Newcastle lacked cohesion and penetration, but forced their way back into it through hard work, spirit and determination. Whether you believe Harvey Barnes’ wonder goal and Jacob Ramsey’s late strike paper over the cracks or reveal a togetherness – a grit and determination that bodes well for the future – depends on the individual.

Ramsey comes off the bench to fire Newcastle level! 🔥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/UBWAfCQyy4

For the second weekend in a row, Newcastle had just two shots on target and scored two goals. At the other end of the pitch, they have allowed their opponents 61 shots in just three games, the highest in the division. That is not going to be sustainable long term. Something Jaissle acknowledged.

“It shows where we have potential,” he said. “There are elements to improve offensively.

“The learning curve is there. There were some elements missing from our performance but there was a strong response. The lads showed big character, big personality and big commitment... It is always better to get a point and see the potential to improve.”

A reality check is not necessarily a bad thing. There has been a lot of hype and excitement on Tyneside and a self-congratulating tone to their own end of summer appraisals.

But this was a reminder of the team’s limitations and the fact that only three of their eight summer signings started the game, with two more coming off the bench, underlined they are a work in progress.

In truth, that is fine. It is the start of September and the Premier League campaign is only three games old. They have a new manager and a new-look team. There has been a significant amount of change in a very short period of time.

It was not the easiest summer, and despite the insistence from senior figures at the club that they had always remained calm and methodical during their summer reset, there was a whiff of crisis only a few weeks ago.

When Eddie Howe quit as manager and Bruno Guimarães, the captain, forced his move to Arsenal at the start of August, Newcastle looked in disarray. So, to have started the season unbeaten from three games against Liverpool, Tottenham Hotspur and Bournemouth is encouraging.

It is also worth highlighting just how good the visitors were. In the first half Bournemouth were superb, rushing Newcastle, forcing mistakes and pouring forward in numbers. In Alex Scott, just as he was in their victory here last season, Bournemouth had the best player on the pitch.

That opens up another conversation. Newcastle played like this a lot at home in Howe’s final season in charge, especially in the second-half of the campaign, but tended to lose not draw the game.

On this occasion, they secured a decent point with a late equaliser thanks to substitute Ramsey, who looked good when he replaced the off-colour Lewis Miley.

Bournemouth will feel they should have held on. They had taken a deserved lead through Marcus Tavernier, who took advantage of a static and ball-watching Amar Dedić to bundle home from close range.

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of this Saturday lunchtime fixture between Newcastle United and Bournemouth at St James’ Park.

The hosts have made a determined start to the 2025-26 season under new head coach Matthias Jaissle. They conceded a last-minute penalty to draw 2-2 with Liverpool on the opening weekend of the Premier League campaign, sealed a hard-fought 3-2 victory over West Bromwich Albion in the Carabao Cup, and then produced an inspired second-half performance to win 2-0 away at Tottenham in their previous top-flight outing.

Despite anxiety in the summer after losing Eddie Howe and multiple key players such as Sandro Tonali, Bruno Guimaraes and Anthony Gordon, the Jaissle era has begun very encouragingly. New signings including Lukas Hornicek, Amar Dedic and Nico Gonzalez have seamlessly slotted into the starting XI, Lewis Hall has been typically brilliant, while Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa look reborn up top after both forwards endured difficult campaigns last season.

Marco Rose’s Bournemouth tenure has started in frustrating circumstances. They had been leading 1-0 against Manchester City in their first top-flight fixture this campaign, but conceded two late goals to dramatically lose 2-1. Bournemouth were also left kicking themselves last weekend against Everton, after a defensive mix-up between Ryan Christie and Marcus Tavernier following a corner delivery gifted James Tarkowski a 91st-minute equaliser, allowing the visitors to salvage a 1-1 draw at the Vitality Stadium.

At opposite ends of the country, over 350 miles separate these two sides. Away days in English football can’t really get any longer. The travelling Bournemouth support will hope their loyalty can be repaid with a first Premier League win of the season under Rose, while Newcastle will aim to continue their unbeaten start and carry on the positive momentum created by Jaissle.

Kick-off is at 12:30, with team news coming shortly.

#1464. VAR a scourge on the Premier League as Forest denied by off-field meddling

Almost £3.5bn was splurged on transfers this summer in a league supposedly described as the best in the world, so why does VAR continue to prove so ineffective and divisive?

Seven years after its introduction, it remains a scourge on the Premier League and here at the City Ground was another exhibit of maddening off-field meddling.

Tottenham Hotspur avoided a third successive defeat after the crucial intervention of VAR prevented Neco Williams from securing Oliver Glasner his first win as Nottingham Forest’s head coach.

The big moment occurred in the 65th minute. Morgan Gibbs-White’s chip over Antonin Kinsky should have been dealt with by Sandro Tonali and Jan Paul van Hecke but both players got themselves in a muddle and Williams bundled the ball in from almost on the goal-line.

Replays appeared to show the ball went in off Williams’ knee and he was protecting his face with his hands to avoid a stray boot. The VAR review ruled that Williams had handled the ball, yet in this billion-pound industry there was not one camera angle which proved entirely conclusive.

On this occasion the VAR official was Peter Bankes, recommending to referee Craig Pawson that the goal be disallowed. Williams said: “It’s a goal. VAR is there when there is a clear and obvious error and for me that is not clear and obvious. I’ve seen the images and the replays and at not one moment did I think I handballed it because I never did. I headed it in between my arms. I’m at a loss at that one, it’s disappointing. If you’re going to pause it, it’s going to look like it hit my arm but it didn’t hit my arm.”

Glasner and the other Forest players were also incensed, and once again supporters are questioning how critical moments in matches are being decided by officials sitting at Stockley Park. “I think the VAR can’t intervene when he is guessing,” said Glasner. “I told the referee after the game that I felt the goal should have stood.

“The VAR should say to stay with the onfield decision because it is about strengthening the referee. If it’s not 100 per cent clear, stick to the onfield decision.  We had a briefing before the season that the threshold for VAR intervention this year should be very high which is why this is wrong.”

While Tottenham were perhaps fortunate to pick up their first point, they are still waiting to score their first Premier League goal of the season. They did not manage a shot on target.

The grand £350m rebuild is proving a slow-burner and it is only Mykhailo Mudryk who will have cause to remember such a dull affair. Signed on loan from Chelsea on deadline day, Mudryk made his first appearance since November 2024 after being suspended by the Football Association following a positive test for performance-enhancing meldonium.

The Ukrainian forward was introduced with 16 minutes left, with his manager Roberto De Zerbi determined to reinvigorate his career.

Tottenham are still waiting for lift-off but De Zerbi remains convinced that his team will eventually click, particularly in attacking areas.

One of their summer arrivals, Omar Marmoush, wasted their best chance in the 16th minute by drilling a shot wide of the post. De Zerbi said: “In the last third we have to improve. We have to maybe keep more calm when we are very close to doing something important.

“If we improve in the last third I think we can score many goals because we have the players with big qualities. We could have scored three or four goals.

Considering we were only all working together on Thursday for the first time, this is the right spirit and the right way to move on.” On Mudryk, De Zerbi said: “He’s working to reach the best physical condition and he needs time.”

After the disallowed Williams goal, Forest were feeling further aggrieved soon after when Rodrigo Bentancur appeared to pull back substitute Igor Jesus in the penalty area. These are two teams clearly in period of transition and patience will be required from both sets of supporters.

The big headline news from Tottenham is that Mykhailo Mudryk is on the bench.

Signed from Chelsea on deadline day on an initial loan, Mudryk was once branded as a future Ballon d’Or winner by Roberto De Zerbi after they worked together at Shakhtar.

Mudryk has not played a competitive match since November 2024 after being suspended by the Football Association following a positive test for performance-enhancing meldonium.

Enzo Fernández’s record deal to Manchester City was facilitated by English-founded agency Unique Sports Management, it can be revealed.

Fernández sealed a £125m move from Chelsea on deadline day, equalling the UK transfer record of Alexander Isak to Liverpool a year ago.

Football Association documents due to be published later in the season will show Unique to have played their part in the biggest transfer of the summer.

Fernández is represented by The Elegant Game, headed by ex-Argentina international Javier Pastore, although he is not registered with the FA for transfers in England.

Unique, which also represented Anthony Gordon for his move to Barcelona, were brought in to close the deal, which was agreed between clubs on deadline day afternoon.

The English-founded agency have Marc Guéhi, who moved to City in January, on their books and their summer deals included Gordon to Barca, Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea and Taylor Harwood-Bellis to Aston Villa. Troy Parrott, who scored the winner for Real Betis against Jose Mourinho’s Real Madrid, is also in the Unique stable.

Will this be third time lucky for Tottenham Hotspur after their £300m+ summer reset?

In typical Tottenham fashion, their start to the Premier League season has not been straightforward with two defeats, five goals conceded and none scored so far.

The popular opinion is that it will eventually click, but Tottenham’s supporters are still scarred by those two successive 17th-placed finishes.

Forest have won their last four games against Spurs, so it will be an early sign of promise if Roberto De Zerbi can secure a positive result here.

Enzo Maresca believes streetwise Enzo Fernández will give Manchester City an extra winning edge – as he told his record £125 million signing to forget about the size of the fee.

City made the Argentina midfielder the joint most expensive purchase in Premier League history with their deadline day swoop from Chelsea.

Maresca has opted against naming Fernández among his captains’ leadership group, which features Ruben Dias, Erling Haaland, Marc Guéhi and Gianluigi Donnarumma.

But the Italian – who knows Fernández well from their time together at Stamford Bridge – is confident his fierce competitive instincts will bring an added dimension to his side.

“I don’t know if it’s streetwise but he knows how to win,” Maresca said, who is in line to hand Fernández his debut against Coventry on Saturday. “When you want to compete or win, it’s much more important to have players that already know how to do that than players who have never done it in the past.

“Enzo is not the only one. This squad has many players who know how to win titles and how to compete and this is what we are looking for.

“I know Enzo quite well and I know what he can bring to the team. He is a winner, [has] a winner’s mentality and knows how to win [after] the World Cup, Club World Cup [success].

“I just said he is a winner and when you belong to the squad and another winning player arrives, they are always happy.

“I can promise you that in the last four or five days, four or five players from the squad were asking if was coming or not because they wanted him to be with us. It’s very important that he is with us.”

Maresca said he planned to use Fernandez predominantly as a No 6 or No 8 depending on the game. “I see Enzo as a six, a little bit more deep, or [an eight] a little higher arriving in the box,” he said.

Good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of the Saturday afternoon 3pm kick-offs of which we are treated to a rare number this week as Sky and TNT Sports decide to inconvenience only 10 sets of matchgoing supporters rather than the usual 12 or 14. The matches start, purely alphabetically, with unbeaten Brentford hosting Sunderland, Leeds United travelling to Brighton and Hove Albion’s Amex Stadium where they have never won and have come away with only three points in their seven visits, the something’s-got-to-give quasi derby between winless Fulham and pointless Palace, leaders Man City hosting Coventry City for the Sky Blue Cup and Tottenham head to Nottingham Forest in pursuit of their first point to spoil the gaiety of a nation.

We have Mike McGrath reporting from the Etihad and John Percy at the City Ground and I will endeavour to keep you up to date with developments at the other three grounds via various methods. Forest vs Spurs seems the most consequential of the fixtures, not because either manager is in any danger but because now the window has closed it should give us a clearer picture of how Roberto De Zerbi plans to marshal his surfeit of wingers into a coherent attack that can break their goalscoring duck and how he proposes to organise a back four that have shipped five goals.

Fulham and Palace have come in for a lot of criticism regarding their recruitment and while I can understand the frustration of the former’s fans for doing so much business with Real Madrid, I think Gonzalo García is a proper player and will shine over the course of the season.

Palace, I think, are paying the price for the January splurge on Brennan Johnson and Jorgen Strand Larsen, not just the inflated fees but the sizeable wages on players who contributed almost nothing. I was at Leeds vs Brentford last week and there was plenty to admire about both sides but fear for Leeds’ so-far commendable resilience at their Amex knacker’s yard and wonder whether Sunderland will be able to live with Brentford’s pace. Manchester City vs Coventry, meanwhile, probably will not give us the Bouaddi-Fernández-Anderson £325m midfield from the start but we might be given a glimpse.

#1463. Virgil van Dijk is spot on: Liverpool's brittle defence leaves them looking like a vulnerable mess - it is unsustainable and MUST be fixed, writes LEWIS STEELE

Published: 12:00 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 17:38 EDT, 5 November 2026

Liverpool's defensive woes are not sustainable, insists skipper Virgil van Dijk who says the team cannot accept losing in the way they did at Fenerbahce.

The Reds lost 3-2 having twice led in Istanbul, with individual errors and lapses in concentration costing them.

Andoni Iraola’s men have now suffered back-to-back defeats after also losing to Arsenal – and they have conceded three goals in each of their last three European games, against LASK, Villarreal and Fenerbahce.

When this statistic was put to Van Dijk, he said: ‘(Our defending) is definitely not sustainable. That’s why it is a very disappointing night, for many reasons but definitely the goals we conceded and the manner we conceded them as well. There is work to do.

‘It is very, very tough. Three set pieces as well. We have been very good at them so far this season but we switched off and were not ready for the first and second balls. Yeah, it is a tough one to take.

‘I mentioned after the last game, we as a group have to go through good moments but also lesser good moments. That will only form a bigger bond, it will be only beneficial.

Liverpool suffered a disappointing 3-2 Champions League loss to Fenerbahce on Wednesday

Captain Virgil van Dijk insisted Liverpool's poor defending is not 'sustainable' after the game

‘No one wants to lose games especially how we did today but it should only help us in the near future. We should not accept losing, especially in the manner we did today.’

Asked if he was angry, the Dutchman said: ‘Yes. But I didn’t show it today because everyone looked disappointed and they have a reason to be, they should be disappointed. We cannot lose in the manner we did today. But we did that and it is down to Fenerbahce as well.’

Van Dijk is right. The defence has been all over the place at times this season – especially in Europe.

Iraola thought he had won the game with a masterstroke triple substitution just after the hour mark when Cody Gakpo assisted Alexander Isak two minutes after the pair joined Florian Wirtz in entering the field.

But in trying to win the game – which is commendable – Iraola left the back door open. It felt ajar all night as Fenerbahce continually had joy down the flanks.

Van Dijk was asked if the deafening atmosphere of the Istanbul crowd played a part and said: ‘It is very difficult for everyone on the pitch because you can’t communicate easily.’

That could be an excuse but these players are world class and cannot put too much blame on the atmosphere.

Jeremy Jacquet has been imperious since joining from Rennes but the Frenchman had his first bad game in a Liverpool shirt, while Van Dijk was not too much better.

Milos Kerkez (above) and Kostas Tsimikas are proving a serious problem at left back

September 9: Liverpool 2-1 Atletico Madrid

Alisson, too, has left questions to be asked over his performances of late. After giving the ball away cheaply for Arsenal’s winner on Sunday, he was at fault for Fenerbahce’s decisive goal by dilly-dallying over whether to come for a cross. He should have gobbled it up.

But the real problem is at full back. Milos Kerkez and Kostas Tsimikas are not good enough – not now, anyway. That should be first on the priority list in future transfer windows.

Ronald Araujo, rested on the night, was missed.

The approach of ‘you can score, we will score more’ has been used – intentionally or not – in most European games this term. When it comes off, as it did in 6-3 and 4-3 wins over LASK and Villarreal respectively, it is exciting.

When it doesn’t, Liverpool just look a vulnerable mess. Work to do for Iraola ahead of a trip to Selhurst Park and Crystal Palace on Sunday, where Pierre Sage is fighting for his life.
