In addition to VEGFR1 and VEGFR2, ECs express VEGFR3. Previous studies have shown that VEGFR3 is strongly expressed by capillary and venous ECs; however, this receptor cannot bind VEGF (VEGFA), only VEGFC and VEGFD, which are key molecules for lymphangiogenesis but less relevant to blood vessel angiogenesis. Vegfr2IECKO-E8.5–P7 ECs showed very strong upregulation of VEGFC (Extended Data Fig. 11a), which could signal to VEGFR3 in the absence of VEGFR2. Loss of VEGFR3 in growing retina ECs has been shown to induce angiogenesis, suggesting that VEGFR3 negatively regulates VEGFR2 signalling32. However, single Vegfr3IECKO-P1–P7 ECs also had decreased ability to migrate and reach the leading edge (Extended Data Fig. 11l–n). Arterial ECs and smooth muscle cells express high levels of VEGFC33,34,35 a ligand that can bind both VEGFR2 and VEGFR3. Compared with Vegfr2IECKO-P1-P7 ECs, Vegfr2/3IECKO-P1-P7 ECs had a very similar zonal distribution in capillaries and veins (Fig. 5b) but a 3.4-fold lower frequency in arteries (Fig. 5c); this suggests an important role for VEGFC to VEGFR3 signalling in arterial mobilization or survival, but only when VEGFR2 signalling is absent. Loss of both VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 did not compromise the proliferation of surviving ECs in any vascular segments (Fig. 5d).

We also observed that Vegfr2KO ECs had decreased VEGFR3 expression only at the angiogenic front, where VEGFA levels are highest. By contrast Vegfr1/2KO ECs showed strong downregulation of VEGFR3 in all vascular segments, except in arteries (Fig. 5e). Vegfr1/2/3IECKO-P1-P7 ECs behaved similarly to Vegfr1/2IECKO-P1-P7 ECs, except for a pronounced decrease in formation of arterial vessels (Fig. 5f–h). Taken together, our findings show that in the absence of VEGFR2 signalling, VEGFR1 is required to sustain VEGFR3 expression and growth and migration of capillary ECs. In arteries, VEGFR3 continues to be expressed after loss of VEGFR1 and VEGFR2 and regulates development of arteries when the other VEGFA receptors are missing. Notably, vein ECs can survive and clonally expand in the complete absence of all VEGF receptor signalling (Fig. 5i).

Our study challenges the longstanding view that VEGFR2 signalling is indispensable for endothelial proliferation, migration and sprouting during angiogenesis1,22. By using iFlpMosaics to induce ratiometric genetic mosaics of wild-type and Vegfr2KO ECs, we demonstrated that these mutant cells are capable of surviving, proliferating and competing with wild-type ECs during the entire embryonic and postnatal organ growth period (Extended Data Fig. 12). Contrary to previous studies suggesting that VEGFR2 is required for all forms of vascular differentiation and development10,12,36, our findings indicate that VEGFR2-independent mechanisms support angiogenesis in certain vascular beds, particularly the long-term development of venous and perivenous capillaries.

We identified significant organ-specific differences in adaptation to acute loss of VEGFR2 signalling (Extended Data Fig. 12a), thereby extending previous findings37,38. Whereas angiogenic retina ECs were strongly affected, brain ECs were the least affected, retaining high angiogenic potential, partially because of VEGFR1 compensation (Extended Data Fig. 12b). By contrast, postnatal heart, kidney and liver ECs were more sensitive to acute withdrawal of VEGFR2, showing partial depletion of Vegfr2KO ECs in capillaries, as well as a partial reduction in proliferation. The postnatal lung showed a distinct response, with no major changes in EC proliferation or cluster composition but instead a shift in transcriptional programs towards inflammation and metabolic adaptations. These findings highlight the heterogeneity of endothelial responses across different vascular beds and suggest that organ-specific factors influence EC resilience to perturbations in VEGF signalling.

The long-term adaptation of Vegfr2KO ECs was a notable observation. Although these cells initially had a competitive disadvantage during early embryonic and postnatal sprouting angiogenesis stages, they ultimately expanded and outcompeted wild-type cells in venous and perivenous regions, indicating that alternative pathways support their survival and proliferation in this niche. Veins are known to provide a continuous source of ECs for capillary angiogenesis and later arterialization20,23, and this venous dominance of Vegfr2KO ECs allows them to compete with wild-type cells over time. Our scRNA-seq analysis of different vascular beds further showed that ECs with prolonged loss of VEGFR2 exhibited a significant shift towards a venous transcriptional signature (venousization), marked by upregulation of many venous genes, including Nr2f2, a master regulator of veins development24,39. Vegfr2KONr2f2KO ECs were significantly less able to expand, particularly in veins, showing that venousization is a key adaptation mechanism that enables Vegfr2KO ECs to persist and contribute to vascular development (Extended Data Fig. 12c,d).

In addition to venousization, our findings demonstrate the compensatory roles of VEGFR1 and VEGFR3 in supporting survival and growth signalling when VEGFR2 is absent (Extended Data Fig. 12b). Previously, VEGFR1 has mainly been reported to negatively regulate VEGFR2 signalling during angiogenesis, because its soluble secreted version sFLT1 or VEGFR1 is a decoy receptor of VEGF1,22. In our mosaic Vegfr1KO and Vegfr1/2KO experiments, sFLT1 levels in the microenvironment were normal; this led us to find that membrane or full-length VEGFR1 acted as a positive regulator of angiogenesis and partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss, supporting both EC survival and migration. The mosaic single loss of VEGFR3 also showed that this receptor was a positive regulator of EC migration towards the leading edge. This was consistent with results obtained using VEGFR3-blocking antibodies40; however, our findings were contrary to results from pan-endothelial Vegfr3KO genetics experiments32 in which the receptor was lost from all ECs. In this case, VEGFC and/or VEGFD bioavailability in the whole body increases, thereby increasing VEGFC–VEGFR2 signalling, whereas in low-frequency Vegfr3KO mosaics this does not occur. In addition, Vegfr2/3KO ECs mobilized less to the angiogenic front and had decreased arterialization when compared with Vegfr2KO ECs. The ability of these alternative VEGF receptors to sustain EC survival, migration and proliferation at the single-cell level indicates potential functional plasticity and compensation within the VEGF signalling network, as suggested previously by studies using classical full-tissue conditional genetics12,32,37.

An important implication of our study is that EC sensitivity to VEGFR2 loss varies depending on the vascular context and the time since the loss. We found that acute loss of VEGFR2 during active angiogenesis resulted in significant EC depletion in the first 3 days, particularly depletion of tip cells and other ECs at the angiogenic front, where VEGF signalling is highest. However, Vegfr2KO ECs in VEGF-low areas and those that had undergone long-term adaptation were able to persist and even contribute to a substantial portion of capillary vessels, particularly those around veins. This suggests that ECs experiencing prolonged VEGFR2 deficiency undergo venousization in VEGF-low areas, enabling them to survive and then grow in the absence of canonical VEGF signalling. Our tumour models showed that Vegfr2KO ECs could form tumour vessels, particularly if they had previously undergone venousization during embryonic angiogenesis. The use of ratiometric and trackable iFlpMosaics was key to obtaining these findings.

Our work may also provide biomarkers and insights into resistance mechanisms to anti-VEGF therapies5,41,42,43. Adaptation of ECs to VEGFR2 loss by engaging alternative venous-related angiogenic pathways may also occur in tumours. If this is confirmed, therapeutic strategies that simultaneously block the compensatory and venous-related pathways identified here may be necessary to overcome resistance to anti-VEGF treatments.

In conclusion, our study reshapes our understanding of VEGFR2-dependent angiogenesis by demonstrating that ECs possess intrinsic mechanisms to adapt to long-term absence of VEGFR2 signalling. The discovery of endothelial venousization and compensatory VEGF receptor signalling provides a new framework for investigation of alternative modes of vascular development and resistance to anti-VEGF therapies.

All mouse husbandry and experiments were conducted using protocols approved by local animal ethics committees and authorities (Comunidad Autónoma de Madrid and Universidad Autónoma de Madrid CAM-PROEX 164.8/20, PROEX 293.1/22 and PROEX-288.7/24). The mouse colonies were maintained in racked individual ventilation cages according to current national legislation. The mice had dust- and pathogen-free bedding and sufficient nesting and environmental enrichment material for development of species-specific behaviour. All mice had ad libitum access to food and water in environmental conditions of 45–65% relative humidity, temperatures of 21–24 °C and a 12 h/12 h light–dark cycle. For preservation of animal welfare, mouse health was monitored with an animal health surveillance programme that followed the recommendations of the Federation of European Laboratory Animal Science Associations for specific-pathogen-free facilities

We used Mus musculus lines mostly on the C57BL6 genetic background, with some having a fraction of 129SV, or B6CBAF1 or DBA genetic backgrounds. Mice were backcrossed to C57Bl6 for several generations. To generate mice for analysis, we intercrossed mice aged between 7 weeks and 30 weeks. We did not anticipate any influence of mouse sex on our data, and both female and male mice were analysed. The initial sample size was determined taking into account the ‘3 Rs’ for animal experimentation and the expected experimental variability based on protocols (published and our own; refs. 13 and 14). The final sample size was defined a posteriori after statistical analysis of the data. Sample size and related statistical analysis methods are indicated in the figure legends or source data. No randomization or blinding was used, and the animals or tissues were selected for analysis on the basis of their genotype, the detected Cre- or FlpO-dependent recombination frequency and the quality of multiplex immunostaining.

The following mouse lines were used and intercrossed: Tg(Cdh5–CreERT2)44, Tg(iSuRe–HadCre)14, Vegfr2flox (ref. 45), Vegfr1flox (ref. 46), Vegfr3flox (ref. 47) (for this work, we also generated a new Vegfr3flox allele in the Vegfr1/2flox background, as indicated below), Nr2f2flox (ref. 48), iMb2–Mosaic16, Apln–FlpO15 and the iFlpMosaic lines13 (R26-iFlpMTomato-2A-Cre/MYFP and Tg-iFlpChromatin–Mosaic).

To generate a new Vegfr3flox allele combined with Vegfr1/2flox we injected Cas9, donor DNAs containing LoxP sites and guide RNAs (TGTTAAAGACACGCATACCT/AGG and AGATGGGGTGAATAGCTCCG/TGG) into mouse eggs of the Vegfr1/2flox iSuRe–HadCre Cdh5–CreERT2 line. Founders containing LoxP sites flanking exon 1 in the same chromosome were screened by PCR, and inducible Vegfr3 deletion was confirmed by PCR and immunostaining for the VEGFR3 protein (Extended Data Fig. 11l,m).

For induction of CreERT2 activity in adult mice, 1 g tamoxifen (Sigma-Aldrich, P5648_1G) was dissolved in 50 ml corn oil (stock tamoxifen concentration, 20 mg m−1), and aliquots were stored at −20 °C. Animals received intraperitoneal injections of 100 µl of this stock solution (total dose: 2 mg tamoxifen per animal at 80 mg kg−1), as indicated in the figures. To activate recombination in pups, we injected 4-OHT at the indicated stages at a dose of 40 mg kg−1. For double (VEGFR1/2, VEGFR2/3) or triple (VEGFR1/2/3) mutants, 4-OHT was administered to pups at 15 mg kg−1. For activation of recombination during embryogenesis, pregnant dams were induced with 0.25 mg 4-OHT supplemented with 0.125 mg progesterone at E10.5 and E12.5. All mouse lines and primer sequences required for genotyping are provided in Supplementary Table 1.

Lewis carcinoma cells were obtained from ATCC and cultured in DMEM (Gibco) containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 1× penicillin–streptomycin and 2 mM glutamine at 37 °C, 5% CO2. The cell medium was changed every other day, and cells were passaged every 3–4 days. Cells were routinely screened for mycoplasma contamination. Cells were used for tumour inoculation when they were at 75–80% confluency. Cells were trypsinized and resuspended in Matrigel solution (Biosciences). Age-matched (15–20 weeks) and sex-matched mice were injected subcutaneously with 5 × 105 tumour cells suspended in Matrigel (Corning, 354234). Mice were euthanized after 15 days, and tumours (less than 2 cm3) were extracted, fixed and processed for immunostaining.

For immunostaining of mouse retinas, eyes were dissected from mouse pups and fixed by incubation with agitation for 20 min in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) (diluted from a stock of 16% PFA; EMS 15710). After two washes in PBS (5 min each), retinas were microdissected from the eyes; 4 incisions were made to enable later flat mounting, and the retinas were refixed in 4% PFA for 45 min with agitation. After two washes in PBS, retinas were blocked and permeabilized by incubation for 1 h in PBST (0.3% Triton X-100, 3% FBS and 3% donkey serum in PBS). Samples were then incubated with primary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) diluted in PBST overnight at 4 °C with agitation. The next day, retinas were washed 5 times for 20 min in PBST diluted 1:2. Then, they were incubated in the same solution for 2 h at room temperature with Alexa-conjugated secondary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2). After washing (3 × 15 min) in PBS containing 0.15% Triton X-100, retinas were washed (2 × 15 min) in PBS and flat mounted in Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech). For combination of rabbit anti-ERG-647 with other antibodies produced in rabbit, retinas were incubated with the Alexa 594 AffiniPure Fab Fragment Donkey Anti-Rabbit secondary antibody, then with 5% rabbit serum for 30 min at room temperature, and finally with rabbit anti-ERG-647.

For collection of organs and histological analysis, mice were euthanized in CO2 chambers, and 10 ml of PBS was injected into the left ventricles, followed by perfusion with 3.7–4% formaldehyde (ITW Reagents, 252931) at pH 7. The explanted organs were postfixed for 2 h in 4% PFA (Thermo Scientific, 043368.9M) in PBS at 4 °C with gentle rotation. After three washes in PBS for 10 min each, the organs were stored overnight in 30% sucrose (Sigma) in PBS. The organs were then embedded in optimal cutting temperature compound (Sakura) and frozen at −80 °C. Cryosections of 30 µm were cut on a cryostat (Leica), washed three times for 10 min each time in PBS, and blocked and permeabilized in PBS containing 10% donkey serum (Millipore), 10% FBS and 1% Triton X-100. The primary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) were diluted in the same buffer and incubated with sections overnight at 4 °C. This step was followed by three 10-min washes in PBS and incubation for 2 h with conjugated secondary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) and 4,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) in PBS at room temperature. After three washes in PBS, the sections were mounted with Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech). For combination of rabbit anti-ERG-647 with other antibodies produced in rabbit, retinas were incubated first with the other primary rabbit antibodies, followed by Alexa 594 AffiniPure Fab Fragment Donkey Anti-Rabbit secondary antibody, then rabbit epitopes blocked with 5% rabbit serum for 30 min at room temperature, and finally incubated with rabbit anti-ERG-647.

For confocal scanning, immunostained organ sections or whole-mount retinas were imaged at high resolution with a Leica SP8 Navigator confocal microscope fitted with a ×10 or ×40 objective. Individual fields or tiles of large areas were acquired. All images shown are representative of the results obtained for each group and experiment. Animals were dissected and processed under identical conditions. Phenotypes or signal intensities were compared using images obtained with the same laser excitation and confocal scanner detection settings. We used ImageJ/Fiji v.1.54f to threshold, select and quantify the objects in confocal micrographs.

For arteriovenous mapping of ERG-labelled control and mutant ECs (Extended Data Fig. 3a), a semiautomatic Fiji script (available at https://github.com/RuiBenedito/Benedito_Lab) was developed. First, six regions of interest were manually defined by the user: artery, vein, mature capillaries between the established arteries and veins, intermediate capillaries, angiogenic front and leading edge. ERG labelling was used to segment endothelial nuclei and classify each nucleus according to reporter or marker positivity (determined by the percentage of pixels within each nucleus above a given intensity threshold level), and the XY coordinates of nuclei were extracted. Then, arterial, venous, distal and proximal arteriovenous boundaries were defined by the user to determine the relative position of each segmented nucleus to each arteriovenous field boundary; this enabled compilation of data extracted from different arteriovenous fields into a single XY dot plot or heatmap.

The data collected in Fiji were post-analysed in R (v.4.5.2) for generation of graphs representing the spatial distribution of the cells of interest. For the XY plots and heatmaps, samples were randomly subsetted to enable us to display equal numbers of control and mutant cells (MYFP+ versus MTomato+ in the Apln–FlpO, iFlpMosaic background, and MTomato− versus MTomato+ in the Cdh5–CreERT2, iSuRe–HadCre background); this was to make clear the zonation differences between control and mutant cells. For visualization with XY dot plots, 2,000 randomly selected cells of each group were plotted; for the heatmap generation, the maximal number of cells (determined by the cell type (control or mutant) with fewer cells) was used. The percentage of each cell type in each arteriovenous region was calculated given its spatial distribution per field (Extended Data Fig. 3a).

We generated Fiji macro Script_Reporter_MarkerDetection_Mapping.ijm for spatial mapping of ERG and/or quantification of EC colocalization with reporters (MYFP or MTomato) and other markers (Ki-67) as in Figs. 1, 2, 5. R scripts were used for data quantification and heatmapping (Script_Spatial Heatmap; Figs. 1, 2, 5 and Extended Data Figs. 3, 4, 11) and are available at GitHub (https://github.com/RuiBenedito/Benedito_Lab). Fiji, Adobe Photoshop CC 24.1.0 and Adobe Illustrator CC v.27.1.1 were used for downstream image processing, analysis and illustration.

To quantify the clonal expansion of single ECs expressing the iSuRe–HadCre and the Tg-iFlpChromatin–Mosaic alleles, we segmented and analysed images with MTomato+H2B-Cherry+, MTomato+H2B-EGFP+ or MTomato+HA-H2B-Cerulean+ signals with the Clone_Identification_Quantification script, deposited at GitHub (https://github.com/RuiBenedito/Benedito_Lab/).

Postnatal and adult tissues were dissociated before fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). Enzymatic digestion was carried out at 37 °C for 20 min using a solution containing 2.5 mg ml−1 collagenase type I (Thermo Fisher), 2.5 mg ml−1 dispase II (Thermo Fisher) and 50 μg ml−1 DNase I (Roche). Following dissociation, samples were pelleted by centrifugation (450g, 4 °C, 5 min). Pellets were gently resuspended in 1× blood lysis buffer (BioLegend, 420301) and incubated on ice for 5 min for lysis of erythroid cells. After lysis, cells were passed through a 70-μm cell strainer and centrifuged again (450g, 4 °C, 5 min). Cells were resuspended in antibody incubation solution (PBS without Ca2+ or Mg2+, supplemented with 2% dialysed FBS; Biowest, X0515), with primary antibodies (APC rat anti-mouse CD31 and APC-Cy7 anti-CD45; Supplementary Table 2) only or with the addition of Hashtag oligo (HTO) antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) when scRNA-seq was performed. Samples were then incubated at 4 °C with gentle agitation for 20 min.

After immunolabelling, cells were centrifuged (450g, 4 °C, 5 min), washed with antibody incubation solution, centrifuged again and resuspended in sorting buffer (10% FBS in PBS without Ca2+ or Mg2+). Stained cells were maintained on ice until acquisition. DAPI (5 mg ml−1) was added immediately before FACS analysis. Cells were analysed using an LSRFortessa cell analyser or sorted using a FACS Aria Cell Sorter (BD Biosciences). For an example of the FACS gating strategy, see Extended Data Fig. 1a. BD FACSDiva v.8.0.1 and FlowJo v.10 were used for data acquisition and analysis.

For RNA-seq analysis, APC rat anti-mouse CD31 (which labels ECs), APC-Cy7 rat anti-CD45 (which labels blood cells) and HTO antibodies (BD Biosciences) (Supplementary Table 2) were used together to hashtag and distinguish the different organ Tomato+CD31+ ECs when loaded on the same 10x Genomics port (Extended Data Figs. 6a and 8a). After antibody incubation, samples were washed twice with antibody incubation solution, centrifuged (450g, 5 min, 4 °C) and resuspended in sorting buffer (10% FBS in PBS without Ca2+ or Mg2+). Stained cells were maintained on ice until acquisition. Immediately before FACS analysis, DAPI (5 mg ml−1) was added, and the cell suspension was passed slowly through a 70-µm cell strainer attached to a 1-ml syringe for removal of aggregates. Live, DAPI-negative, CD31+CD45− and endogenous-reporter-positive cells were sorted into cold 1.5-ml microcentrifuge tubes containing 300 µl of sorting buffer. Cells were collected using a 100-µm nozzle at 20 PSI in high-purity mode with a flow rate of fewer than 3,000 events per second to preserve cell viability and minimize contamination. After sorting, cells were pelleted at 500g for 5 min at 4 °C and resuspended in 30–40 µl cell-capture buffer (Ca2+- and Mg2+-free PBS supplemented with 0.04% ultrapure bovine serum albumin; Thermo Fisher, AM2616). Viability and cell concentration were determined using a Countess 3 Automated Cell Counter (Thermo Fisher Scientific) before loading of the 10x Genomics port.

Single-cell suspensions were loaded on to the 10x Genomics Chromium Controller system for encapsulation into emulsion droplets. The 10x Genomics Chromium single-cell 3′ RNA-seq library preparation and sequencing were carried out at the CNIC Genomics Unit according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Each port was loaded with 20,000 to 50,000 cells. Final libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 platform, with software v.1.7.2.

scRNA-seq data were aligned and quality controlled by the CNIC Bioinformatics Unit using Cell Ranger (v.8 and v.9). Clustering, cell type identification and downstream analysis were performed by I.G.-G. The following pipeline was applied for transcript alignment, quantification, quality control and cell type classification.

Reference transcriptomes were generated using the Ensembl GRCm38 mouse genome, build version 98 (sep2019.archive.ensembl.org). Genes metadata were obtained from the corresponding Ensembl BioMart archive. To enable downstream analysis of gene deletion efficiency and soluble versus full-length isoform abundance, we appended Vegfr2 (also known as Kdr) exon 3, Kdr exon 30, Vegfr1 (also known as Flt1) exon 13b and Flt1 exon 30 to the reference transcriptome as custom metadata features. Gene annotations were obtained from the corresponding Ensembl BioMart archive. Raw sequencing reads from gene expression libraries, hashtag oligonucleotides and targeted transcript sequences were aligned and quantified using Cell Ranger (v.8 and v.9).

Downstream analyses were performed using R (v.4.5.0) and the Seurat package (v.5.5.1; https://satijalab.org/seurat/)49. Cells were filtered for removal of low-quality profiles and technical artifacts using the following criteria: 2,000–30,000 total unique molecular identifiers (UMIs), 800–6,000 detected genes, mitochondrial transcript content less than 25%, fewer than 65% of reads mapping to the top 50 expressed genes and fewer than 0.1% haemoglobin transcripts. Cells with fewer than 15 hashtag UMIs were excluded to improve sample assignment accuracy. To enrich for endothelial populations and exclude hematopoietic contamination, we also required cells to express Cdh5 (normalized expression greater than 0.1) and no or very low expression of Ptprc (normalized expression less than 0.1). Cells identified as doublets on the basis of hashtag antibody signals were removed. Demultiplexing by organ was performed using sample-specific hashtag oligonucleotide signals (Supplementary Table 2) and after confirmed by organ-specific EC markers, and all downstream analyses were conducted separately for each organ ECs.

Mitochondrial genes, haemoglobin genes and transgenes were removed before clustering to avoid biasing of normalization and dimensionality reduction. Filtered count data were log-normalized and scaled before analysis. Dimensionality reduction was performed using principal component analysis, and batch effects across independent ports were corrected with the Harmony algorithm50.

We clustered cells by constructing a shared nearest neighbour graph and applying the Louvain community detection algorithm to identify distinct cell populations. The optimal number of principal components for dimensionality reduction was determined using an elbow plot, and clustering resolution parameters were selected on the basis of the EC complexity observed in each organ.

Clusters and cells were classified using the SingleR function from the SingleR package v.2.10.0 (ref. 51). Putative doublets were identified as cell clusters that had high total UMI or gene counts or unusual gene coexpression or were located in principal component analysis outliers. Cells classified as singlets were retained and reclustered. Final cluster identities were manually curated on the basis of known EC subtypes and literature-based markers. The FUNCTION_Dotplot_Markers custom function in R was used to find and plot top marker genes per cluster to determine cell identities.

To assess the rate of exon deletion in Vegfr2flox/flox samples, we computed the number of UMI reads aligned to each exon, including the floxed region and the terminal 3′ exon or untranslated region (which is typically overrepresented in 10x Genomics 3′ libraries). Only reads with valid barcodes, UMIs and matching strand orientation were retained.

Read counts for floxed exons were normalized to total UMI counts per cell. These values were added to the Seurat metadata. Deletion efficiency was visualized using dot plots and violin plots, comparing expression of the whole transcript (including the 3′ untranslated region). These visualizations were generated using the custom R function FUNCTION_violin_dotplot_deletion_FC.R, which combines violin plots of single-cell expression distributions with dot plots displaying total average expression numbers and signed fold change between conditions.

To obtain the ratio between the soluble (sVegfr1) and full-length (flVegfr1) isoforms, the normalized reads from exon 13b (the last exon in the soluble form) were divided by the normalized reads of exon 30 (the last exon in the full-length version).

We quantified differences in cell type composition between control and mutant samples for each organ by comparing relative proportions across conditions. For UMAP visualizations (both split and integrated), equal downsampling of the two conditions was performed to ensure identical cell numbers, thereby avoiding sampling bias in visual comparisons.

Differential gene expression between conditions was visualized using volcano plots. These were generated using R functions (FUNCTION_VolcanoPlot) developed in-house that built on the EnhancedVolcano package (v.1.26.0)52. For volcano plots and heatmaps, statistical analyses were performed using Seurat’s FindMarkers function, with Wilcoxon rank-sum test and Bonferroni correction for multiple testing. GSEA was performed using FGSEA with a custom wrapper function (FUNCTION_Fgsea_TableFgsea) based on the FGSEA package. For hallmark pathways, statistical analyses were performed using the multilevel Monte Carlo approach implemented in fgseaMultilevel (R package fgsea v.1.34.2)53 and Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction for multiple testing.

Genes used for differential gene expression analysis were prefiltered using FUNCTION_FilterLowExpressionGenes_onlyTable; this removes genes with low and highly heterogeneous expression patterns across cells, which are often inconsistently detected between datasets and potentially reflect technical artefacts such as ambient RNA contamination. The function acts as an empirical, distribution-based filter to improve robustness of downstream differential expression analysis. Differential expression heatmaps were generated using a custom function (FUNCTION_Find_PlotGenesHeatmap_FC_Metadata), implemented in-house and based on the pheatmap package.

Most numerical data shown in charts were first compiled and processed with Microsoft Excel 2019 and 2024 and then analysed and plotted with GraphPad Prism v.10.1.0. All bar graphs show mean ± s.d. Experiments were repeated with independent animals, as stated in the source data file or figure legends. Comparisons between two sample groups with a Gaussian distribution were performed using unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests. Comparisons among more than two groups were made by one-way or two-way analysis of variance followed by multiple comparison tests. Data points were analysed and plotted with GraphPad Prism. No randomization or blinding was used, and the animals or tissues were selected for analysis on the basis of their genotype, the detected Cre- or FlpO-dependent recombination frequency and the quality of multiplex immunostaining. For mosaic analysis, only samples with less than 50% recombination were selected. The sample sizes were chosen according to the observed statistical variation and published protocols.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

RNA-seq data can be viewed at the Gene Expression Omnibus under accession code GSE331295. Unprocessed FACS raw data files and original microscopy images of the data are available upon request. All other data supporting the findings in this study are included in the main article and associated files. Source data are provided with this paper.

a, Schematic of the iFlpMosaic and iSuRe-HadCre genetic systems used to induce and map genetic mosaics. Flow-chart depicting the main steps in image analysis used for the digital mapping of the identified cells, and the generation of heatmaps or XY dot plots, with an example of the analysis for a control retinal AV field with AplnFlpO, iFlpMTomato-Cre/MYFP or Cdh5-CreERT2, iSure-HadCre genetics. Definition of the 6 regions of interest, ERG-based segmentation (endothelial nuclei), nuclear-classification according to reporter or marker expression and relative distance of each nucleus to the AV limits are determined using a custom made semi-automatic FIJI script (steps i-iv). Once a minimum of 2000 cells per reporter group (Tomato+/−, YFP+) are analysed, data is then post-analysed in RStudio to determine the cell distribution of each reporter group in each region and the contribution of Tomato+ cells to each region when compared to control (YFP+ or Tomato- cells) (step v). XY dot plots (step vi) and heatmaps (step vii) are then generated. Note that dot plots (shown in vi) have a maximum of 2000 + 2000 mapped cells plotted as dots, to allow their spatial visualization, whereas heatmaps (shown in vii) are generated with maximal number of mapped cells (with equal cell number in control and mutant group).b,c, Representative confocal micrographs showing the loss of VEGFR2 protein (b), and its downstream target ESM1 (c), 24 h after 4-OHT administration. Data are presented as mean values +/−SD. For statistics see Source Data File 1. Scale bars are 25 μm.

a, Schematic of the genetics and cell sorting gating strategy to isolate the cells used to perform the scRNAseq contrasts shown in Fig. 3 and this figure. b,c, UMAP showing the different brain endothelial clusters and their proportions (b) and the expression of canonical tip cell marker genes in the activated cell cluster (c). d,e, Umaps and violin plots showing the expression of two genes known to be highly expressed by sprouting tip cells, and downregulated after Vegfr2 deletion in brain ECs. f, Violins showing a tip cell genes score based on the combined expression of several tip cell genes (PlexinD1, Kcne3, Esm1) in brain ECs. g, Violin plots showing expression of the terminal exon 30 (highly detected in the 3′10x genomics library sequencing) and the upstream deleted floxed exon 3, used to assess Vegfr2 deletion efficiency from P4 to P7 in lung ECs. Red negative values indicate fold changes between conditions. Green and red labels above the dots show the absolute average expression (not log). h, UMAP and accompanying histobar plot illustrating the distribution and proportion of lung endothelial cell clusters within each condition. i, Dot plot showing the expression of key marker genes for the different lung EC clusters. j, UMAP projection of the control and Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 lung ECs. The associated bar plot shows the log2 ratio of the number of Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 divided by the number of control cells per cluster. k, Volcano plot of showing top DEGs in lung ECs. Coloured genes correspond to highlighted pathways or processes of biological relevance. l, List of hallmark pathways deregulated in lung Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 ECs. m, Heatmap showing the average log2 fold change of apoptosis-related and tip-cell genes in lung ECs between Vegfr2KO (P4–P7) and control samples. n, Violin plots showing expression of the terminal exon 30 (detected in the 3′10x genomics library sequencing) and the deleted floxed exon 3, used to assess Vegfr2 deletion efficiency from P4 to P7. Note that in some cells there is still some residual Vegfr2 mRNA given the short-term deletion nature of the assay, or some contamination with mRNA from wild-type kidney ECs. Red negative values indicate fold changes between conditions. Green and red labels above the dots show the absolute average expression (not log). o, UMAP and accompanying histobar plot illustrating the distribution and proportion of kidney endothelial cell clusters within each condition. p, Dot plot showing the expression of key marker genes for the different clusters. q, UMAP projection of the control and Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 Kidney ECs. The associated bar plot shows the log2 ratio of the number of Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 divided by the number of control cells per cluster. r, Volcano plot of showing top DEGs. Colored genes correspond to highlighted pathways or processes of biological relevance. s, List of hallmark pathways deregulated in kidney Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 ECs. t, Heatmap showing the average log2 fold change of apoptosis-related and tip-cell genes in kidney ECs between Vegfr2KO (P4–P7) and control samples. For volcano plots and heatmaps (k, m, r, t), statistical analyses were performed using Seurat’s FindMarkers function, with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test and Bonferroni correction for multiple testing. For hallmark pathways (l, s), statistical analyses were performed using the multilevel Monte Carlo approach implemented in fgseaMultilevel (R package fgsea) and Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) FDR correction for multiple testing.

a, Schematic of the iSure-HadCre, Cdh5-CreERT2 genetics used to analyse the ability of ECs with short-term (2–3 days before implanting the tumor) deletion of Vegfr2 to contribute to Lewis Lung carcinoma (LLC) tumor vessels. Quantifications show that upon short-term deletion, VEGFR2KO ECs(Tomato+ERG+) contribute less to intratumoral vessels when compared to vessels in extratumoral region of the tumor. b, Schematic of the iFlpMosaic genetics used to analyse the ability of ECs (ERG+ nuclei) with long-term (since embryogenesis) deletion of Vegfr2 to contribute to LLC tumor vessels. Quantifications show that upon long-term deletion, the disadvantage of VEGFR2KO ECs(Tomato+ERG+) to contribute to intratumoral vessels when compared to vessels in extratumoral region of the tumor, is smaller than upon short-term deletion. Note that the Apln-FlpO allele also drives the recombination of the iFlpMosaic allele in other cell types besides ECs, and hence the need to use ERG staining (labels the EC nuclei). Data are presented as mean values +/− SD. For statistics see Source Data File 1. Scale bar 250 microns.

Arrows indicate Tomato+Ki67+ cells (yellow) or Tomato+Ki67- (white). g, Representative confocal micrograph of Vegfr1/2KO-P4-P7 retinas immunostained with ERG and respective quantification charts, showing a further decrease in EC/vascular density when compared to Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 retinas. h, Representative confocal micrographs of Vegfr1/2KO-P4-P7 retinas immunostained for cleaved caspase 3 (CC3), and respective quantification chart showing a similar increase in EC apoptosis to Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 ECs. i, Newborns survival plot showing that double deletion of Vegfr1 and Vegfr2 induced at P1, leads to 100% lethality of pups before P20. j, Representative confocal micrograph of retinas with mosaic deletion of Vegfr1 in ECs from P1 to P7. Heatmap, XY dot plot and chart showing the position and relative % of Tomato+ (KO) and Tomato negative (WT) cells. k, Representative confocal micrographs of retinas from Vegfr1 heterozygous floxed (flox/wt; n = 3 pups) and Vegfr1 homozygous mice, with complete (n = 6 pups) or mosaic deletion (n = 5 pups) in ECs induced at P1 with 4-OHT. a, Single cell RNAseq and histological analysis of Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 ECs (gene deletion induced at P4 and analysis at P7) in distinct organs revealed common but also distinct transcriptional programs and functions for VEGFR2. b, Loss of VEGFR2 affects the migration of ECs towards VEGF produced by hypoxic tissues, during the first wave of angiogenesis. This leads to the accumulation of Vegfr2KO ECs in more mature vessels and veins, which provides for a continuous source of mutant ECs during subsequent waves of angiogenesis derived from veins. The additional loss of VEGFR1 compromises capillary angiogenesis, whereas the additional loss of VEGFR3 compromises arterialization. c, The comparison of scRNAseq data from ECs with short-term (P4 to P7) and long-term (embryonic to P7) deletion of Vegfr2 revealed that over time Vegfr2KO ECs undergo significant transcriptional changes and upregulate the expression of many venous genes (venousization), particularly Nr2f2. d, The upregulation of Nr2f2, and venousization, enables Vegfr2KO-E8.5-P7 ECs to compete with wildtype ECs over time, and form veins and many other venous-derived vessels, such as capillaries, tip cells and even arteries. Note that these cells adapt over time to the loss of VEGFR2 and become more capable of angiogenesis than Vegfr2KO-P1-P7 ECs. The additional loss of the master regulator of vein specification Nr2f2, prevents the venousization and growth of Vegfr2KO ECs.

Antibodies for immunostaining and hashtagging.

#1441. Cole Palmer's England lifeline: Three Lions ask Chelsea about star's fitness in clear sign Thomas Tuchel is considering calling him up after warning over last squad withdrawal

Published: 18:32 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 19:13 EDT, 5 November 2026

England have privately asked Chelsea for the latest on Cole Palmer ahead of Thomas Tuchel revealing his squad for the Nations League clashes with Croatia and Spain.

Palmer is under consideration for another call-up, having withdrawn from duty during the last international break with a minor muscular injury.

Tuchel responded by appearing to question his desire to represent his country, warning he 'misses way too many camps' as the 24-year-old skipped all four England fixtures in September and October.

Palmer had played a full 90 for Chelsea away at Bournemouth before that break, which he then used to fly abroad to the Caribbean with his girlfriend, Olivia Holder, after withdrawing from England duty. He was accompanied by a personal rehab coach on that trip, and was provided with an injury-specific training and recovery plan by his club.

Palmer started in Chelsea's first fixture when the Premier League returned at home to Brentford with Blues boss Xabi Alonso insisting they were right to take care of their star player themselves.

Chelsea star Cole Palmer is under consideration for England UEFA Nations League call-up

He withdrew from the last squad, leaving boss Thomas Tuchel questioning his commitment

Palmer, who was injured, went to the Caribbean with girlfriend Olivia Holder on the last international break

It has been described as standard procedure for England to make medical checks on players with clubs. While it does not guarantee a call-up, it indicates how Tuchel has been weighing up offering Palmer another chance as he names his next squad on Friday morning.

Palmer was not the only player to withdraw from England duty in the last break, with Declan Rice, Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford and Tino Livramento among other dropouts.

Yet Palmer's issue was a contentious topic after it represented a chance for him to return to England's thinking following his 2026 World Cup omission. His representative did not answer when asked whether he would happily accept another call-up after Tuchel's previous comments.

Palmer has played an important role for Chelsea early in this season with three goals and three assists in the Premier League.

He scored a penalty in their last win over Manchester United, which took him to 50 goals in 105 games in the top flight for the Blues. He has started every league game under Alonso this term with Sunderland at the Stadium of Light this Sunday.

#1440. Everton Women Unwrap New Partnership With Nestlé Confectionery

Everton Women has announced a new multi-year partnership with Nestlé Confectionery, bringing one of the world's most recognisable food and beverage companies into the Club's growing portfolio of commercial partners.

The agreement will see Nestlé Confectionery become the 'Official Chocolate and Grab Bag Sweet Partner of Everton Women' and an 'Official Supplier of Hill Dickinson Stadium', with household favourites including KitKat, Smarties, Rowntree's, Aero, Lion, Yorkie, Milkybar and Quality Street set to feature across both venues.

At Goodison Park, Nestlé Confectionery will have a prominent presence through pitchside LED advertising, big-screen exposure and matchday activations designed to engage supporters, alongside opportunities to showcase its products at food kiosks and points of sale.

Supporters and visitors to Hill Dickinson Stadium will also be able to enjoy Nestlé Confectionery's popular range of products, extending the brand's presence across both of Everton's iconic stadiums.

The agreement represents Everton Women's second dedicated commercial partnership, following last year's deal with GGM Gastro, with further Everton Women's-focused partnerships set to be announced.

The growing interest from major businesses reflects the opportunities being created around Everton Women, with the team's move to Goodison Park offering prospective partners a unique combination of footballing heritage, an iconic stadium and access to new audiences as the women's game continues to develop.

Andrew Middleton, President of Business Operations at Everton, said:  “We are delighted to welcome Nestlé Confectionery as a partner of Everton Women and an Official Supplier of Hill Dickinson Stadium.

“Like Everton, Nestlé’s brands have been part of family life for generations, making this a natural fit for our supporters and matchday experience. Together, we will create engaging moments across both venues and bring these iconic products closer to our audiences.

“This partnership is another important step in Everton Women’s continued growth, and we look forward to working with Nestlé to bring it to life.”

Gail Stove, OOH Confectionery Lead for Nestlé UK & Ireland, said: "Nestlé Confectionery is excited to be an Official Partner of Everton Women and Official Supplier of Hill Dickinson Stadium.

"We can’t wait to share our beloved brands with visitors at these brilliant venues.

“Working collaboratively with Everton Football Club, we’ll bring the No.1 confectionery single within the leisure channel, KitKat® 4 Finger, along with other iconic Nestlé Confectionery brands for everyone to enjoy.”

Further details of Nestlé Confectionery's planned matchday activations and opportunities for Everton supporters to engage with its brands will be announced in the coming months.

#1439. How James McAtee became Nottingham Forest's tough-tackling 'quarterback': The heart-to-heart with Oliver Glasner, summer boot camp and an Adam Wharton blueprint

Published: 21:00 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EDT, 5 November 2026

Quarterback is not a word necessarily associated with somebody once dubbed the 'Salford Silva' but then James McAtee has changed immeasurably since leaving Manchester City 15 months ago.

That moniker was handed down when the diminutive midfielder was much younger, effortlessly gliding through City’s academy, excelling in tight spaces, never losing possession. Scoring heaps, too.

That is who Nottingham Forest thought they were purchasing for £30million in August 2025, a statement signing to play high up the pitch. And yet as last season unravelled, and the sackings piled up – four managers in all – McAtee mustered only two Premier League starts throughout the campaign.

He was given four minutes across almost four months at one stage and was an unused substitute in both encounters with City. That will change on Saturday, McAtee one of the first names on the Forest team sheet, owing much to one conversation with Oliver Glasner that changed the course of his career at the City Ground.

So to the quarterback. The most important position in a Glasner team. That was how the Austrian envisioned McAtee’s evolution, the path to regular matches, and within months he has become the heartbeat of a team that is deserving of significantly more points than the six they have amassed so far.

Those who oversaw McAtee's development at City are not shocked by the calm use of possession and incisive passes through the lines yet did not predict him flying into challenges and blocks, only two midfielders in the division having completed more tackles than his 14 so far. He has turned into a terrier.

James McAtee in his 'quarterback' role for Nottingham Forest, where he has become the heartbeat of the team

At Manchester City he was dubbed the 'Salford Silva' and was more effective higher up the pitch

This has been a product of a full summer’s work on a rented pitch in Stockport, close to the family home. Forest's sporting director George Syrianos had made it clear that McAtee needed to become more physically robust and, after a five-day holiday, he spent a regimented two-and-a-half hours a day training, including 60-minute weight sessions in the afternoons.

When he arrived back for pre-season, McAtee had put on just over 2.5kg of muscle and lost 1kg of fat. He turned up a new man and that served to rubber stamp Glasner’s idea of permanently moving him into the engine room.

The Forest boss spoke to the 24-year-old about how he had developed Adam Wharton at Crystal Palace into an England international and that the plan here would be exactly the same.

This month’s Nations League ties will come too soon for that yet there are those within the FA who are confirmed admirers of McAtee and expect him to earn future caps. That he skippered the Under 21s to last year’s European Championship title, was player of the match in the final against Germany and named in the team of the tournament holds real weight inside St George’s Park.

Aesthetically, he is the picture of what the FA have wanted to create over the past decade: a nimble yet tough midfielder who guards the football with his life and wriggles out of trouble without fuss. And whose game understanding means he knows when to force the issue – McAtee has created the same number of chances as Rayan Cherki (18) this season.

The only central midfielders to have attempted more passes into the box than McAtee’s 60 are Bruno Fernandes, Granit Xhaka and Pascal Gross.

City will be some test on Saturday evening and there is plenty for him to prove, having worked under Enzo Maresca with the club’s Under 21s and a lingering feeling of what might have been at the Etihad Stadium.

As for England, they are blessed with real quality coming through in central midfield, with Alex Scott at Bournemouth leading the charge to unsettle the axis of Elliot Anderson and Declan Rice.

Scott could return from a thigh injury sustained during the last international break this weekend, a fitness problem that enraged his club.

McAtee skippered the England Under 21s to last year’s European Championship title, was player of the match in the final against Germany and named in the team of the tournament

The 24-year-old bulked up over the summer and is now able to mix it in the Forest engine room

Beyond those three it is very much up for grabs. James Garner is a recent Thomas Tuchel favourite, largely owing to his work ethic, with Wharton overlooked for the World Cup.

The man picked ahead of all those, Manchester United’s Kobbie Mainoo, was not afforded a kick in the United States. McAtee’s defensive and offensive stats this season outstrip the others in that chasing pack. They all know that there is definitely a claim to stake for somebody.

It’s Rice, Anderson, Scott and another at this point. Whether McAtee can kick on beyond nine consecutive Premier League starts is up to him. Crucially, he is in control of his own destiny more than ever before.

At City, he patiently waited for chances that barely came. In his debut year at Forest, players considered safer bets jumped the queue as the club battled relegation. But under Glasner, he has been harnessed, given the assurances that one sub-par performance does not mean a spell on the bench. McAtee has always been somebody who needs love to flourish and has finally found some.

#1438. Palmer and Rogers complete 12-minute rescue mission to save Chelsea

Xabi Alonso needed the cavalry – and referee Jarred Gillett – to stop Chelsea making a quick exit from the Carabao Cup and, boy, did they come up trumps for him.

Chelsea had looked to be heading out of the competition shortly after half-time, but, in Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers, Alonso has a cheat code that is capable of masking even the worst defending.

Alonso’s side have shared 26 goals in the five games they have played this season. It has certainly been an entertaining start by Chelsea’s latest manager.

Palmer, Rogers and Pedro Neto stepped off the substitutes’ bench to complete a stunning rescue mission against Leeds United. Palmer scored twice, Neto once and Rogers helped himself to at least a hat-trick of assists. He claimed it was four, but the record books may say three.

When it was announced Palmer had been awarded the player of the match, Rogers responded by saying: “Mate, I got four assists. I can’t believe that! That’s mental. He scored a pen!”

"Mate, I got four assists!" "That is criminal!" Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer arguing over the POTM award! 🤣 pic.twitter.com/X2PkPnSGDk

Chelsea had looked down and out, when, just three minutes after Alonso’s quadruple half-time change, Leeds doubled their lead. But four goals in an incredible 12-minute spell turned the tie on its head and it was Alonso’s substitutes who Chelsea had to thank.

Palmer, with some help from Gillett, was the first to come to the home side’s rescue. Four minutes after Brenden Aaronson had put Leeds 2-0 up, Gillett pointed to the penalty spot after Daniel James had stood on the foot of Pep Chavarría.

It looked like a harsh decision on Leeds and proved to be almost as big of a game-changer as Alonso’s substitutions. Palmer stepped up to score the resulting penalty.

Cole Palmer pulls one back for Chelsea from the spot! 🎯 pic.twitter.com/BUv6h1wTPQ

“Nobody in the stadium, not one player was asking for a penalty and he gave the penalty,” Daniel Farke, the Leeds manager, said. “All of a sudden their players came into the game. The momentum was on their side. Situations can change the whole momentum of the game.”

Stamford Bridge sensed a comeback and in the 55th minute, Rogers nudged the ball into the path of Palmer who produced a brilliant curling finish to beat Michael Zetterer, the Leeds goalkeeper.

TWO goals in TWO minutes for Cole Palmer and Chelsea are level! 🥶 pic.twitter.com/sgDd3YUgA6

Reece James then went close, before Neto completed the turnaround on the hour mark. Palmer found Rogers, who in turn picked out Neto and he sent Stamford Bridge wild by sending his shot into the corner of the net.

"This is a comeback of comebacks!" Pedro Neto scores and Chelsea have turned it around eleven minutes after going 2-0 down! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/FTPuWcFqEX

As Farke waited to make a quadruple substitution of his own, Danny Welbeck got in on the act by collecting the ball from Rogers, spinning and scoring.

Class from Danny Welbeck 😤 pic.twitter.com/FUFKxlzXDz

That should have been that and the atmosphere could not have been more different from half-time, when Chelsea fans had booed off their side after watching them fall a goal behind.

Reggie Watson, Chelsea’s 16-year-old debutant, Malo Gusto, Estêvão Willian and Jamie Gittens were hooked at half-time by Alonso, who said: “For sure, I take responsibility for all of them. No player to blame. It’s the decisions that we took.

“I know that probably I haven’t taken the right decisions for them to show their best level. It’s something that I will analyse and learn from. So it’s my responsibility and we had to make decisions at half-time. And we have seen another second half with another quality.”

Goalkeeper Mike Penders was one of the nine changes made by Alonso. He produced a superb double-save to first keep out Aaronson and then recover to tip Tarik Muharemovic’s header out from the corner.

Conor Coady was impressed with that Mike Penders double save in the first half 👏 pic.twitter.com/6NJqFDvnzk

But the Belgian flapped at the corner, which gave Harry Wilson a second chance to get his delivery right. And he did just that by finding Muharemovic at the back post to head the ball into the net.

Valentín Barco survived Alonso’s changes, but was partly at fault for Leeds’s second goal just after the break. He lost the ball and Ethan Ampadu galloped away from Rogers before crossing. Lukas Nmecha got the slightest of touches and Aaronsen smashed the ball into the net.

"Chelsea cut apart AGAIN !" Brenden Aaronson makes it 2-0 to Leeds 🔥 pic.twitter.com/LlJNpqXHav

The substitutes then took over, as Chelsea shocked the visitors before Leeds substitute Dominic Calvert-Lewin gave his team hope by reducing the deficit with 15 minutes remaining.

Any thoughts of a Leeds comeback were quickly erased, however, as Barco netted his first Chelsea goal from a Rogers pass, which may have taken a slight touch to deny him a fourth assist in the record books. Welbeck added a sixth in time added on.

Valentín Barco gets Chelsea a FIFTH! 🫨 pic.twitter.com/XnhgvhBpL9

On the defeat by Chelsea, Farke said: “The referee had the idea to give a penalty. No one in the stadium was asking for it, no one of their players was asking for it, but he spotted a situation where he thought he would give a penalty.

“All of a sudden they scored the goal, then their players came into the game at half-time, the whole stadium after being relatively quiet for 60 minutes they of course were there then. The momentum was all of a sudden on their side. In football small situations can change the whole momentum of a game and this happened.”

"100% I meant it!" 😅Morgan Rogers says he is really enjoying his football after he helped Chelsea beat Leeds 6-3 in the Carabao Cup! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/7uUQb6eIla

Here’s a reminder of the assist in question. Did Rogers mean it? Let us know in the comments beneath this live blog...

TWO goals in TWO minutes for Cole Palmer and Chelsea are level! 🥶 pic.twitter.com/sgDd3YUgA6

"Mate, I got four assists!" "That is criminal!" Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer arguing over the POTM award! 🤣 pic.twitter.com/X2PkPnSGDk

On the message from the manager at half-time, Palmer told Sky Sports: “Just up the intensity, play a bit more, become more alive because I think the first half was flat, everyone agreed in the changing room, so we stepped up.

Asked whether Alonso’s message was delivered calmly, he said: “At the start, but then he got a bit angry. But it was alright.”

On Chelsea’s half-time changes, Conor Coady said on Sky Sports: “I think the credit goes down to [Alonso]. He made a bit of a statement by doing that at half-time. Four subs is a lot to do at half-time but it was needed. Listen, we said about the first half that it was kind of like the players hadn’t played with each other, and then the big guns came on... They were electric at times.”

A crazy match which was decided by Chelsea’s superb substitutes. Alonso took action at half-time and was rewarded with six goals in a madcap second half. Palmer hauled Chelsea back into the game, Rogers collected a handful of assists and Neto scored the go-ahead goal. You wonder what this match will do for the likes of Estevao and Gittens, though.

Chelsea 6 Leeds United 3 (Welbeck) Pure reflexes from Welbeck, who diverts Barco’s wild effort beyond Zetterer.

Palmer has the hat-trick ball on his mind and attempts an audacious chip but just gets his angles wrong. Any guesses who laid on the chance? Rogers. Of course.

Fans in the away end have resolved they have seen enough and are now heading towards the exits. Stach attempts to launch a counter but his raking cross-field ball is far too heavy.

Rogers drifts out to the left and wins Chelsea a valuable corner. James walks over to take it to rapturous applause from supporters there.

Leeds look to break but Wilson mistimes his run and is caught offside.

There will be six minutes of time added on.

Chance! Okafor darts inside of Neto and spins in a teasing ball to the back post but neither Calvert-Lewin nor Tanaka are able to reach it.

Shouts for a Leeds penalty fail to pique the interest of referee Gillett. Gudmundsson was felled on the left of the box but the contact looked minimal.

A tap on Barco’s head from Wilson provokes some histrionics from the Argentine but Jarred Gillett calms all parties down.

Leeds are still pushing. Stach’s effort from eight yards out is closed down before Tanaka’s strike from the edge of the box is smothered by James.

Alonso goes into the book, apparently for straying too far outside of his technical area.

Chelsea 5 Leeds United 3 (Barco) Rogers lays on his fourth assist of the match, driving towards the byline before flashing a searching ball across the face of goal which Barco spears past Zetterer at the far post. That should be that, right?

Valentín Barco gets Chelsea a FIFTH! 🫨 pic.twitter.com/XnhgvhBpL9

Gudmundsson replaces debutant Bard down Leeds’ left.

Chelsea 4 Leeds United 3 (Calvert-Lewin) Game back on? Okafor is afforded far too much space down the left by a tiring Chelsea back line and his cross finds Calvert-Lewin who plants the ball past Penders to reduce the deficit to just one goal. What a tie this has turned into!

Leeds win a corner, which falls to Stach on the edge of the box but his effort is charged down.

It will be a source of acute anguish for Farke that Chelsea’s fourth goal came before he could make his four changes: Stach, Calvert-Lewin, Tanaka and Okafor eventually replace James, Nmecha, Longstaff and Aaronson. Conversely, it should be to Alonso’s credit that he took action early - his substitutes have decided this tie.

Chelsea 4 Leeds United 2 (Welbeck) Rogers gallops on to a simple ball down the right channel and his cutback (towards Palmer) is picked up by Welbeck who spins before firing beyond Zetterer, leaving three Leeds defenders sprawled in front of him. He cares not, and absorbs the love of the crowd in the near corner.

Class from Danny Welbeck 😤 pic.twitter.com/FUFKxlzXDz

Palmer goes close after having found a yard of space on the edge of the box. His strike spears through a thicket of limbs in Leeds’ box but Zetterer pulls off a strong save to deny the Englishman a quickfire hat-trick.

Chelsea 3 Leeds United 2 (Neto) Just 11 minutes after going 2-0 down, Chelsea find themselves ahead. Palmer threads a through-ball through the middle for Rogers, who slides in front of his marker to an open Neto who sweeps the ball beyond Zetterer. Leeds punished for leaving themselves two vs two at the back there.

"This is a comeback of comebacks!" Pedro Neto scores and Chelsea have turned it around eleven minutes after going 2-0 down! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/FTPuWcFqEX

Chelsea have got their tails up and Palmer almost lays on a go-ahead goal but James cannot turn in his cross from the left.

Chelsea 2 Leeds United 2 (Palmer) Wow! Palmer has turned this game on its head. And it’s so, so simple. Acheampong’s throw-in is knocked down by Rogers into the path of Palmer who works in from the right, passing the ball around a Leeds defender and past a rooted Zetterer.

TWO goals in TWO minutes for Cole Palmer and Chelsea are level! 🥶 pic.twitter.com/sgDd3YUgA6

Chelsea 1 Leeds United 2 (Palmer) Palmer makes no mistake. He goes right, and while Zetterer guesses the right way he cannot get there and Chelsea are back in business.

Cole Palmer pulls one back for Chelsea from the spot! 🎯 pic.twitter.com/BUv6h1wTPQ

Chavarria is caught by James in the box and the referee points to the spot. That came from nowhere.

Chelsea 0 Leeds United 2 (Aaronson) Amapadu deserves so much credit here. He steals the ball from Barco high, bursts beyond Rogers on the right and while Nmecha cannot turn in his cutback, Aaronson arrives late to stroke the ball past Penders and double Leeds’ lead.

"Chelsea cut apart AGAIN !" Brenden Aaronson makes it 2-0 to Leeds 🔥 pic.twitter.com/LlJNpqXHav

Alonso resolves he has seen enough and rings the changes at the interval. Palmer, Rogers, James and Neto enter the fray in place of Estevao, Watson, Gittens and Gusto.

Big cheers from the Chelsea fans at half-time, as Cole Palmer, Pedro Neto, Morgan Rogers and Reece James have all come on to warm up and are stripped off ready to play. Alonso is sending on the cavalry.

The delayed kick-off has knocked us out of kilter with tonight’s Champions League matches, but here are the live scores:

Liverpool 2 Atletico Madrid 1Paris St-Germain 4 Slovan 0Napoli 0 Arsenal 0Sporting CP 1 Galatasaray 1

Boos at half-time from the Chelsea fans. Their team were pretty awful, but booing so early in the season. Really?

There is only one minute of time added on and Watson earns himself a booking for a late challenge on Wilson before the half-time whistle is blown. It will be interesting to see how long Alonso waits before turning to his bench.

Justin, James and Wilson have got a lot of joy down Leeds’ right, rotating in Chavarria’s orbit. It has been difficult for Chelsea to pin them down and Gittens’ attacking threat has been blunted as he attempts to track their movements.

Better from Chelsea. Watson does well to regain possession high and Estevao takes over, darting towards the by-line. His cutback is directed towards Welbeck but he is beaten to the ball by a Leeds toe and it is played behind for a corner which comes to nothing.

Chelsea are really struggling to build up a head of steam, with individual mistakes proving costly.

Gittens and Estevao both end up on the left and the former works infield before firing a shot at Zetterer which the German parries behind for a corner. Perhaps Chelsea’s most dangerous moment of the half.

The corner is played short with the ball eventually falling to Barco on the edge of the box but his mis-hit effort trickles wide.

Gittens rescues an overhit Acheampong cross and finds Barco on the edge of the box, but the Argentine’s effort is charged down. Leeds spring a counter and their sweeping move up field earns them a corner.

Wilson floats another delivery to the back post to Muharemovic, but he cannot replicate his earlier goal.

Farke will be delighted with what he has seen so far. It is all well and good Chelsea allowing Leeds the ball, but they have to break incisively when openings arise, and they have not done that.

Big chance for Leeds! James bursts down the right and the Welsh winger dinks in a cross to the far post which Justin cannot get past Acheampong, but while Longstaff is first to the second ball, he can only sky the shot over the bar.

Leeds’ goal has stirred something inside them and they look motivated to score a second. Ampadu launches a long throw from the left which ricochets off a couple of players before rolling out for a Chelsea goal-kick.

Chelsea 0 Leeds United 1 (Muharemovic) Set-pieces have been a massive feature of Leeds’ game this season and here they take the lead with the simplest of corner routines. Wilson floats the ball to the back post where Muharemovic is waiting, unmarked, and he loops a header over Penders into the net. Such a shame for the Chelsea keeper as he had just pulled off a stunning double-save.

"The set-piece routine does it again!" Tarik Muharemović puts Leeds in front against Chelsea! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/UxeJ3xgL56

Barco slips on the far side and in doing so concedes a corner rather comically, to the delight of the travelling supporters. The delivery is met by Lacroix and Leeds are unable to create anything from the second phase of the set-piece.

There is an intriguing duel developing down Chelsea’s right as Bard looks to contain Estevao. The French wing-back has done a decent job so far.

Estevao attempts to free himself of Bard’s clutches and drifts inside, Chavarria then almost picks him out with a cross from the left but Leeds just about clear their lines.

Justin plays in a cultured through-ball from a wide-right position to James but Chavarria does well to snuff it out. Leeds are making the pitch as big as possible and spaces are beginning to open up as they did at Fulham on the opening weekend.

Although Penders’ shot-stopping has not yet been tested, he has shown some nifty footwork, sweeping up any loose balls that make it past Chelsea’s back three/five.

Big chance! Chelsea spring a surprise attack as Chavarria sets Gittens away down the left. He works the ball infield to Welbeck who lays on a great chance for Estevao but Justin darts back to take the ball off the Brazilian’s toes. A brilliant piece of last-ditch defending.

Gittens gets a shot away, a tame effort straight at Zetterer from 22 yards out as he cuts in from the left. The correct intent, though.

Leeds look to circulate the ball across their back line. As mentioned pre-match, Chelsea will not mind letting their opponents get on the ball as they set out-of-possession traps. Aaronson eventually dribbles off the pitch on the far side.

Chelsea’s Argentine midfielder, Valentin Barco, is being booed by the Leeds fans every time he touches the ball. Barco will already be used to getting that treatment, as it has even happened to him while he’s been a substitute this season.

In other news, there’s a real Borussia Dortmund vibe to this Leeds away kit.

Leeds supporters boo Argentina World Cup squad member Barco’s every touch, and another Leeds foul, this time Justin on Gittens, prompts a second Chelsea free-kick.

A couple of early touches for Watson who plays a neat pass around the corner. Ampadu then lands a late tackle on Lacroix and Chelsea earn a free-kick in their own half.

Although there are still some empty seats, we are finally under way. Chelsea in their customary all blue, kicking from right to left. Leeds in their yellow away strip.

Chelsea and Leeds emerge from the tunnel, led out by Colwill and former Chelsea defender Ampadu. Here’s a reminder of the teams in full:

Chelsea Penders; Gusto, Acheampong, Lacroix, Colwill, Chavarria; Watson, Barco; Estevao, Gittens; Welbeck

Substitutes Martinez, Hato, Fofana, James, Neto, Palmer, Quenda, Rogers, Pedro

Leeds United Zetterer; Justin, Bijol, Muharemovic; James, Ampadu, Longstaff, Bard; Wilson, Aaronson; Nmecha

Substitutes Trafford, Gudmundsson, Elvedi, Bogle, Tanaka, Stach, Okafor, Calvert-Lewin, Bahoya

Daniel Farke believes Leeds can go far in the Carabao Cup this year 💪 pic.twitter.com/26ueAAUHoZ

On the Brazilian winger’s opportunity tonight, Hasselbaink said on Sky Sports: “He has to find his place. This is his opportunity... It’s not really an out-and-out left-wing [position] or a No 10 as he can play, but [with] good players it doesn’t matter where you put them on the pitch. He will find his spaces and he will be direct as he was when he came in against Arsenal. He is going to play for his place because he wants to play week-in, week-out.”

As recently as March, a giant mural of Estêvão Willian appeared on the side of a building outside Stamford Bridge as the teenager threatened to become Chelsea’s number one poster boy.

He may no longer hold top billing outside the club, following a summer in which Chelsea spent a club-record £117m on Morgan Rogers to complete a fearsome front three alongside Cole Palmer and João Pedro.

A giant mural of the Brazilian teenager appeared on the side of a building close to Stamford Bridge in March.

But inside Stamford Bridge, nothing has changed. Estêvão remains one of Chelsea’s star boys and is part of an “untouchable” group of players that also includes Palmer, Rogers and Pedro. Sources believe Estêvão is a player the club will look at rewarding with an improved contract in the coming months.

Having already earned his Chelsea “untouchable” status, the next challenge for the 19-year-old winger – once nicknamed “Messinho” – is to make himself undroppable.

Estêvão may not be a perfect fit for Xabi Alonso’s three-at-the-back formation that features two 10s – Palmer and Rogers – behind a striker. But the boy from Brazil is certainly not being squeezed out and Chelsea’s manager has spoken of the need to be flexible.

Much has been made of Chelsea’s willingness to let the opposition have the ball under Xabi Alonso, but tonight they will likely be forced to dictate proceedings. In Leeds, they face one of only two sides who have completed fewer passes than them in the Premier League.

1. Ian Hamilton in 1967: 16 years, four months and 15 days2. Kingsley Whiffen in 1967: 16 years, five months and six days3. Reggie Walsh in 2025: 16 years, six months and 11 days4. Reggie Watson in 2026: 16 years, seven months and 14 days5. Tommy Langley in 1974: 16 years, nine months and one day

Asked how he will approach the Carabao Cup this season, Daniel Farke said: “We’ll try to win it. That’s the quickest way to Europe and to some glory. Of course knowing that the Premier League will always have the priority and knowing that we are as successful as possible there, especially to reach our first goal to establish ourselves [at] this level.

“We are not the favourites to win the Carabao Cup, we know this. Challenging, difficult games, but of course we travel to London in order to go through in the next round without doing anything stupid at this stage of the campaign because you also have to rotate a bit more and integrate a few new players. Nevertheless, we want to be at our best and anyhow possible we also want to go through to the next round.”

Tonight represents an opportunity for 16-year-old Reggie Watson to announce himself at senior level. The central-midfielder caught Alonso’s eye during pre-season when the Spaniard said of him: “Reggie Watson, a great midfielder. He thinks, he’s very collective, he’s very generous on the effort, intelligent with the ball”.

“For his age, I’m really impressed with him.”

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of tonight’s Carabao Cup third-round tie between Chelsea and Leeds United. This is a rematch of last season’s FA Cup semi-final which Chelsea edged by a single Enzo Fernández goal, but plenty has changed since then. Xabi Alonso has taken over the reins at Stamford Bridge and made a promising start, reeling off three wins before losing to Arsenal in an absorbing contest last Sunday. Chelsea are not involved in European competition this season, so the domestic cups represent an avenue to silverware, as well as an opportunity to tinker.

In Alonso’s way, though, stands a Leeds team whose manager, Daniel Farke, told the media on Tuesday that his side are aiming to win the Carabao Cup. Farke has overseen an impressive run of form, having lost only two of their previous 16 competitive matches in a stretch that extends back to March. Two wins at Nottingham Forest preceded draws against Brentford and Brighton to keep Leeds undefeated this term. Farke has suggested he will rotate in west London to “integrate new players” having brought in seven new recruits during the summer.

If Leeds are to reach the next round, they must reverse a heavily one-sided head-to-head record against their hosts, who have won each of their past 10 cup meetings (three in the League Cup, seven in the FA Cup). In fact, Chelsea have lost at this stage of the competition just once in the past 15 years, and that was against Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City four seasons ago.

Alonso broke up the exhilarating “JP Morgan” band (João Pedro, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers) for Chelsea’s victory over Luton Town in the previous round, handing starts to Danny Welbeck and Estêvão. Players such as Jamie Gittens and Geovany Quenda are also waiting in the wings and may get chances to impress tonight. Mike Penders could also be in line for a start between the sticks.

#1437. Why Enzo Maresca is sticking with 'awe-inspiring' Gianluigi Donnarumma despite Leipzig horror show, growing catalogue of errors and a worrying downward trend

Published: 12:00 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 07:07 EDT, 6 November 2026

There was a Manchester City fan on Thursday’s Ryanair flight back home from Leipzig wearing a Gianluigi Donnarumma sticker on his coat, portraying the Italian as Don Vito Corleone. The sticker, a bit worn and a bit crumpled, was peeling off. A metaphor exists within that somewhere.

Tough times for Donnarumma, a calamitous night in the Champions League – beaten at his near post by Ridle Baku's cross for one goal, fumbling another routine effort at the feet of a striker and allowing a straightforward shot to squirm through his fingers – just adding to the feeling that the past few weeks have not reflected kindly on him.

Question marks around Donnarumma’s suitability between the sticks are becoming more pronounced after a catalogue of mistakes this season. One against Paris Saint-Germain when Maghnes Akliouche’s shot was too hot (some would argue two after neglecting his near post for Desire Doue’s opener) and then Nicolas Jackson shooting through him at Aston Villa last month.

Each time, Enzo Maresca has publicly recognised the errors and intimated that nobody needs to rake over them in detail with his No1, who is experienced enough to know he must do better.

Now Leipzig. ‘It’s not a concern,’ Maresca said of the latest gaffe. The manager’s defences of Donnarumma are racking up and what City are witnessing is fundamental problems from somebody described as the best the world has to offer.

Maresca has rejected the idea that summer signing Geronimo Rulli, a 34-year-old Argentina international, could take over the gloves, claiming that City line-ups are always ‘Gigio plus 10’. Rulli understood his lot when joining from Marseille, to feature in domestic cup competitions, and was happy with that.

Gianluigi Donnarumma had a night to forget in Leipzig this week, making at least three individual errors

But Man City boss Enzo Maresca will stand by his goalkeeper, claiming that City line-ups are always ‘Gigio plus 10’

Happy in a way that James Trafford was not, after making it clear that one season as Donnarumma’s understudy was not palatable.

He has flourished at Leeds United so far this season, leading to some observers criticising Hugo Viana for letting him go, only to blunder for a goal at Bournemouth last weekend. Worth remembering that it does happen to all of them at some point.

Trafford did not appear ready for the big time last year when starting the season ahead of the wantaway Ederson and City had their eyes on Donnarumma months before landing him – a £26million deal struck just as Ederson left for Fenerbahce.

Trafford will be ready soon and is pushing Jordan Pickford hard to be England's No1, but definitely wasn’t back then.

With Trafford gone and Maresca seemingly ruling out his No2 taking over – while also making a vague reference to taking stock over the international break – it appears that City would have no option but to stick with Donnarumma if they did actually want to bring about a change. January signings seem remote in the current climate of guilty verdicts and appeals.

But there is something outstanding that Donnarumma does offer, one that does set him apart. Maresca categorised the stunning one-handed save from Leipzig’s Christoph Baumgartner as one nobody else could make.

And while some hyperbole might be at play there, very few could lay claim to producing that kind of moment on a semi-regular basis.

Repelling Baumgartner is up there with Donnarumma’s instinctive save from Bryan Mbeumo at a crucial juncture on debut last year and thwarting Alexis Mac Allister in a victory at Anfield. The sort of awe-inspiring saves thousands pay money to witness.

Very few goalkeepers can claim to make wonder-saves as regularly as Donnarumma does

Donnarumma's impressive shot-stopping in the Premier League is evidenced by this graphic of every shot he has faced since joining City (red circles = goals, blank circles = saves)

Nobody across the Premier League has a higher save percentage than Donnarumma’s 71.5 since his arrival from PSG. More scientifically, only Bart Verbruggen and Senne Lammens have prevented more goals in that time – a metric measured by the xG of shots compared to how many goals were conceded.

Donnarumma has prevented seven goals (1.4 this season), with Brighton’s Verbruggen at 9.7 and Manchester United's Lammens at 8.1 across the same period. These are broadly encouraging numbers for City, despite Donnarumma's save percentage dipping to 69.7 this season – eighth among his peers, with Trafford way out in front on 79.5.

City will need to keep a careful eye on that downward trend from a 27-year-old who they brought to the club to act as the anchor, to bail them out in a way that Ederson struggled. That was the trade-off for his limited footwork, being incapable of playing through the opposition lines in a way the Brazilian could.

The wonder saves cancel all of that out. Donnarumma has been the goalkeeper’s goalkeeper for those alone. But were the certainty around that aspect of his game to waver on a longer-term basis, City should have decisions to make.
