a, Correspondence between the GB cell-state annotations used in this study and the GB meta-modules defined by Neftel et al.10. Each malignant cell was scored for every Neftel meta-module by signature scoring on log-normalized RNA (excluding the cell-cycle modules G1/S and G2/M), and assigned to its highest-scoring module. Shown is the proportion of cells in each cell state that map to each Neftel et al. meta-module. b, Cell-state prediction accuracy of the classifier in Fig. 1b, trained on gene expression from a random 80% of 16,423 metacells (9,464 GB, 6,959 TME; 12 patients). Accuracy is shown for the held-out 20% (n = 3,285) using gene expression, and for all metacells using gene accessibility. Cell states are predicted less accurately from accessibility than from expression, most pronounced for malignant states, indicating elevated epigenetic plasticity. c, Uncertainty (entropy) of expression-based cell-state predictions per metacell (n = 16,423 metacells). Low uncertainty across all cell states confirms that expression profiles support confident state assignment. d, Evaluation of cell-state prediction accuracy of the cell-state classifier as in b, however trained on human neurodevelopmental cell types of a multi-ome brain atlas (12 donors; early fetal, late fetal and post-natal stages48), evaluated based on gene expression (held-out 20%; n = 512 metacells) and gene accessibility (n = 2,559 metacells). Cell-state predictions show comparable accuracy across modalities, except in progenitor populations. e, Epigenetic plasticity across neurodevelopmental metacells (n = 2,559), analysed as in Fig. 1c,d. Top: Epigenetic plasticity score (prediction entropy) across the cell types in d. Bottom: Percentage of cells from each expression-defined state (columns) assigned to each state from gene accessibility (rows). Off-diagonal values reflect accessibility compatible with several transcriptional states. As expected, radial glia and NPCs show the highest epigenetic plasticity (P = 7.5 × 10−59, two-sided t-test). f, Schematic of the canonical neurodevelopmental lineage relationships among the cell types analysed in d,e. Radial glia sit at the apex and give rise to three differentiation routes: Towards neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes, with plasticity decreasing along each route as cells mature. g, Global correlation between gene expression and accessibility in GB metacells (Pearson r across n = 21,369 genes), stratified by cell state. The concordance of correlation levels across GB cell states suggests that state-specific differences in epigenetic plasticity are not driven by differences in the global coupling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility. h, Average epigenetic plasticity per patient (n = 12) for the cell states in b, computed with the linear model of Fig. 1e after downsampling each state to equal cell numbers. Plasticity trends match those in Fig. 1e, indicating that the observed differences are not driven by variation in cell abundance. i, Average epigenetic plasticity score of GB states (n = 9) across patients. Although individual patients exhibit variation in plasticity across states, the average plasticity is comparable across patients (one-way ANOVA, P = 0.53). j, Donor-associated variation in epigenetic plasticity within defined cell neighbourhoods, shown as the ratio of the standard deviation of mean plasticity scores across donors to the standard deviation across all cells. Values were computed using k = 10 or k = 30 neighbours for each metacell (n = 4,813 and n = 11,868 metacells respectively), considering neighbourhoods represented by at least three donors, and stratified by state. Donor-associated variation was lower than overall local variation in plasticity across all malignant states. Box plots in c,e,g–j show median and IQR, 1.5 × IQR (whiskers), and outliers. Illustration in f created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Two-phase training scheme. Phase 1: Topic construction by joint training of the core autoencoder modules. scDORI embeds paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq profiles in a shared latent Topic space, from which three modules reconstruct the data. Module 1 maps Topic proportions to peak accessibility through a linear decoder with batch-specific adjustments. Module 2 predicts gene expression from the denoised Topic-specific accessibility of Module 1, using a learnable gene–peak linkage matrix restricted to a fixed genomic window around each gene. Module 3 reconstructs TF expression through Topic-TF weights. The three modules are trained jointly, minimizing the sum of their reconstruction losses together with regularization terms. Phase 2: Fine-tuning for eGRN inference. A fourth module infers Topic-specific TF–gene-regulatory links. In silico TF–peak binding scores, signed for activation or repression, are weighted by Topic-specific peak accessibility (Module 1) and propagated to target genes through the gene–peak links (Module 2). Learnable TF–gene-Topic weights adjust these links according to TF–target expression co-variation, and activating and repressive contributions are combined into a net regulatory score that predicts gene expression from Topic-level TF expression (Module 3). The encoder, gene–peak links, and Topic–peak decoder are optionally frozen during fine-tuning, with sparsity constraints on the learned TF–gene weights. b, Training runtime of scDORI as a function of dataset size, shown for Phase 1, Phase 2, and both phases combined, measured on subsampled multi-ome data from the GB atlas. Runtime scales to datasets of millions of cells. Empirical runtimes on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU (32 GB). c, Assessment of peak–gene link predictions in three cell lines (IMR90, K562, GM12878) of the published ENCODE dataset76,77, converted to semi-synthetic single-cell multi-ome data as in18 and scored against curated experimentally supported enhancer–gene links from BENGI33 as ground truth. Benchmarks span nine evidence x cell-line combinations available in BENGI, drawn from seven evidence sources derived from chromatin configuration, perturbation, and genomic interaction assays. AUPRC is shown for recovered peak–gene pairs with scDORI and SCENIC+. scDORI achieved higher AUPRC than SCENIC+ in all nine comparisons (P = 2.0 × 10−3, one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 9 paired comparisons). Illustration in a created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Average Topic activity in malignant and TME states. Extended version of Fig. 2c showing data for 31 Topics (all Topics with max activation > 0.1 across cells). Key biological functions of each Topic based on GSEA are shown. Raw values and complete pathway analysis are reported in Supplementary Table 2. b, Activity of GB-associated Topics in all cells visualized on the UMAP representation of Fig. 1a. State-specific, inter-state, and pan-state Topics are labelled accordingly. c, Activity of GB-associated Topics across patients. Shown is the number of patients with at least 1% of their cells exhibiting activity (>0.05) for each Topic. All GB Topics are active in at least 4 out of 12 patients, confirming that Topics capture universal regulatory programs of GB.

a, UMAP visualization of ATAC peaks in the patient atlas using Topic–peak scores (from scDORI Module 1) as embedding. (Left) Z-scored accessibility of peaks in each GB state. (Right) Topic–peak score for selected Topics. Topics identify distinct groups of co-accessible peaks within each GB state, reflecting different gene-regulatory programs active in those states. b, Genomic distance distributions between peak–gene pairs inferred by scDORI or MOFA29. For each peak in a MOFA factor, we picked the closest gene that was also part of the same factor. Red lines mark the cis-distance (150 kb) constraint applied to scDORI. Black lines indicate the ±1 Mb assessment window, and interchromosomal peak–gene pairs are shown separately on the left. c, Comparison of cell type prediction in our GB dataset using three latent space embeddings: scDORI (50 Topics), MOFA (50 factors), and SCENIC+ (AUCell-based TF activity scores from 195 TFs). Logistic regression models were trained to predict cell type labels from the latent embeddings of each method, using n = 9,464 GB and n = 6,959 TME metacells as input. scDORI achieved higher mean per-cell type accuracy (88.0%) than MOFA (80.3%; 17/17 cell types, P = 8 × 10−6) and SCENIC+ (85.2%; 11/17 cell types, P = 2.7 × 10−3), with the advantage over SCENIC+ concentrated in malignant states. P-values were obtained from a one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test. d, Stability of scDORI gene programs across random initializations. Shown is the Jaccard similarity between the top 500 genes of the most active Topic in each GB state, comparing the reference run (Run 0) against three additional runs trained with different random seeds. A randomized version of the reference Topic–gene set serves as a negative control. Gene programs are recovered consistently across runs. e, Activity patterns of selected scDORI Topics derived from our patient atlas projected onto a reference single-cell GB atlas from Neftel et al.10. Colour denotes average Topic activity, and bars on the left show the proportion of cells from each state in our atlas among the top 5,000 cells for each scDORI Topic. The mapping of scDORI Topics to GB cell states is highly concordant across datasets. f, Activity of selected scDORI Topics within malignant cells of the Neftel GB atlas in e, visualized on a UMAP embedding. Neftel state annotations and Leiden-clustered subpopulations are indicated. g, Performance of scDORI and SCENIC+ eGRNs in predicting DEGs between the Neftel GB cell states shown in e, following the GRaNPA21 framework. For each state pair a logistic regression model was trained to predict whether each gene is up- or downregulated based on the signed TF–gene links in each eGRN. Genes were split into four cross-validation folds, with test genes held out from training. AUPRC is shown for all state pairs. Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d. Both methods outperform randomized control eGRNs (P = 3.1 × 10−5 for each, one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 15 pairs) and perform comparably to each other. h, Performance of scDORI and SCENIC+ in predicting DEGs between the Leiden clusters shown in f, computed as in g. AUPRC is shown for every cluster pair, considering either scDORI or SCENIC+ eGRNs. Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d. Both methods outperform randomized control eGRNs (P = 4.4 × 10−19 and P = 4.3 × 10−19, respectively; one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 104 pairs).

a, Quality control of the gain-of-function screen described in Fig. 3. Shown are distributions of UMI counts, detected genes, and mitochondrial read fractions, stratified by seeding density (High: 14,000 cells/cm2; low: 9,000 cells/cm2) and biological replicate, separately for each PDGC line (S24, P3XX, and BG5). b, Cells recovered after quality control and barcode demultiplexing. Left: Relative contribution of each cell line, replicate, and seeding density to the total of 261,566 cells. Right: Fraction of cells recovered per TF perturbation, shown for the pooled dataset and for each patient line. TF representation is balanced across lines. n = 3 (BG5) and n = 6 (S24, P3XX). c, Expression bimodality coefficients (BC) of all screened TFs in OE and control cells from b. Each dot is a TF (n = 55). Violin centre line, median; error bars, extrema. Expression is bimodal (BC > 0.555) for every TF in the OE populations and for 54 of 55 TFs in the controls, reflecting heterogeneous expression of the targeted TFs and motivating exclusion of low- and high TF-expressing cells from respective populations in each OE-versus-control comparison. Inset: ASCL1 expression in control and ASCL1-overexpressing cells. d, Effect of the endogenous-expression filter on control cell heterogeneity in b. Each dot is one TF from the OE screen (n = 55), showing the change in state proportions (left) or in average entropy (right) after removing control cells with high endogenous expression of that TF (above the tenth percentile). Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d. Filtering left state heterogeneity essentially unchanged: change in entropy did not differ from zero (P = 0.14, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 220) and mean changes in individual state proportions were at most 0.025. e, Proportion of cells from each GB state in unperturbed control populations across pooled or individual PDGC lines in b. Total cell counts per condition indicated above. All GB states are, to varying degrees, represented in control cells across all lines. f, Validation of state regulator ranking by scDORI and SCENIC+. For each GB state, the average change in state probability (Δ state score, OE versus control) is shown for the top N predicted regulators of that state, with the average change in the remaining TFs (54 − N) plotted below for comparison. Shaded regions indicate s.d. intervals. Regulators nominated by scDORI induced their predicted state more strongly than those nominated by SCENIC+ (P = 8.2 × 10−10, one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 40 state × N combinations, scDORI higher in 34 of 40), most notably for the neuronal-like and AC-like states. g, Induction of Topic programs after gain-of-function of scDORI-predicted regulators of each Topic. For each top regulator (scDORI regulator score > 0.25), the change in activity of its predicted Topic is shown (Δ Topic score, OE vs. control). Dot size denotes the number of PDGC lines in which the effect was significant (label-permutation test, Benjamini–Hochberg FDR < 0.05) and colour denotes the scDORI regulator score. Regulators of nearly all Topics induced their predicted Topic program. All Topic-level effects per TF are provided in Supplementary Table 3. h, Concordance of Topic- and state-level effects after OE of scDORI-predicted regulators. Each point corresponds to one TF-Topic prediction, positioned by the change it induced in that Topic (x-axis) and in the corresponding state (y-axis), relative to control cells. TFs predicted to regulate several Topics appear once per Topic. Colour denotes the predicted Topic and dot style the significance category (label-permutation test, Benjamini–Hochberg FDR < 0.05). Most regulators induced Topic and state changes consistent with scDORI predictions (Supplementary Table 3). i, Number of DEGs per TF OE condition versus the number of OE cells, per cell line in b. The dashed line depicts a linear regression fit. DEG count scaled positively with the number of OE cells (Spearman r = 0.87, P = 1.9 × 10−50, n = 162 TF × cell-line conditions), reflecting increased statistical power with greater cell coverage. j, Number of upregulated and downregulated genes in TF-overexpressing cells relative to control cells in each PDGC line in b. Bars show the mean ± s.d. of each direction. n = 3 (BG5) and n = 6 (S24, P3XX). Top 100 DEGs per condition are reported in Supplementary Table 3.

a, Availability of TRs across GB states. Left: Schematic illustrating how a TR can be selectively expressed in its native Topic but epigenetically primed in cells of alternative states. Right: Mean chromatin accessibility (colour intensity) and mean expression (dot size) of indicated TRs across GB Topics. Bars on top indicate availability of TRs in Topics of alternative states, either by expression (scaled expression>0.5; purple) or epigenetic priming (scaled accessibility>0.5, scaled expression<0.3; green). b, Average expression (left) and chromatin accessibility (right) of the top TRs (activity score>0.05) of each target Topic within cells of each source Topic. TR expression is largely confined to Topics of the same GB state, whereas TR accessibility extends broadly to Topics of alternative states, indicating epigenetic priming for future activation. c, TAP between Topic pairs, scaled by the number of expressed TFs in the source Topic and by the weight of self-regulatory links in the target Topic. Asterisks denote significant links, defined as those exceeding the 95th percentile of a null distribution from 1,000 randomized GRNs (one-sided permutation test). OPC-NPC-like (25, 34) and AC-like (9, 44) tTopics show multiple strong links towards alternative state Topics, whereas links from neuronal-like Topics remain largely within their own state. Full list of TAP scores provided in Supplementary Table 4. d, Changes in TAP scores when using TR accessibility or expression in source Topic for computation. Positive values indicate TAP links mainly influenced by epigenetic priming of TRs, which encompass many of the links between different states. e, Number of top TRs from alternative states (activity score>0.5) that are epigenetically primed in each GB state. The epigenetic priming of alternative state TRs reflects transition potential patterns. f, Variance component analysis of TAP scores across Topic pairs. Each bar shows the proportion of variance explained by a single biological feature, fitted separately in an ordinary least squares model and stratified by whether the target Topic belongs to the same/related state (yellow; n = 77 Topic pairs), an alternative state (orange; n = 212), or any state (purple; n = 289). Regulatory links inferred from the eGRNs explain the largest share of TAP variance. For transitions towards alternative states, epigenetic priming of TRs contributes more than their expression level. g, TRS values between pairs of Topics. Neuronal-like Topics (24, 37) exert the highest repressive effects towards alternative state Topics. Asterisks label significant TRS links, estimated as in c. Full list of TRS values provided in Supplementary Table 4. h, Repression exerted by each source Topic towards the top 50 marker genes from each state identified by the linear model in Fig. 1b, instead of TRs. Similar to TR-level repression, neuronal-like Topics (24, 49) exert the strongest repression towards genes of alternative states. i, Cumulative repression exerted by individual source Topics towards genes of alternative Topics or states. Neuronal-like Topic 24 exerts the strongest repression against alternative identities. j,k, Net transition potential between Topics, as determined by the difference between TAP and TRS values between Topic pairs. Three distinct regulatory mechanisms underlie net transition potential interactions with alternative Topics: (i) predominant repression (Topic 24), (ii) predominant activation (Topics 9 and 34), and (iii) limited activation or repression (Topic 19). Raw values are provided in Supplementary Table 4. Illustration in a created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Schematic of dorsal telencephalon development, depicting neurogenic and gliogenic differentiation trajectories from radial glia towards differentiated neuronal and glial cell types. The shown differentiation hierarchy was reconstructed from available lineage-tracing studies49,50,51. NPC: Neural progenitor cell, OPC: Oligodendrocyte precursor cell, GPC: Glial progenitor cell. b, Activity of selected Topics inferred by scDORI from a developmental brain atlas (n = 12 donors)48. Colour denotes average Topic activity scaled across cell types of dorsal telencephalic origin, collected during early fetal, late fetal, and post-natal development stages. Topic-regulated programs are labelled on the right, determined based on Topic activity patterns, associated genes, and TF regulators. UL: Upper-layer, DL: Deep-layer. Full list of inferred Topics reported in Supplementary Table 5. c, TRs identified in developmental Topics in b recovered canonical lineage regulators, including PAX6 and GLI3 in radial glia114, SOX11 in fetal neurons115, CUX2 in UL neurons116, FOXP2 in DL neurons117, SOX9 in astrocytes118, OLIG1 in OPCs119, and MYRF in oligodendrocytes120, indicating high-confidence prediction of bona fide fate regulators. d, TAP, TRS and net transition potential (TAP–TRS) between pairs of developmental Topics in b. Shown are the respective values scaled by the number of TFs in the source Topic and self-activation in the target Topic. Asterisks denote significant links, defined as those exceeding the 95th percentile of a null distribution from 1,000 randomized GRNs (one-sided permutation test). Progenitor Topics show broad transition potential toward downstream lineages, whereas terminally differentiated cell type Topics show little or no transition potential towards alternative lineages, often constrained by repression. These results reflect the canonical differentiation hierarchy shown in a, as well as dedifferentiation potentials described for OPCs and astrocytes51,52, demonstrating that our transition model captures biologically coherent relationships. Illustration in a created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Schematic of the approach used to compute spatial co-activity of Topics across 97 matched tumour sections profiled by Visium spatial transcriptomics. For every section and Topic pair, the pairwise Euclidean distance between Topic A and Topic B spots is computed. Spatial co-activity is defined as the fraction of sections in which the closest 10% of spot pairs are spatially overlapping. Because spatial distance is symmetric by construction, net transition potentials (TAP–TRS) are symmetrized before row-wise Pearson correlation. b, Number of Visium sections and patients represented per Topic pair in the analysis described in a. All Topic pairs were covered by at least 20 sections derived from at least 7 patients, supporting the generalizability of the reported spatial co-activity patterns. Data are presented as mean ± s.d. c, Average spatial co-activity between Topic pairs computed as described in a (right), compared to their symmetric net transition potentials (left). Topic pairs with high net transition potential tend to be spatially co-active, as evidenced by row-wise correlations (Pearson r, right bar). Asterisks denote correlation P < 0.05. A full list of spatial co-activity values between Topics is provided in Supplementary Table 6. d, Schematic of how temporal co-activity of Topics was computed across pseudotime-aligned clonal trajectories. For each Topic pair, we averaged the cosine similarity of their temporal profiles across the top 10% of trajectories in which the two Topics were most temporally proximal, and compared the resulting matrix to net transition potential using column-wise (r1) and row-wise (r2) Pearson correlations, which capture incoming and outgoing transition relationships, respectively. e, Number of clonal populations per patient considered for the temporal analysis in d. A total of 57 clonal trajectories from all 12 patients were considered. f, Average temporal co-activity of Topics as described in d,e compared to net transition potentials (left). Topic pairs with high net transition potential tended to be temporally co-active for incoming and outgoing transitions, as evidenced by column-wise (top bar) and row-wise (right bar) correlations. Asterisks denote correlation P < 0.05. A full list of temporal co-activity values between Topics is provided in Supplementary Table 7. g, Correlation between Topic spatial co-activity and symmetric net transition potentials associated with each source Topic (n = 17). TAP and TRS values were computed using Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs, a union scDORI eGRN pooling links across Topics, SCENIC+ eGRNs, or random eGRNs. Dot colour represents the source Topic. Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs result in significantly higher correlation with spatial co-activity patterns than those derived using alternative GRNs (P = 0.0057 vs. Union; P = 0.0117 vs SCENIC+; paired two-sided t-test). h, Same as in g, but correlating temporal co-activity patterns in f and net transition potentials. Values denote the average between column-wise (incoming links, r1) and row-wise (outgoing links, r2) correlations for each Topic. Net transition potential values estimated with Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs positively correlated with temporal co-activity, significantly outperforming those derived from alternative methods (P = 0.0052 vs. Union; P = 0.0026 vs SCENIC+; paired two-sided t-test). i, Average epigenetic plasticity of cells in each Topic (as in Fig. 1c, top 5,000 cells per Topic) compared with (i) the cumulative net transition potential towards alternative state Topics (Topic-driven plasticity) and (ii) the total repression exerted by each Topic, both computed from Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs, a union scDORI eGRN pooling links across Topics, or SCENIC+ eGRNs. Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs best recapitulate observed epigenetic plasticity, with modelled plasticity and repression showing significant positive (r = 0.71, P = 0.002) and negative (r = −0.512, P = 0.036) correlations, respectively. Yellow boxes indicate P < 0.05. Box plots in g,h show median and IQR; whiskers are 1.5 × IQR. Illustrations in a,d created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Predicted regulatory roles of indicated neuronal-like TFs based on scDORI. Heat map colours indicate differences in the number of activated and repressed marker genes of each Topic (top 250). Dot size and colour denote TF-driven regulation of target TRs (TAP/TRS analysis, Supplementary Table 4). Repressors are predicted to broadly silence non-neuronal-like Topics, while activators selectively induce neuronal-like programs. b, OE levels of neuronal-like TFs in a at day 3 post-transduction in S24 PDGCs, quantified by qPCR, normalized to GFP vector controls (n = 3 independent transductions). Data are presented as mean ± s.d. c, Proportion of scDORI or SCENIC+ predicted target genes showing concordant changes in both ATAC-seq and RNA-seq after OE of neuronal-like TFs as in b. PBX1 and SOX4 were excluded because of insufficient changing gene sets (<500). Despite differences in regulon size across methods, the proportion of targets responding to perturbation was comparable. d, Percentage of target gene-regulatory directions accurately (green) or incorrectly (brown) predicted by scDORI or SCENIC+ based on gain-of-function perturbations in b. scDORI more accurately predicted regulatory directionality than SCENIC+, particularly for repressed targets. e, Percentage of Topic peaks (Topic-association score>0.95) opened after OE of neuronal-like TFs as in b, determined by ATAC-seq. Significance determined by one-sided hypergeometric test (BH-corrected FDR < 0.05). Only the pioneer TF ASCL1 induced a strong and significant increase in chromatin accessibility across neuronal-like and OPC-NPC-like Topic regions. f, Expression of top neuronal-like state regulators in GB states (left) and TME neurons (right) in our patient atlas. Dot colour and size indicate average expression and percentage of TF-expressing cells. MYT1L is the only TF exclusively expressed in neuronal-like GB cells at levels comparable to TME neurons. g, Genomic distribution of MYT1L-bound regions (n = 20,620) in S24 PDGCs determined by CUT&RUN after 8 days of MYT1L OE (n = 3) (top). Intensity of CUT&RUN peaks within ± 1 kb from peak summit in OE and control conditions (bottom). h, Differentially accessible regions (DARs) after MYT1L OE compared to control PDGCs in neurospheroid monoculture or co-culture with primary cortical cells (n = 3 each). Shown are the proportion of opening and closing regions, bound or not bound by MYT1L, and their genomic annotation. MYT1L predominantly closes chromatin by binding enhancer and promoter regions. i, Representative genome browser examples of MYT1L-bound TRs closed after MYT1L OE, as in b,g. j, Precision of MYT1L downstream target prediction, assessed at the level of target TFs and all target genes. Predicted MYT1L targets were derived from an average scDORI eGRN across neuronal-like Topics and compared against those of a SCENIC+ eGRN trained on neuronal-like cells. Blue boxes indicate the proportion of predicted targets directly bound by MYT1L (CUT&RUN as in g). Colours denote directional concordance with ATAC-seq and RNA-seq changes after MYT1L OE as in b. scDORI outperformed SCENIC+ in MYT1L regulon prediction, particularly at the TF level. Illustration in b created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Chromatin and transcriptional changes induced by primary cortical co-culture on S24 PDGCs compared to neurospheroid monoculture (n = 3 each). Enriched Topic programs in differentially accessible genes (DAGs; nearest gene to differentially accessible peak, FDR < 0.05) and DEGs (fold change>1.5, FDR < 0.05) as determined by GSEA, and the percentage of opening and closing Topic peaks (Topic-association score>0.95) are shown. Dot colour and size denote GSEA normalized enrichment score (NES) and significance, respectively. Asterisks indicate significant changes in Topic peaks (one-sided hypergeometric test, BH-corrected FDR < 0.05). Co-culture broadly opens chromatin across multiple Topic regions, consistent with a plasticity-promoting environment. b, MYT1L levels after Dox-based manipulation in S24 PDGCs co-cultured with primary cortical cells, in therapy-naive and therapy-exposed contexts. (Left) Normalized MYT1L counts from bulk RNA-seq during MYT1L induction (day 6, on) and after withdrawal (day 6 post-dox removal, off), compared to matched controls. (Right) MYT1L levels quantified by qPCR in PDGCs pre-exposed to ionizing radiation or temozolomide (TMZ), with and without MYT1L induction (day 6), compared to untreated controls. n = 3 biological replicates per condition, except for Dox control (n = 2). Data are presented as mean ± s.d. c, Average state association score of differentially closed and opened genes after MYT1L OE in S24 PDGCs with and without prior therapy exposure (ionizing radiation or temozolomide), as in b. Therapy-induced effects are shown below. Colour indicates z-scored state score. MYT1L represses non-neuronal-like gene signatures even under therapeutic pressure. d, Overlap of DAGs induced by MYT1L OE under therapeutic pressure with DAGs from MYT1L OE alone or treatment alone, all identified relative to untreated, unmanipulated controls as in b. Stacked bars show the proportion of closing (left) and opening (right) DAGs attributable to MYT1L OE alone, treatment alone, both, or neither. Most MYT1L-induced chromatin changes are preserved under both treatments, indicating that the plasticity-restricting function of MYT1L is largely retained under therapeutic pressure. e, Chromatin changes in Topic-associated regions and genes after MYT1L OE in therapy-exposed PDGCs in b, computed as in a with respect to untreated, unmanipulated controls. MYT1L-driven effects (Fig. 5f) are conserved under therapeutic pressure, albeit modestly attenuated. f, Representative western blots of MYT1L protein levels in S24 (n = 6 independent experiments, P = 1.8 × 10−6 OE vs control) and P3XX PDGCs (n = 5 independent experiments, P = 0.035 OE vs control), 7 days after MYT1L OE compared to controls, with fold-change quantifications. Uncropped Western blots are shown in Supplementary Fig. 2. (Bottom) MYT1L expression by qPCR 3 weeks after MYT1L knockout (KO) in BG5 PDGCs compared to controls (n = 3 independent experiments, P = 0.072 KO vs control). Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d.; two-sided t-test. g, Enriched Topic signatures in DEGs of MYT1L OE (S24, P3XX) or KO (BG5) compared to controls (n = 3 each), 3 weeks post-transduction, as determined by GSEA. Dot colour and size denote NES and significance, respectively. Neuronal-like identity is enriched after OE and depleted after KO. h, Selected pathways enriched after indicated MYT1L manipulations by GSEA. Dot colour and size denote NES and significance, respectively. All significantly enriched pathways are reported in Supplementary Table 10. MYT1L gain-of-function upregulates neuronal and synapse-related pathways, whereas loss of function upregulates stem cell pathways. i, Morphological changes after MYT1L OE in S24 PDGCs in neural microenvironments. (Left) Representative images of PDGC morphology in co-culture with primary hippocampal neurons (day 7; representative of ROIs quantified at right) and in mouse cortex xenografts (two-photon live imaging, 21 days post-injection; 6 z-stacked regions per mouse, n = 3 MYT1L OE and n = 2 control mice). (Right) Quantification of primary branches and total neurite-like projections from in vitro co-culture experiments (n = 16 control vs n = 17 MYT1L OE ROIs with 7–10 quantified cells per ROI; n = 3 independent experiments). MYT1L OE significantly increases the number and complexity of neurite-like projections. Data shown as mean ± s.d.; P-values for two-sided t-test are shown. Scale bar=100 µm. j, Tumour microtube (TM) interconnectivity in S24 PDGCs monocultures after MYT1L OE (n = 48 control vs. n = 37 MYT1L OE ROIs; n = 3 independent experiments) or knockdown (KD) (n = 47 control vs n = 44 MYT1L KD ROIs; n = 3 independent experiments). MYT1L OE reduced, and KD increased average TM length, yielding fewer and more connected morphologies, respectively. (Right) Total cell counts per ROI confirm comparable cell numbers across conditions. Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d.; P-values for two-sided t-test are shown. Scale bar=200 µm. k, Proliferation time-course of PDGCs after MYT1L OE (S24; n = 5 independent experiments x 10 wells each) or KO (BG5; n = 3 independent experiments x 30 wells each) determined by Alamar Blue assay, normalized to day 0. MYT1L OE and KO significantly reduce and increase proliferation, respectively. Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d.; P-values from two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test are shown. l, Representative fluorescent microscopy images of tdTomato-labelled S24 PDGC spheroids transduced with Dox-inducible constructs of full-length MYT1L (left), MYT1L DBD fused with a VP64 activator domain (centre), or MYT1L DBD fused with an EnR repressor domain (right). Images of uninduced and dox-induced spheroids were taken on day 7 after embedding and binarized based on intensity. Dashed lines delineate spheroid size at day 0. Total number of spheroids and corresponding growth quantifications are shown in Fig. 5h. Scale bar=1,000 µm. m, Fold change in proliferation of S24 PDGCs after 7 days of OE of the indicated MYT1L constructs in l, normalized to uninduced controls. Full-length MYT1L and DBD–EnR reduced proliferation, while DBD–VP64 enhanced it. n = 8 wells x 3 independent experiments; Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d.; P-values for two-sided t-test against uninduced controls are shown. Illustrations in b,e,i,j created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Schematic of MEOX2 manipulation in S24 PDGCs co-cultured with primary cortical cells. MEOX2 OE was induced by Dox addition (MEOX2 on) and subsequently removed after Dox removal (MEOX2 off). b, MEOX2 expression levels after Dox-based manipulation in PDGCs as described in a. Normalized MEOX2 counts in bulk RNA-seq data of PDGCs 6 days after MEOX2 induction and 6 days after MEOX2 removal, compared to controls at equivalent time points (n = 3 each, except Dox+ control n = 2). Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d.; P-values for one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test are shown. c, Chromatin-accessibility effects of MEOX2 induction and withdrawal in co-cultured S24 PDGCs as in b. Enriched Topic programs in DAGs (nearest gene to differentially accessible peak, FDR < 0.05) as determined by GSEA and the percentage of Topic peaks (>0.95 Topic-association score) opening and closing are shown. Dot colour and size denote GSEA NES and significance, respectively. Asterisks indicate significant changes in Topic-associated peaks (one-sided hypergeometric test; BH-corrected FDR<0.05). MEOX2 induces broad chromatin opening that is retained after withdrawal. d, Pseudotime-ordering of two clonal trajectories depicting transitions from neuronal-like cells toward AC-like or OPC-NPC-like states (n = 3109 and n = 5804 cells each). Trajectories are divided into stages defined by distinct Topic activation patterns: Stage 1, neuronal-like Topics; Stage 2, neuronal-like transition Topics; Stages 3–4, alternative state Topics. White lines demarcate stage boundaries. Average chromatin accessibility and expression of TFs active in cells of each stage are shown along the pseudotime axis. Links going in the opposite direction to the trajectory are shaded. Stage 1 is dominated by repressive links targeting alternative state TFs, which are progressively lost as the trajectory advances. f, Repressive effects from TFs in each Topic towards top repressors in neuronal-like Topics. TFs active in non-neuronal-like Topics broadly repress neuronal-like safeguard repressors. Illustration in a created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

#1400. Man United's secret plot to poach Sir Alex Ferguson from Aberdeen, 40 years on - from phone calls with a fake Scottish accent to clandestine meetings at M74 services on Bonfire Night

Published: 04:53 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 08:07 EDT, 6 November 2026

It is 40 years ago today since Manchester United appointed Sir Alex Ferguson as manager and ushered in the most successful era in the history of the club.

The parallels with the current situation at Old Trafford are striking. United have made their worst start to a league season since then, with just one win from their opening nine games, and Michael Carrick is fighting to save his job, just as Ron Atkinson was on the brink in November 1986.

United had rejected Big Ron’s offer to resign towards the end of the previous season. However, with the team only staying out of the relegation zone on goal difference, the club decided to sack him following a 4-1 League Cup defeat by Southampton.

Atkinson felt the seeds of a decision that would change the course of United’s history had been sown a few months earlier when he was working as a TV pundit at the World Cup in Mexico and Aberdeen boss Ferguson was in temporary charge of Scotland, following the sudden death of Jock Stein.

‘Lawrie McMenemy, also on the World Cup beat as a TV pundit, revealed he had heard Alex Ferguson had already been tapped up for my job,’ Atkinson later wrote in his autobiography.

‘I haven’t lost any sleep about the shenanigans surrounding my premature departure. I don’t blame Alex one bit. It’s all part of the management game. Somebody is inevitably waiting to nick your boots in this business.’

It is 40 years since Manchester United secretively lured Sir Alex Ferguson from Aberdeen

Club director Mike Edelson put on a fake Scottish accent to get through to Ferguson's office at Aberdeen, posing as Gordon Strachan's assistant

Atkinson’s suspicions were founded on a conversation between Ferguson and United director Sir Bobby Charlton in Mexico. Ferguson confirmed the chat, but disputes its significance.

‘That’s not true,’ Ferguson wrote, addressing Atkinson’s claim in his book Managing My Life. ‘Although Bobby did speak to me at the side of the pitch before Scotland’s fiasco of a game in Uruguay, the furthest he went was to ask that if I ever decided to move to England, I should let him know. I don’t think that could be considered an offer.

‘Apart from the brief contact with Bobby, there was nothing but rumour to link me with Old Trafford before November 5.’

Charlton’s recollection also suggests it was incidental. ‘I was working for the BBC and I went to watch Scotland train,’ he told Daily Mail Sport in 2011. ‘He saw me through the fence and came over to say hello. We only spoke for a minute or so, but I liked him.

‘I also recall going to Aberdeen once, to open a garage of all things. The people there were panicking. “You’re not here to take our manager, are you?” The whole city seemed to be in love with him. I stored that away, too.’

Atkinson viewed Charlton as an adversary in the boardroom. When he returned from Mexico keen to complete the signing of England centre back Terry Butcher from Ipswich, using money earmarked from the £2.3million sale of Mark Hughes to Barcelona, Charlton was the main opponent to the move.

Chairman Martin Edwards pulled the plug citing a lack of funds due, in part, to building a new museum at Old Trafford. ‘We’ll bring the museum up for a corner then!’ Atkinson replied.

Having decided a change of manager was needed, United favoured Ferguson over Terry Venables, but were anxious to make sure the 44-year-old wanted the job having drawn a blank with McMenemy, Bobby Robson and Ron Saunders before appointing Atkinson five years earlier.

Club director Martin Edwards spoke with Fergson and met him with a secret delegation at M74 services in Lanarkshire

Ferguson pictured with Graham Hogg (right) in his first week of training at Man United

Edwards, Charlton and fellow directors Mike Edelson and Maurice Watkins hatched a bold plan to get through to Ferguson’s office at Aberdeen by posing as Gordon Strachan’s accountant.

Edelson, who put on a Scottish accent to make the call, said: ‘It suddenly got very embarrassing when the receptionist started asking me personal questions about how my wife was. The other three were rolling around. But she put me through, Alex answered, I quickly explained who I really was and then put him on to Martin.’

Ferguson recalled taking the call in his office. ‘Martin Edwards gave me his number so I could ring him back and thus be assured of the authenticity of the call. I could scarcely contain myself as I dialled the Manchester number. Would I be interested in the job at Man United? Yes, I told him without hesitation.’

Ferguson immediately told his No 2 Archie Knox, but admitted that when he told his wife Cathy she was ‘devastated’ because the family were happy in Aberdeen.

It was her reluctance to move to London that had previously persuaded him to reject Arsenal and Tottenham but this time the opportunity was too good to refuse.

Ferguson arranged to meet the four-man delegation from United at 7pm that night at Hamilton Services on the M74 in Lanarkshire, where they would recognise each other using their car registrations. ‘It really was a case of flashing headlights,’ said Edelson.

Edwards got into Ferguson’s car and the others followed to the home of Cathy’s sister Bridget in the Bishopbriggs suburb of Glasgow.

Ferguson revealed he was offered a ‘disappointing’ salary that was less than he earned in Scotland and had no transfer budget. United also refused his request to buy the family home to ensure a quick sale, or pay back a £40,000 loan from Aberdeen, but he accepted the job anyway.

Ferguson surrounded by photographers in his first game in charge - they lost 2-0 against Oxford United at the Manor Ground

He became the most successful manager in English football history, winning 13 Premier League titles

United’s directors drove back to Manchester that night and Edwards sacked Atkinson at 10.30am on the morning of November 6. Edwards then caught a 2pm flight to Aberdeen with Watkins, who was also United’s solicitor, to conclude the deal with Aberdeen chairman Dick Donald.

Meanwhile, Atkinson was clearing his desk and saying his goodbyes at United before organising a farewell drinks party at his home in Rochdale which was attended by a number of United stars and went on a lot longer than planned.

‘It turned into an all-night rave with more than a hundred people packed into the house and lasted until 5am,’ Atkinson recalled.

There were a few sore heads when a nervous Ferguson gathered the players together on November 7. He was well aware of the drinking culture at Old Trafford and what he felt was Atkinson’s liberal attitude, based on information fed to him by Strachan, who had left Aberdeen for United two years earlier.

‘He cited all sorts of problems with the team, particularly the drinking and the alleged indifference of Big Ron to its damaging effects,’ Ferguson wrote.

‘The training, Gordon suggested, was a shambles, with nothing done until Ron had a session on his sunbed as a preliminary to joining in a small-sided practice game.’

Clamping down on the boozing was one of the first items on Ferguson’s agenda, but not before he banished bus driver Derek Sutton from sitting on the bench following his first game at Oxford 48 hours after being appointed.

It ended with a 2-0 defeat followed by a goalless draw at Norwich as Ferguson made an inauspicious start to a glittering career spanning 26-and-a-half years. His first game at Old Trafford brought a first win, beating QPR 1-0.

In a new book, Fergie: The Lost Tapes, author Wayne Barton has gone through 400 hours of recordings and unearthed a long-forgotten address by the new manager to United fans that day which has echoes of the farewell speech he made on the pitch in 2013.

‘Hello, Alex Ferguson here. I don’t need to tell you how important this day is to me. This is the greatest experience of my life, to be in front of this platform and this stage.

‘Since I’ve arrived here, I’ve been so aware of the traditions and success of this great club. My job is to make sure that success continues and to make us the greatest club in Britain.

‘The real supporters of Manchester United are the greatest in the world - don’t let anyone forget it.’

#1399. Thomas Tuchel faces fight to win trust of England players

Thomas Tuchel faces a fight to regain the full trust of his England players, despite claiming that “99.9 per cent” of supporters do not talk about the semi-final defeat by Argentina.

Telegraph Sport reported that players were shocked and disappointed by Tuchel’s approach to the final 30 minutes of the World Cup semi-final.

It can now be revealed that doubts linger among England players over Tuchel’s ability to get the best out of his squad and ultimately lead them to glory in the next European Championship.

There is also some lasting unhappiness over Tuchel’s perceived unwillingness to take ultimate responsibility for England’s World Cup exit and his claim that ball possession was not in “the DNA” of the nation’s players.

Tuchel has spoken of fostering a “brotherhood” within the England squad, but a source told Telegraph Sport: “He still has work to do to get all the players fully behind him again. What happened at the World Cup and some of his comments caused some damage that has not just disappeared.”

Tuchel has no concerns over the commitment of his players and said: “I have no doubt how keen they are. No doubt. I know them, I was seven weeks with them. We had a qualification campaign together, we are 18 months together, I have no doubt that we step up and produce performances in the next cycle. I’m responsible for that.”

One player who did not travel to the World Cup and is not part of Tuchel’s latest England squad for four Nations League games is Morgan Gibbs-White. His partner, Britney De Villiers, took a swipe at Tuchel by posting an image on Instagram that referenced the fact the Nottingham Forest man is the only Premier League player to have created five or more chances in every match he has played this season.

There is no immediate sign that Tuchel is ready to change his approach, as he refused to accept the country were angered by his tactics and substitutions in the Argentina game.

In an attempt to gloss over the nature of England’s missed opportunity in the United States, Tuchel claimed that the bronze-medal victory over France was “one of the nicest experiences ever” for supporters and that he did not lose any sleep over his World Cup squad selection.

Tuchel’s defence of the World Cup campaign also included the revelation that his Football Association bosses had assured the England head coach that his job was safe before the last-16 victory over Mexico.

“I tell you something, like 99.9 per cent of the fans don’t speak about substitutions, tactical twists,” Tuchel said. “They speak about where they have watched the Mexico game, they speak about the second half, the energy of the Croatia match, they speak about how nerve-wracking it was to watch our match against Congo and where they celebrated.

“This is how it should be, this is what a World Cup is for, to connect with the people and to give them experiences that they will not forget. And this is the feedback that I get.”

Asked if he had received any negative feedback at all since the World Cup, Tuchel answered: “No. Not at all. Do you think that’s necessary? I had some quite bad stuff between Argentina and France. [But] No [not since I’ve been back in England].”

The FA publicly backed Tuchel after the defeat by Argentina, but the German has now revealed that he was privately told his job was safe well before that.

Even if England had lost to Mexico and failed to reach the last eight of the World Cup, Tuchel has claimed he would not have been sacked. He said: “There was a moment, a very special moment, before the Mexico game where we had a talk and my bosses told me ‘we know that anything can happen in a football match, we know that anything can happen in a match in Mexico, in a World Cup match, but don’t worry, we see what’s going on and we want to continue like this’.

“It was a beautiful moment for me as a coach. I felt this kind of freedom to take my choices and to just coach freely, and there was never a doubt in my mind that we would continue together and there was obviously never a doubt in their mind.”

England secured their best World Cup finish since 1966 by winning the bronze-medal game against France in a chaotic match in Miami.

“If you look at the 6-4 against France, people talk about it like it’s one of their nicest experiences ever, to watch a football match,” Tuchel said. “So maybe I have to compromise in my wish for control, for a little bit more chaos, embrace the chaos, and maybe it brings out the best.”

Tuchel has named his first England squad since the World Cup for four Nations League games against Spain, Czech Republic (home and away) and Croatia. He has recalled Cole Palmer and Trent Alexander-Arnold to his squad, but insists he has lost no sleep over not taking the pair to the World Cup.

“I was very happy with the [World Cup] squad selection, we put a lot of effort and emphasis into the squad selection,” Tuchel said. “And I had a lot of sleepless nights, but I had not one sleepless night about our selection, because I was more than seven weeks with this group of players, and they were nothing but fantastic. I think the spirit that we built and the mentality that we showed brought us to the place that we got.

“It feels unfulfilled, but, yeah, that’s how it is. We need to move forward with the decisions in the Argentina game. And sometimes as a coach, you can only win if you win. So now we know the result, and we didn’t win. Of course, I reflect and, of course, I’m very critical of myself. But the question that is also still lingering around is, who knows what would have happened? Who knows if we hadn’t made any substitutions what would have happened? And would we have the same sleepless nights?

“So, there’s not much sense in torturing ourselves, looking back. It’s moving forward, but the team, like I said, did brilliantly. And I will not allow 30 minutes against Argentina to override how we view this World Cup.”

Tuchel had warnings for Palmer and Alexander-Arnold, as he said: “It is one thing to be nominated, by the way, with Cole and getting your ticket back in the squad, but it’s another thing to play and keep your place. It’s about when he comes and he needs to show these kinds of performances.”

On Alexander-Arnold, Tuchel added: “Now it’s time to fight for his place. He always said he’s up for a fight, especially for England. So it’s a need to prove that.”

Tuchel said that Alexander-Arnold has been called up as a right-back, rather than a midfielder. Asked if the Real Madrid player offers enough defensively, he answered by saying: “He has to, he has to. It’s necessary. My conviction is that he will, but he has no choice.”

Tuchel has now finished his broadcast duties. It was quite a strange performance from him. I don’t recall ever seeing him read from notes before. His little joke about his bosses telling him off was awkward and felt rehearsed, and the stuff about 99.9 per cent of England fans talking about Mexico and the second half against Croatia was delusional.

It was also jarring to hear him claim that the FA had basically assured Tuchel that his job was safe straight after England beat Mexico. It was a special night, undoubtedly, but did it really deserve that sort of reaction?

“I wanted to give Jarrad a chance. It was a 51 per cent decision on Jarrad.

“I don’t have a clear picture on what he is all about and have a very clear picture on what Levi can bring us.”

“It makes no sense to nominate three, four, five number 10s. It just does not help anyone. We can see the form that Morgan [Gibbs-White] is in.

“It’s one thing to be nominated, but it’s another thing to perform. This also counts, especially Cole needs to step up to justify the nomination.”

“The minimum I can do is back my bosses. They have my full support on that.

“I’m grateful that I can talk about football because that’s my little bit of knowledge, not sports politics.”

“That’s the beauty of high-level sport, you can’t always win and it makes you feel alive. Not in a very nice way, still you feel that pain of these high-pressure moments.

“As soon as you enter knockout football, it’s a new level of pressure.”

Tuchel has now claimed that people say the 6-4 against France is “maybe one of their best experiences (watching football) ever”.

Again, not something anyone has said to me. Where is Tuchel finding these people?!

Tuchel on Alexander-Arnold: “He comes as a right back.” Sounds like he agrees with Mourinho that the Real Madrid player is not a midfielder.

Tuchel: “There was never a doubt in my mind that we would continue together and there was obviously never a doubt in their (the FA’s) mind.”

Tuchel says that 99.9 per cent of fans don’t talk about substitutions. He says they speak about the Mexico game and the Croatia game, their emotions and where they watched the matches.

FA technical director John McDermott, who has taken a position at the back of the room to listen, had a little laugh when Tuchel joked that he got told off in his FA review for “my substitutions.”

Tuchel says he felt the “full support from my bosses”.

Warning for Palmer: “It’s one thing to get your ticket back, but it’s another thing to keep it.”

He’s expecting Palmer to step up and show him his Chelsea form.

“When you are a coach, you only win when you win...There’s not much sense torturing ourselves by looking back. I will not allow 30 minutes of the World Cup to determine how we view the World Cup.”

Tuchel says he has no regrets over not taking Palmer and Alexander-Arnold to the World Cup. He says he didn’t have a single sleepless night over his squad selection.

Tuchel says the direction in sports is always forwards and never backwards. “The target is to win the home Euros, of course.”

Tuchel says his feelings on the World Cup are mixed. He thinks there are very positive things to take from the World Cup, but says it was also unfulfilled. He says it’s important to recognise that England won a bronze medal, but says he acknowledges they did not push it over the line.

He says the downside of having the belief they could go and win it is that it hurts even more that they did not.

Tuchel has said the France third-place game “directs the narrative” of what’s coming for England.

Tuchel will be happy with this so far. Very gentle start from the broadcasters.

We will be hearing from Tuchel very soon. Lots to discuss but the Palmer and Alexander-Arnold call-ups and his World Cup reflections are at the top of the list.

#1397. Bloodthirsty Brighton feast on rattled Arsenal

Overpowered and overrun, Arsenal were subjected to the sort of gruelling treatment they usually inflict on their opponents. Mikel Arteta’s side did not look anything like Premier League champions here, as Brighton and Hove Albion produced a stunning performance full of swarming energy and breathless bravery.

In the biggest test of their season so far, Arsenal fell woefully short of the standards they have set themselves over the past few campaigns. This sort of thing simply does not happen to Arteta’s side. Well, it did not happen. Not before this monstering on the south coast, where the Brighton fans were whipped into a frenzy by the brilliance of Fabian Hürzeler’s players.

Brighton were everything that Arsenal are expected to be: aggressive, inventive and dominant across the field. They even scored with a set-piece, as one of Arsenal’s great strengths became a sudden weakness. Everywhere Arteta looked, the foundational truths of his team were being shaken by a Brighton storm. It was their first defeat by a three-goal margin since May 2023, also against Brighton.

Remarkably, this is now the third consecutive season in which Brighton have beaten the reigning Premier League champions. They are rarely happier than when they are on the hunt against more illustrious opponents, working as a team to snap at heels and then attacking in numbers. They are known as the Seagulls, but they played more like a pack of bloodthirsty wolves. The ferocity of their off-the-ball work, especially in the first half, was extraordinary.

Not for a long time have Arsenal been as rattled as they were here. David Raya misplaced passes, Gabriel Magalhães lost duels and Bruno Guimarães chased the ball in vain. It was Brighton’s Pascal Gross, rather than Arsenal’s Martin Odegaard, who shaped the game in midfield. It was Brighton’s Charalampos Kostoulas, rather than Arsenal’s Kai Havertz, who offered incisive class in attack.

Gross and Kostoulas both struck from range in a one-sided first half, before Chema Andrés added the third after the break. At half-time, Arteta had sprinted down the tunnel towards the dressing room. Whatever messages he gave to his players, they either did not sink in or did not work. By the end, Arsenal were lucky the scoreline was not even more humiliating.

Arteta’s players had come through some tricky assignments in winning their first seven matches of this season, but this was their toughest test yet and they failed it badly. They did not handle the emotions of the occasion particularly well, either: in stoppage time, a frustrated Declan Rice kicked out at Malick Yalcouyé. He was perhaps fortunate to avoid a red card.

It was the first time that Rice and Guimarães had started alongside each other for Arsenal and it quickly became clear that their £180m partnership will need some work. Arsenal would have hoped their experience in the Premier League would allow for an instant connection but, evidently, that is not the case. Guimarães was hooked after 60 minutes, but might easily have been removed at the break.

Both managers had a similar assessment of the match and how it was won: Brighton did the basics far better than Arsenal. “How we wanted to approach this game was getting into it through small wins,” Hürzeler said. “Everyone speaks about a goal or chance as a win, but a small win can be the first throw-in, the first corner, win the first header, win the first tackle. These small things. If you win these small steps, and celebrate them as a win, then you can gain bigger and bigger wins.”

It was typical of Brighton that one of their new signings produced an excellent performance in midfield. Andrés, a 21-year-old Spaniard signed from Stuttgart at the end of the transfer window, looks to be the latest gem identified by their data-led recruitment model. No one inside the Amex Stadium was thinking about Carlos Baleba, sold to Manchester United, when Andrés made his tackles and won his headers.

Another new signing, centre-back Luka Vuskovic, was similarly impressive at the back. Signed for £46m from Tottenham Hotspur, Vuskovic looks more than capable of going to the top of the game.

This was perhaps the first occasion this season in which Arsenal missed William Saliba, the injured centre-back who has been so fundamental to their success in recent years. The Frenchman can always be relied on to provide calmness and composure at the back, even under intense pressure. Without him, Arsenal were uncharacteristically jittery.

“The amount of technical errors we did in our own half...” Arteta bemoaned. “We didn’t respect any principle of play that you have to get out of those man-to-man situations. That put us always on the back foot.”

Gross, who at 35 is playing as well as ever, opened the scoring with a low shot from range after 31 minutes. Kostoulas then struck the second, from a similar distance, after some end-to-end action resulted in Arsenal’s midfield and defence melting away. The third was the most simple, as Andrés headed in at the back post from an inswinging corner.

Arsenal did have some chances, with Havertz missing the best of them, but there was never a sense that Brighton were vulnerable. The pressure on the home side was never sustained. For Arteta, who now has an extended international break in which to ruminate on this defeat, it all made for an unfamiliar and unexpected pain.

Mikel Arteta said his Arsenal players failed to “respect the game” as their perfect start to the season was ended in stunning style by a brilliant Brighton performance.

Arsenal’s capitulation on the south coast led to their first defeat of the campaign and Arteta admitted that Brighton had a different “edge” and “bite” throughout the match. The Arsenal manager also said the 3-0 loss represented a “big lesson” for his players.

“There are certain basics you need to accomplish in football, especially in the Premier League, that we were very far from,” Arteta said. “From the first throw-in you could sense it, it was so clear.

“It was a really disappointing result and performance. Brighton were another gear up from us. We were extremely poor technically and were not respecting the game.

“It is not going to take away what the team has done in the last six or seven weeks since coming back from the World Cup. What we have done and the way we have competed, and the amount of games we have won, has been remarkable. But this is a big lesson for all of us to understand what it takes to win at this level.”

Arteta added that his team did not “respect the principles of play” that were required against Brighton’s intense pressing, and also said his players were guilty of numerous technical errors.

“Credit to Brighton for what they have done because they have overcome us and they had another edge,” Arteta said. “There are a lot of moments when the ball is 50/50 and it changes hands and most of the time it was for them.”

Brighton are the Premier League’s top scorers this season with 16 goals in five matches so far, and this emphatic victory took them up to third place in the table.

“It was a special win,” Fabian Hürzeler, the Brighton head coach, said. “Not only because we played the best team in England but because of the performance. I am really proud of my team. It’s always important to enjoy these moments. We were horrible to play against. My players really trust each other on the pitch.”

Two things, one give credit to them. In the manner that they played and committed to every single action. We were below the standards that are required for us but in the Premier League as well.

When you miss chances like we did it becomes impossible. I want to congratulate Brighton for what they’ve done. It’s a big lesson for us to learn. If I have to describe how the team has played and competed in the last six or seven weeks, has been expectational but today has been a big lesson.

A very disappointing result and performance. Full credit to Brighton the manner they went about the game, they were a different gear from us. We didn’t do the basics right for long periods, especially in the first half. We didn’t win enough duels, and any second balls and that stretches you.

We were poor technically when we had the ball in our own half, we didn’t apply the principles that you need against a team that wants to press you man to man.

Arteta: "There are certain basics that you need to accomplish in the Premier League that we were very far from. The amount of technical errors we did... we didn't respect any principle of play. We were always on the back foot. They had another edge."

Beating the current champions and maybe the best team in England is something special. The result is nice but the performance is what makes it special, the boys showed real courage, real intensity and they were horrible to play against because we did the basics right.

Intensity, intensity, winning the personal duels...we have to have the belief to compete with the best teams in the league. My players really trust each other on the pitch. If one player is out then another can replace him.

Overall we wanted to be really good in every phase. We needed to be at the highest level. We go game by game. After the international break we have a lot of games. After wins like this we have to stay humble and understand why we had this win. We have to keep on going.

I thought we showed great intensity, waited for mistakes and punished Arsenal. It was a strong performance, a very complete performance.

We won the ball high up and attacked really fast. After the last two wins we are full of confidence and wanted to finish really strong before the international break.

I feel really good. I can’t complain. I just try to help the team when I can. I really enjoy life in Brighton, I’m loving it.

The bad blood is adding to the intensity of the occasion.

Ipswich don’t play like a team that is short of confidence and quality. You might assume, if you haven’t seen much of them, that they are destined for a season of toil but there is definite quality with Gary O’Neill’s ranks, including Abdul Fatawu, who has been magnetic in drawing your eye to him. They might be a goal down but they are playing as if they are a goal in front.

Arsenal had just enjoyed a spell of control, but trail to a goal from one of the league’s in-form players. Gross whips a shot from just outside the box around Raya and in off the post.

Brighton have the lead at the Amex and it’s their captain, Pascal Gross, who has provided it. Superb long-range effort, in off the near post. On the overall balance of play, Brighton deserve that. It’s reward for their courage and willingness to go after Arsenal, rather than sitting back.

It took almost 20 minutes but Arsenal have found their feet in this game now. They are starting to find avenues through Brighton’s aggressive pressing and have made a few promising runs in behind, through Havertz and Saka. This is a high quality match.

No goals at the Amex, but Brighton are the team making the running, Arsenal struggling to play out from their own half and are yet to register a shot on goal.

Barry kept himself onside and turned the ball into the back of the net with his stomach. He did well to avoid a handball.

Bright start from Everton and they have the goal they deserve, albeit it came in fortuitous circumstances. James Tarkowski’s volley clattered into Thierno Barry and the deflection took it away from Christian Walton in Ipswich’s goal. Barry now has five goals for the season and, while he is raw, it’s an invaluable contribution.

A storming response to a bad night at Leeds from Newcastle, and it looks like being a long afternoon for Hull. Two down in seven minutes.

What a start for Newcastle United and what will really please manager Matthias Jaissle is the way both goals have come from his players winning important tackles.

The German was incensed by the lack of physicality and intensity in the heavy defeat to Leeds on Monday but the first goal for Joe Wilock came when Lewis Miley won a tackle on the edge of the Hull penalty box.

The second came when Sven Botman came away with the ball just inside his own half. On both occasions Harvey Barnes provided the assist. A short, intricate pass to Willock inside the box and then a surging, twisting run from the halfway line and the perfectly timed pass to Lewis Hall who stroked a first time shot into the bottom corner.

Hull have been outfought so far which is precisely the response Newcastle’s manager had demanded.

The home team are pressing high and all over Arsenal in the early stages. Raya has just made a save to deny Kostoulas.

Brighton have started brilliantly against the champions. They are hunting like wolves, pressing Arsenal with remarkable intensity. We have played seven minutes and I don’t think the ball has left Arsenal’s half.

Big chance for Everton to take the lead, but after great skill to turn his man at the edge of the box Brennan Johnson shoots wide with only the goalkeeper to beat.

The perfect start for Newcastle with all their injuries: Joe Willock has put the home side in a strong position against Hull with a clean strike inside three minutes.

We are under way at the Amex, St James’ Park and the Hill Dickinson.

Another famous face in the stands at Hill Dickinson Stadium today but this time it’s not about politicians. Wayne Rooney is here to watch his boyhood club and he will be hoping Everton can go into the international break unbeaten. An extra special cheer too before kick-off for Jarrad Branthwaite, who has just been called up for England duty. Plenty of Premier League clubs would like to sign Branthwaite, if they were given half a chance, but David Moyes has made it quite clear that Branthwaite: “Isn’t for sale - I want to keep my best players.”

He was not part of the match-day squad at Sunderland but Ben White’s injury has opened up a place, and Dowman fully deserves it after his two goals against Ipswich in the League Cup. Sam Dean has the story of his rise to stardom as well as what Arsenal are doing to nurture such a special talent.

Brighton are wearing a special “125 anniversary” kit today, to mark 125 years since the club was formed in 1901. It’s inspired by the colours of their first ever kit, which means an all-blue shirt, pale gold shorts and dark socks. Personally I would not allow such nonsense. But I don’t make the rules.

Spurs scored two late goals to salvage some pride against Aston Villa, but it is another defeat for Roberto De Zerbi’s team who have two points from five games. This Emi Buendia screamer put the game out of reach.

Emi Buendia, that is a BEAUTIFUL strike 😮‍💨📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/nNplbL7mpd

It has been a term tossed around liberally at Newcastle United since Matthias Jaissle arrived as manager, but what does “vertical football” actually mean?

It is the new buzzword in football analysis, the latest fashionable phrase to describe a “new” style of football, and it has been referenced multiple times by both Jaissle and Ross Wilson, the sporting director, since the German coach’s appointment last month.

For some of us of a certain age, vertical football just seems like clever new terminology to describe an old idea.

Subs: Pope, Schar, Bamba, Toure, Thompson, Pivas, Salia, M Miley, Mills

We are getting to the stage where we really need to start asking questions about Tino Livramento’s injury record.

The right back was due to start for Newcastle against Hull City this afternoon – his first start since April – but has picked up another injury.

That will surely mean he is out of the England squad for the Nations League having also picked up a tournament-ending injury at the World Cup in the summer before the first group game.

Livramento only played 17 Premier League games for Newcastle last season, scuppering his chances of a summer move to Arsenal, missing huge chunks of the season with groin and hamstring issues.

Injuries are already cutting deep into the Newcastle squad, with four teenagers on the bench for the visit of Hull. None have played in the first team before and three of them – Michael Mills, Mason Miley and Kyrian Thompson are just 17–years-old.

Newcastle wanted a younger team this season but not this young. It was interesting to hear Matthias Jaissle talk before the game. He knows how tough this season could be with so little experience in the side.

Everton XI: Pickford; Maitland-Niles, Branthwaite, Tarkowski, Mykolenko; Garner, Armstrong; Grealish, Dewsbury-Hall, Johnson; Barry

Subs: Travers, King, Keane, O’Brien, George, Hackney, Alcaraz, Dibling, Graham

Subs: Scherpen, Furlong, Greaves, Florentino, Nunez, Akpom, Flemming, Philogene, Maeda

Lewis Dunk is a surprise absentee for Brighton, it can only be because of injury, and Hurzeler has preferred Diego Gomez to the lively Yalcouye who was very threatening at Old Trafford and Coventry. He could be a handful off the bench.

Good news for Arsenal: Jurrien Timber is finally fit enough to start a match again. This is his first start since mid-March and his return is timely, given the absence of Ben White through injury. It’s also a first Premier League start for Arsenal for Bruno Guimaraes, who comes into the midfield after his impressive performance off the bench at Sunderland last weekend.

The one he wore in Only Fools and Horses episode Yuppy Love. Of course, Bloom could actually talk about his wealth rather than one of those old five pound notes he found the other day...

Very excited for this one today. Arsenal have won all seven of their matches so far. Only once before in their history have they won their first eight games of a season - that was in 1903, when they were playing in the Second Division as Woolwich Arsenal. pic.twitter.com/iNBxoHl4Gc

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of today’s Premier League 3pm kick-offs, with Brighton vs Arsenal the pick of the three matches.

Brighton are the league’s top goalscorers so far this season and have amassed the most expected goals, but the champions have the league’s best defence and are seeking five wins from five to start their title defence. There is some welcome needle between Fabian Hurzeler and Mikel Arteta, dating back to Declan Rice’s contentious second yellow for delaying the restart two years ago, as well as the Brighton manager’s comments about Arsenal’s style of play in March.

That 1-0 Arsenal victory at the Amex coincided with Man City dropping points at home to Nottingham Forest on a pivotal night in the title race. Bukayo Saka scored a deflected shot in the ninth minute, and Arsenal held on from there in an ugly but resolute display.

With Saka, Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz fit and firing, as well as the introduction of Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes to Arteta’s midfield stable, Arsenal’s football has been more technical and enterprising so far this season. Brighton are one of the few teams who will back themselves to play through Arsenal’s press, which should make for an absorbing game.

Elsewhere, Newcastle are looking to bounce back from their shellacking at Leeds at home to surprise package Hull City. Mattias Jaissle’s team took four points from Liverpool and Spurs but there is concern about how many shots they are conceding. Hull remain unbeaten and continue to confound the odds and underlying data, but that surely cannot last forever.

Everton are also one of the division’s unbeaten teams, but will be targeting three points from a home game against Ipswich after three consecutive draws. Ipswich are sitting comfortably on six points after their win at Crystal Palace, though they did have the extra man for the majority at Selhurst Park.

#1396. Towards observing interstitial hydrogen in solution in metal lattices
