a) Projections of the distribution of every fly over the first 15 min of representative 40-min group assays with 5 males and 5 females in a large 190 mm arena with a 21.5 mm central food patch (red circle) formed from agar perfumed with ACV (orange) or an agar control (blue) for D. erecta (left) and D. melanogaster (right). The positions of each fly in every 250th frame are overlaid, projecting a total of 108 frames over 15 min. b) Population occupancy of the central patch over time for 40-min group assays with 5 males and 5 females in a large 190 mm arena with a 21.5 mm central food patch for D. erecta (above) and D. melanogaster (below). Occupancy ranges from 0 with no individuals on the patch to 1 when all 10 individuals of the group are located on the central patch at a given time. Means ± standard error are indicated in black and shaded regions for assays on an ACV (orange) or agar patch (blue). Patch occupancies of individual assays are shown in shaded lines (n = 10 each). c) Fraction of individuals of group assays in (b) within 3 fly body lengths of one other fly (paired, black), in a group of three or more flies (grouped, dark grey), or at a distance over 3 body lengths from any other individual (solo, light grey) over time for D. erecta (above) and D. melanogaster (below). All flies in the entire arena were included in the analysis. Means ± standard errors are indicated. d) Total amount of time at least one group of three or more flies is present in assays with 5 males and 5 females in a large 190 mm arena with a 21.5 mm central food patch formed from agar perfumed with ACV (orange) or an agar control (blue) for D. erecta (D. ere) and D. melanogaster (D. mel). Means (black bars) and individual assays (dots, n = 10 each) are shown. e) Mean number of flies in large arena (190 mm) group assays (5 males and 5 females) present in clusters of three or more individuals throughout the whole 40-min assay for D. erecta (D. ere) and D. melanogaster (D. mel) in the presence of an agar (blue) or ACV (orange) patch. Assay means (dots, n = 10 each) and overall mean (black bar) are shown. f) and g) Mean distance of individuals in large 190 mm arena from the central 21.5 mm food patch formed from agar and perfumed with ACV (orange) or an agar control (blue) (f) and number of patch visits (g) for D. erecta (D. ere, agar n = 70 flies from 7 assays; ACV n = 100 flies from 10 assays) and D. melanogaster (D. mel; n = 100 flies from 10 assays, each) over 40 min. Black bars indicate the mean. h) Fraction of all copulations per large 190 mm arena group assay (5 males and 5 females; n = 10 assays each) that commenced on the central 21.5 mm patch formed from agar perfumed with ACV (orange) or an agar control (blue) for D. erecta (D. ere) and D. melanogaster (D. mel). i) Raster plots depicting the position of each individual fly relative to the Pandanus patch over duration of the assay (n = 6 assays) for D. erecta (left) and D. melanogaster (right). Time on the patch is highlighted in yellow. Greyscale indicates linear distance to the patch with decreasing distance shaded in lighter shades of grey. Individuals are aligned by the time of their first entry to the patch. j) Comparison of the spatial distribution of copulations in the presence of a Pandanus patch (yellow dots) for D. erecta (left) and D. melanogaster (right) (n = 6 assays). k) Mean patch occupancy for all flies for D. erecta (D. ere) and D. melanogaster (D. mel) (n = 6 assays). l) Fraction of all copulations that were initiated on the central food patch for D. erecta (D. ere) and D. melanogaster (D. mel). Each dot represents a separate assay (n = 6) and bars represent the mean. Scale bar indicates relative density. All statistical tests performed were two-sided, where appropriate. Comparisons that were statistically significant are indicated as: *p ≤ 0.05; **p < 0.001; ***p < 0.0001; all other tests were not statistically significant. See Supplementary Table 1 for full statistics.

a) Mean relative distribution of flies in small 38 mm arena group assays with 5 males and 5 females in the presence of a central 21.5 mm food patch (red circle) formed from agar perfumed with ACV (right) or an agar control (left) for D. erecta (above; agar n = 8, ACV n = 7) and D. melanogaster (below; agar n = 6, ACV n = 6). b) Interaction per minute of all five D. erecta males of 5 male and 5 female group assays in small 38 mm arenas with a central 21.5 mm food patch towards any other individual in the arena for D. erecta (D. ere; agar n = 8, ACV n = 7) and D. melanogaster (D. mel; agar n = 6, ACV n = 6). Individual males (dots) and means (black bars) are indicated for assays with ACV (orange) or an agar (blue) patch. c) Interactions of all five males towards any other individual in the arena over the duration of an assay (top, solid line represents mean and shaded line individual assays) and ethogram of each male for either agar (blue; n = 8) or ACV (orange; n = 7) showing individual interactions with other males (open circle) and females (closed circle). Top panels and assays 5,8,11 and 15 are replotted from Fig. 1m. d) Approaches per minute of individual males towards a single female, another male, or an inanimate fly-sized hemispherical visual target (⌀ ca. 3 mm) in a small 38 mm arena with a central ACV (orange) or agar (blue) patch for D. erecta (top; targets: female: agar n = 16, ACV n = 19, male: agar n = 17, ACV n = 20, bead: agar n = 18, ACV n = 15) and D. melanogaster (bottom; targets: female: n = 8, each, male: agar n = 24, ACV n = 26, bead: n = 8, each). Means (black bar) for all assays (dots) are indicated. All males were paired with a single mobile target (another male or female), or a single hemispherical bead positioned at the center of the arena. e) Courtship index of flies in small 38 mm arena group assays with 5 males and 5 females in the presence of a central 21.5 mm food patch (red circle) formed from agar perfumed with ACV (right) or an agar control (left) for different D. melanogaster lines derived from populations in North America (Canton-S (CS); n = 6 assays) and Africa (Cameroon (CO4n); n = 4 assays and Rwanda (RG11n); agar n = 5, ACV n = 6 assays). CS data are replotted from Fig. 1h. All statistical tests performed were two-sided, where appropriate. Those comparisons that were statistically significant are indicated as: *p ≤ 0.05; ***p < 0.0001; all other tests were not statistically significant. See Supplementary Table 1 for full statistics. Schematics in d adapted from ref. 43, Springer Nature Limited.

a) Schematic depicting assay in which a single male was provided a female-sized hemispherical bead (ca. 3 mm) at the center of a small 38 mm arena with a 21.5 mm central food patch (red circle) formed from agar perfumed with ACV or an agar control. b) Fraction of time individual D. erecta (D. ere, left, agar n = 18, ACV n = 15) and D. melanogaster (D. mel, right, n = 8) males (dots) spent within three body-lengths of the hemispherical bead at the center of a small arena in the presence of an ACV (orange) or agar (blue) patch over 20 min. Mean is indicated by black bars. c) Mean velocity of flies in b). d) Frequency distribution of the central hemispherical bead position relative to the heading direction of D. erecta (top, n = 15–18) and D. melanogaster (bottom, n = 8) males in (b) on an agar (blue, left) or an ACV (orange, right) patch. Coordinates are shown using orientations of all males over 20 min with respect to the egocentric orientation of the male, heading towards the bead at 0/2π, while the bead is behind the male at π. e) Schematic of a fly head highlighting olfactory appendages (third antennal segments and maxillary palps) innervated by Orco+ olfactory sensory neurons in green and innervation of antennal lobes in the brain (center). Right: Schematic of optogenetics bead assay comprised of a single male with a female-sized hemispherical bead (⌀ ca. 3 mm) at the center in a small 38 mm arena with a 21.5 mm central agar patch. Arena is fitted with LEDs emitting 625 nm (red) light from top. f) Left: Overlaid trajectories of D. erecta (top, n = 13) and D. melanogaster (bottom, n = 12) Orco>CsChrimson control males reared without retinal over the 2 min prior to (left, pre) and during 2-min (right, LED on) optogenetic activation. Right: Raster of individual bead approaches (circles) for each male in the 2 min prior to and during optogenetic activation (grey shaded area). g) Mean distribution of males in 38 mm arenas with one isolated male in the presence of a central 21.5 mm food patch (red circle) formed from agar perfumed with ACV (right) or an agar control (left) for D. erecta (n = 4). No visual target was provided in these assays. Scale bar indicates relative density. h) Top left: Schematic of grid assay containing a lattice of 13 fly-sized hemispherical visual targets (⌀ ca. 3 mm) arranged in a regular square array in a large 190 mm arena on a large 145 mm food patch (red circle) formed from agar perfumed with ACV or an agar control. Bead sizes are enlarged and not to scale to highlight grid pattern. Top right: Mean distribution of groups of 5 D. erecta males on ACV without lattice of hemispherical visual targets over 20 min (n = 5 assays). Bottom: Mean distribution of groups of 5 D. erecta males in the presence of lattice on an agar (left) or ACV (right) patch (n = 5 assays, each). Scale bar indicates relative density over 20 min. i) Number of times any single D. erecta male within the group of 5 males switched from one hemispherical visual bead target to another on an agar (blue, left) or an ACV (orange, right) patch (n = 5 assays, 5 males each) over 20 min. j) Top: Overlaid trajectories of individual D. erecta males on agar (left) and ACV (right) in the presence of the bead grid (n = 8 assays) over 20 min. Bottom: Mean distribution of individual D. erecta males on an agar (left) or ACV (right) patch in the presence of a bead lattice. Scale bar indicates relative density. k) Overlaid trajectories of groups of 5 D. melanogaster males on agar (left) and ACV (right) in the presence of the bead grid (n = 5 assays) over 20 min. l) Mean number of approaches per male in (k) for each bead in the grid over 20 min indicated by color and size of the circle. m) Four representative assays from (k) for agar (left) and ACV (right), in which bead approaches for each male (rows) are depicted (black dots) over the 20-min assay. n) and o) Total number of beads in the grid visited (n) and approaches per minute (o) for each individual male in (k) on agar (blue, n = 25 males) and ACV (orange, n = 25 males). p) The number of song bouts per bead approached for D. erecta males in grid assay containing a lattice of 13 fly-sized hemispherical visual targets in a large 190 mm arena on a large 145 mm food patch formed from agar perfumed with ACV (orange, n = 8) or an agar control (blue, n = 8). Individual males were alone in the assay chamber and behavior was scored for all approaches during 20-min assay. q) Distance of a male to the immobilized decapitated female (black) and the closest bead in representative grid assay shown in Fig. 2m with the bead in the second row on the left replaced by an immobilized decapitated female over 20 min. Red dotted line indicates one fly length (3 mm) distance. Once male has encountered the female, he remains close to her for the remainder of the assay, moving farther from the rest of the beads. r) Average fraction of time a male spent with each bead prior to encountering the female (black dots) and fraction of time male spent with the female after encountering her (green dots) for all males that encountered the female on ACV (n = 8). All statistical tests performed were two-sided, where appropriate. Those comparisons that were statistically significant are indicated as: n.s.: not significant; *p < 0.05; **p < 0.001; ***p < 0.0001. See Supplementary Table 1 for full statistics. Schematics in e adapted from ref. 43, Springer Nature Limited.

a) Schematic showing virtual reality behavioral setup for tethered flies provided with an oscillating visual target (black dot) and with ACV presented through odor tube. b) Target position in the male visual field (top) and corresponding heading direction (center) and tracking index (bottom) of a representative D. erecta male prior to (black), during (orange), and after (black) presentation of ACV with visual target continuously oscillating after an initial 30 s baseline period. c) Tracking indices (TI) of eight wild type D. erecta males prior to (black), during (orange), and after (black) presentation of ACV with continuously oscillating visual target (black arrow) as in (b). d) Left: Mean tracking index of wild type D. erecta males (n = 8, same males shown in c), prior to (black), during (orange), and after (black) presentation of ACV with continuously oscillating visual target (black arrow). Thick lines represent the mean, shaded areas the standard error. Right: Probability of tracking. e) Same as in d) but with D. erecta males mutant for the chemosensory co-receptors Orco and Ir8a (n = 4) deficient in the major olfactory pathways previously implicated in the detection of ACV volatiles60,61. f) Left: Tracking index of D. erecta males expressing CsChrimson in Orco+ olfactory sensory neurons in the antenna and maxillary palps prior to (pre), during (LED) and after (post) optogenetic activation (n = 3). Lines indicate mean ± standard error (shaded). Right: Probability of tracking. All statistical tests performed were two-sided, where appropriate. Those comparisons that were statistically significant are indicated as: *p ≤ 0.05; all other tests were not statistically significant. See Supplementary Table 1 for full statistics. a) and b) P1 neural activity (∆F/F) of D. erecta (a) and D. melanogaster (b) males plotted against tracking index for five individuals (rows) for the entire experiment (all), during the 30 s baseline period (baseline), and with a continuously oscillating visual target prior to (vis, pre), during presentation of visual stimulus and ACV (vis + acv) and after (vis, post) presentation of ACV with only visual target. Line of best fit (red), Pearson correlation coefficient and p-value are indicated for each plot. See Supplementary Table 1 for full statistics.

a) Schematic of LC10a neurons and region of interest imaged (black box). b) LC10a neural activity (∆F/F) recorded in the right hemisphere of a representative D. erecta (left) and D. melanogaster (right) male tracking an oscillating visual target plotted against the position of the target (black line) in the male visual field colored by the target’s progressive (black) and regressive (grey) movement. ACV was provided throughout. c) Target position in the male visual field (top), corresponding LC10a neural activity (center), and heading direction (bottom) for a representative D. erecta male in the presence of ACV during an initial 10 s baseline period and then with visual target continuously oscillating. d) Schematic of fru+ innervation of the Lateral Protocerebral Complex (LPC, green) and Anterior Optic Tubercle (AOTu, red) and ROI used to image both neuropils simultaneously (black box). e) and h) Left: Neural activity (∆F/F) of aggregate Fruitless (Fru+) neurons in the lateral protocerebral complex (LPC) innervated by P1 neurons. a) Courtship index of D. erecta males paired with a D. melanogaster female in small 38 mm arenas with a central 21.5 mm food patch formed from agar perfumed with ACV. Males were either wild type (black, n = 8) or mutant for the DEG/ENaC sodium channel ppk23 (red, n = 7). Courtship indices for the entire 40 min of the assay (left) or the 10 min following courtship initiation are shown. Black lines indicate mean. Enhanced courtship in mutants is consistent with evidence from other species that ppk23 is essential to detection of heterospecific pheromones, suggesting that D. erecta remain averse to courting D. melanogaster females on ACV due to detection of heterospecific pheromones by ppk23+ sensory neurons. Black line indicates mean. b) Mean velocity of individual female and male D. erecta (left) and D. melanogaster (right) in pairs (1m1f, Dere n = 20, each, Dmel n = 8, each) or groups of 5 males and 5 females (5m5f, Dere agar n = 8, ACV n = 7 assays, Dmel n = 6, each) in small 38 mm arenas with a central 21.5 mm food patch formed from agar perfumed with ACV (orange) or an agar control (blue). Individual (dots) and overall means (black line) are indicated. c) Fraction of time male (left) and female (right) D. erecta (D. ere) and D. melanogaster (D. mel) in b) spent moving when paired (1m1f) or in groups (5m5f) over 40 min in a small 38 mm arena with a central 21.5 mm food patch on agar (blue) or ACV (orange). Black lines indicate mean. d) Mean velocity of individual D. erecta (left) and D. melanogaster (right) males in small 38 mm arenas with a central 21.5 mm food patch formed from agar perfumed with ACV (orange) or an agar control (blue). Individual (dots) and overall means (black line) are indicated (n = 10, each). e) Mean velocity of all other males and females in the group during the 2 s window preceding a male courtship bout, compared to a permuted null distribution of 2-s velocity windows in D. erecta groups on agar (left, n = 8 assays) and ACV (right, n = 7 assays). f) Movement probability of a female target for D. erecta (left) and D. melanogaster (right) 1 male and 1 female pair assays in small 38 mm arenas with a central 21.5 mm food patch for the whole 40-min assay (filled circle) and the five second period before the male engages in courtship (open circle) on agar (blue, Dere n = 20, Dmel n = 8) or ACV (orange, Dere n = 20, Dmel n = 8). All statistical tests performed were two-sided, where appropriate. Those comparisons that were statistically significant are indicated as: *p ≤ 0.05; ***p < 0.0001; all other tests were not statistically significant. See Supplementary Table 1 for full statistics.

Male brains stained for GFP (green) and neuropil counterstain (magenta) visualizing neural expression patterns of transgenic lines labeling olfactory sensory neurons a) and b) (Orco-Gal4), LC10a neurons c) and d) (VT029314-Gal4), and sexually dimorphic neurons expressing the fruitless e) and f) (Fru-Gal4) and g) and h) (Dsx-Gal4) transcription factors. Scalebars: 50 µm.

Group behaviour in a large arena with central food patch. Representative video clips of D. erecta and D. melanogaster groups of five males and five females in large 190-mm arenas with a central food patch filled with agar perfumed with ACV (orange) or an agar-only control (blue). Clips displayed at 30× speed.

Groups in small arena with central food patch. Representative clips of D. erecta and D. melanogaster groups of five males and five females in small 38-mm arenas with a central food patch filled with agar perfumed with ACV (orange) or an agar-only control (blue). Clips displayed at 10× speed.

Behaviour of individual males towards an inanimate bead. Video comparing behaviour of individual D. erecta and D. melanogaster males in a small 38-mm arena towards a central hemispherical plastic bead of 3 mm diameter on ACV (orange) or an agar control (blue). Recordings are displayed at 10× speed.

Optogenetic activation of Orco+ olfactory sensory neurons in the presence of a visual target on agar. Video clips of individual D. erecta and D. melanogaster males expressing the channelrhodopsin CsChrimson under the expression of the Orco promoter in small 38-mm arenas with a small black plastic bead on the central agar patch. The representative videos show male behaviour during an initial 2-min baseline period, followed by 2 min of red LED illumination and a final 2-min period with LEDs turned off again. Displayed at 4× speed.

Group of males presented with a grid of beads. Video comparing the behaviour of five D. erecta males in a large arena with a large food patch filled with agar perfumed with ACV (orange) or an agar-only control (blue) towards a grid of small hemispherical plastic beads. Clips displayed at 10× speed.

Optogenetic activation of P1 neurons in the presence of a moving visual target. Comparison of representative video clips of D. erecta males expressing the channelrhodopsin CsChrimson in P1 neurons (using 71G01 driver) or a CsChrimson only control in a small 38-mm arena with a constantly rotating dot projected onto the floor of the arena of males. Thirty µl of either agar (blue) or agar perfumed with ACV (orange) are added to the center of the arena. Male behaviour is shown before and following onset of red LED light. Clips are shown at 2× speed.

Male courtship tracking of projected dots. Behaviour of a D. erecta male in the presence of 30 µl agar perfumed with ACV (orange) and an agar-only control (blue) towards a constantly rotating dot projected onto the surface of a small 38-mm arena. Representative videos shown at original speed.

Food-odour-dependent tracking of visual stimulus in tethered setup. Clip of a tethered D. erecta male running on a spherical treadmill presented with an oscillating ‘fictive female’ on a conical screen in front of him before and during exposure to ACV odour. For interpretability of his walking direction, the tracked movements of the treadmill are indicated as a continuous blue line. Shown at 0.5× speed.

Correlated burst of courtship activity on agar. Video clip of a group of five male and five female D. erecta in a small arena with a central food patch filled with agar showing how inactivity is interjected with a burst of spontaneous group activity. Displayed at 10× speed.

Courtship with additional moving visual stimuli. Comparison of example videos of a pair of one male and one female D. erecta in a small 38-mm arena supplemented with 30 µl agar perfumed with ACV in the center with and without two constantly rotating black dots projected onto the floor of the assay chamber. Clips played at 2× speed.

Visual social scene replay experiment. Video shows the experimental design of transforming a recording of a group of five D. erecta males and five females on ACV into a visual representation used to replay to pairs of tester males and females followed by two representative replay experiments in which D. erecta pairs are presented with 30 µl agar perfumed with ACV in the center of a 38-mm arena and either a social scene representative of a group on agar or on ACV. Behaviour clips displayed at 5× speed.

#1372. A win to transport Martin O'Neill back to Celtic's European glory days? No, Besiktas was a lesson in why he shouldn't be the manager at all

Published: 11:22 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 12:00 EDT, 6 November 2026

There are clearly a number of ways in which to reflect upon Celtic’s quite discombobulating back-from-the-dead victory over Besiktas in the Europa League on Thursday evening.

Martin O’Neill regarded it as a triumph of heart and spirit and soul that conjured up recollections of ‘the olden days’, when the likes of Juventus, Porto and Olympique Lyon turned up at Parkhead during his first stint in charge and were sent packing with their tails between their legs.

Benjamin Nygren viewed it as a well-earned win notable for the side fighting from start to finish. Callum Osmand, meanwhile, opted to paint it as some kind of masterclass in digging in, staying strong and getting your rewards.

Of course, there are some of us sober-minded sorts who opted not to travel through the looking-glass and saw it for what it was. A disgrace, really. A night in which O’Neill appeared to buy into the overriding view of his paymasters that Europe doesn’t really matter all that much – only to get away with an unfathomable team selection by chucking on a load of subs over the last half-an-hour and hoping for the best.

It was a night, for anyone watching the game remotely objectively, that simply added fuel to the theory that the Northern Irishman is a man out of time and no longer suitable as manager.

He made comments afterwards about the team playing some lovely stuff. Gee-whizz. The first hour – before he summoned Camilo Duran, Osmand and Colby Donovan from the substitutes bench – was absolutely mortifying for Celtic as a club.

Martin O'Neill got his team selection wrong against Besiktas and was lucky to come out on top

It was like the olden days all right. The days when Wayne Biggins was running around up front and punters were throwing Mars bars into the directors’ box.

It’s just fortunate that Besiktas fell into such a false sense of security that they set about turning it into a game of ‘passy’, an exercise in keep-ball, and forgot about what those big white sticks at either end of the park are for.

For long periods, Celtic struggled to get the ball off them. When they did gain possession, they didn’t have the faintest idea what to do with it.

Early in the second period, with the visitors a goal up, a text came through from a foreign contact with an extensive history in the game who was questioning the wisdom of tuning in. ‘Really embarrassing’ was how he described it.

It was all that. And the madness and mayhem of the last 28 minutes or so shouldn’t be used to disguise it.

Celtic supporters paid good money for those Europa League packages and tickets. They need a better explanation than the one O’Neill gave in the aftermath for why they turned up for a make-or-break fixture and ended up watching the stiffs. They should claim a refund for the first 60 minutes.

The 3-2 victory, earned against all odds and much logic, showed precisely what was at stake. Celtic, thanks to Duran’s 87th-minute winner, are just a point off the top 24, which guarantees a spot in the play-offs. They’re also just four points off eighth and the automatic entry into the last 16 that brings.

There was absolutely everything to play for on Thursday. And that begs the painfully obvious question of why O’Neill picked the team he picked.

He says it was all intentional. That fresh legs were needed in the side. That the plan was always to utilise the substitutes the way he did. And the band played believe it if you like.

Camilo Duran is hailed by his team-mates but why he started on the bench remains a mystery

All the Dilly Daydreams buying into this stuff about it being a night for the ages and some sort of example of everything good about Celtic need to give their heads a wobble. This simply reeked of giving a home league game against Kilmarnock on Sunday priority over a big night under the lights.

The Parkhead side are in the state they are in because they have let their standards slip to a ridiculous degree. They have meekly accepted becoming a laughing stock in Europe, a punchbag for the LASKs and the Maribors and the Kairat Almatys.

Given O’Neill’s insistence that UEFA competition should be a major focus, it is crazy that he went into a game of this magnitude with Jordan Lotomba making his first start at right-back, 35-year-old James Forrest reappearing on the right flank for just his second start of the season and Sebastian Tounekti, a bloke that even the dogs in the street know is not cut out for this, on the left.

Lotomba had a mare, giving away the stupid penalty that led to Besiktas’ opener with a stupid tackle. Forrest did produce the team’s first shot on target on 50 minutes but was almost as ineffective as Tounekti. When all three departed the scene on 61 minutes, it wasn’t a moment too soon.

Surely the lightly raced Osmand, terrific after coming on, should have kept his place on the left. On the other side of the pitch, it’s hard to figure what is going on with £9million man Haissem Hassan. If he can’t get in the starting line-up ahead of the ageing Forrest, there’s a problem.

Right now, he’s starting to look a monumental waste of money that O’Neill doesn’t fancy. Indeed, the £20million or so committed to him and Kasper Hogh is starting to look like the most reckless example of silly spending since Edinburgh decided it needed to bring back the tram system.

Hogh should never have started. Duran should have been playing through the centre all day long and hammered that home when moving there after the Dane had been taken off and scoring twice.

Big Kasper is just a jigsaw piece in the wrong box here. A pineapple Danish in a bag of cinnamon swirls. Someone, somewhere will get some enjoyment from him through time, but it doesn’t look like it’s going to be Celtic.

O'Neill's relief at gaining a much-needed win was clear as he embraced assistant Maloney

That’s 15 games without a goal now. People can talk all they like about how O’Neill is not playing to his strengths, but an £11million international player needs to be able to adapt better than this. He was honking on Thursday. Again.

He just looks bereft of confidence, but wouldn’t it have been better to shove him in at home against Killie at the weekend in the hope he can get back on the goal trail rather than pitch him into a big European game and watch him slide ever further into the mire?

Lord knows. With every passing week, the mess the transfer window ended up being comes into sharper focus. Sam Johnstone doesn’t convince in goal and certainly didn’t convince against Besiktas.

It’s hard to know who should play between him and Viljami Sinisalo. Maybe both. A bit like Rab Douglas and Magnus Hedman all over again.

Still, it was good to see Landon Emenalo, Shim Mheuka and £3million Joel van den Berg get an outing in the KDM Evolution Trophy in Dingwall on Tuesday – and end up on the wrong end of a 2-0 hosing from League One Ross County, who had 22 shots on goal and rattled the woodwork more than once.

Yes, there are many things that can be said about the last couple of days at the champions. And lots of things that an admittedly thrilling win against solid opposition can paper over.

One thing remains as clear as it was before Besiktas came to town, though. Under this board and this manager, Celtic are a confusing outfit going nowhere other than backwards.

#1371. Lethal Trent Alexander-Arnold sends Tuchel a statement in England victory

Thomas Tuchel has never been inclined to place much faith in the most famous right-back at his disposal, Trent Alexander-Arnold, once of Liverpool, now of Real Madrid, and – back in an England shirt – still capable of changing games in the blink of an eye.

England always looked likely to defeat a beleaguered Czech Republic team down to 10 men with just 25 minutes played, but it still required one man to conjure the moment of inspiration in this Nations League tie. This was the first cap in 15 months for the right-back now known simply as “Trent” in an England shirt – as well as his Real Madrid jersey – rather than the six syllables of his surname. With the game level at half-time, two minutes into the new half, he twice won the ball before landing a cross on the head of Anthony Gordon for the first goal.

TRENT ➡️ GORDON ⚽️🔥Anthony Gordon can't stop scoring for England, 3 goals in his last 3 games for England 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/xmqPIULJ24

Will the Alexander-Arnold with England experiment survive? One feels that Tuchel will need a little more to convince him to abandon whatever reservations he has about the Liverpudlian. A week short of his 28th birthday, Alexander-Arnold was winning just his 35th cap. His Real Madrid team-mate Jude Bellingham, a second-half substitute, was earning his 58th cap less than two months after his 23rd birthday. Bellingham was on as captain in place of the man he replaced, Harry Kane, scorer of England’s second. Bellingham’s international career has taken a much less rocky path than that of his Real team-mate.

Having missed the World Cup finals this summer, and had little good fortune around previous tournaments, one wonders if Euro 2028 might be the watershed moment for Alexander-Arnold. Either way, against opponents who sit back, he is lethal when it is time for the big delivery. Alexander-Arnold may not have the breadth of England experience that some of his peers have accumulated, but he does have plenty of experience of big games.

“I make that run time and time again,” Gordon said of his anticipation of the Alexander-Arnold cross, “but only a set number of players have that ability, that technique and the bravery to risk a mistake to play that pass. And that’s why I have been dying to play with him [Alexander-Arnold]. He’s been on his own journey but has trained really well this week. He should have played more. Sorry – he would have loved to have played more.”

A Freudian slip from the Barcelona winger, another Liverpudlian in Spain, who himself has barely put a foot wrong for England of late. He has three goals in three games for England, including the World Cup semi-final against Argentina. This was an England team that Tuchel fine-tuned, first to give a rest to Bellingham and in other quarters, too. Lewis Hall started at left-back. Trevoh Chalobah won his third England cap at centre-back. Alex Scott, of Bournemouth, was given his debut off the bench in the second half and Rio Ngumoha won the second cap of his England career, just one month after his 18th birthday.

As for Kane, his 87th goal for England now puts him within two goals of Robert Lewandowski, among four greats in the seven ahead of Kane on the all-time international goalscorers’ list. By the end of this international break the England captain should have equalled Peter Shilton’s record 125 caps. It has been an astonishing career even if it ends tomorrow. Following the missed penalty against Spain, Kane was again the man in the right place at the right time when Morgan Rogers’s shot was blocked in the second half.

“Strange to get an early red card,” Tuchel said. “Not the best for the team and spectators. It’s an awkward one, but we kept going, got a win and that’s what counts.” Not quite a vintage Czech Republic team, either, and when their best player of the opening stages, the attacking midfielder Pavel Sulc, of Lyon in Ligue 1, was dismissed after 25 minutes, it certainly did not become any easier for the home team. Sulc, the Czech player of the year in 2025, had mistimed a tackle on Elliot Anderson, which on a VAR review, the Turkish referee Umut Meler decided was worthy of an upgrade from yellow to red. It was high on the right calf of the England midfielder.

Czech Republic DOWN TO 10 MEN! 🟥Pavel Šulc sees red for a dangerous challenge on Elliot Anderson#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/B2YOLuS0vL

England had looked once more a little open to the counter-attack in the early stages, with Sulc one notable runner. This was not an opponent of the quality of Spain and Tuchel’s players were able to recover the situation. When they lose the ball in the opposition’s half, England tend to look vulnerable.

Even before the red card Rogers had hit a post. Myles Lewis-Skelly, playing in midfield, was booked for a foul on Lukas Serv and was pursued thereafter by the Czech players hoping to get an upgrade on the yellow card. He was substituted at half-time, with Eberechi Eze on in his place.

“I spoke to Ant [Gordon] at half-time,” Alexander-Arnold said later to ITV, “and I said if I’m getting in those spaces make sure you get to the back post. You don’t expect to get it that fast, but it did and it worked.”

Two minutes after the break, Alexander-Arnold suddenly burst into life. He won the ball back in his own area and then drove forward in search of the return. When that did not come, he raced back to win the ball again and unleashed one of those right-footed outswingers to the back post, where Gordon guided in the header. “Really proud to score that,” Gordon said, “because I can’t tell you the number of hours I’ve spent practising headers.”

Kane scored the second just a minute before he was replaced and Bellingham took the captain’s armband and the role as a No 9. One day someone will have to step into those goalscorer’s boots on a permanent basis and try to replace Kane – although it may be a while yet.

Thomas Tuchel has backed Jude Bellingham as a future England captain after giving him the armband in the victory over the Czech Republic.

In the absence of Declan Rice, who was vice-captain at the World Cup, Bellingham assumed the role when he came on for Harry Kane, who is now in his 10th season as England captain and also scored in the 2-0 win in Prague.

Tuchel, who needs to check on Bellingham ahead of Saturday’s game against Croatia after a “niggle,” has praised the midfielder’s attitude during the extended international break one year after he was back from an injury but left out of the squad.

“If you are the captain at the end of these matches, you can be the permanent captain,” Tuchel said when asked whether Bellingham could eventually lead the team. “He was the captain against New Zealand before the World Cup. It is always a reward and always an honour.

“I think he loves to be with us at the moment. That’s what I feel, and we had this small talk today about his role. We felt in our hearts or our stomachs to say ‘let’s go again, let’s start again’ and also our heads told us maybe 30 minutes is enough for this match because he hasn’t played in this quick turnaround through this season. He has done it before, but not in the season, so we didn’t want to be the first ones to try that.

“But even in this little encounter, you can see that he’s confident and happy to help from the bench. So it’s a reward. It’s good. He had a little niggle at the end of the match, so hopefully it’s nothing serious, and he’s available for Croatia.”

Nico O’Reilly is a doubt for the Croatia match in Rijeka and there are also concerns over Ezri Konsa, who was on the bench but not fit enough to play.

Trent Alexander-Arnold provided an assist for Anthony Gordon in the Real Madrid full-back’s first cap in 15 months. Gordon, meanwhile, has now scored in the first two Nations League games of the campaign and is staking his case to be an indispensable player for Tuchel.

“He’s getting there. He’s defending his shirt, he’s defending his position, an excellent performance again after his performance against Spain,” Tuchel said.

“He was very decisive today and had an excellent goal. It was very, very difficult, but the technique and finishing was excellent. He scored against Spain, so he has decisive actions and he’s defending his shirt and his position. He does it on the highest level and he’s a very important player.”

England returned to winning ways with a 2-0 win over Czech Republic in Prague.

Pavel Sulc’s first-half red card after a VAR review of his clumsy challenge on Elliot Anderson took the sting out of the initially lively hosts and Anthony Gordon gave Thomas Tuchel’s men a deserved lead early in the second half.

The forward headed home a fantastic cross by Trent Alexander-Arnold, who was making his first start under the German coach, before skipper Harry Kane scored to settle any nerves.

So who played well for England and who failed to impress? Rate each player with our voting tool, and have your say in the comments.

I thought we were very professional second half. We stepped up and needed to be more dynamic, bring more urgency into our play, which we did. We kept that intensity going and and the effort was till there. Deserved victory.

Strange to get an early red card. Not the best for the spectators, not the best for the team. It’s an awkward one. But we got the win.

To guide it into the goal, there was an awful lot [for Anthony Gordon] to do. Good pass, good goal. Both full-backs were good. The position in the second half suited Trent more than the position in the first half. Lewis was excellent on the other side.

We have used all the outfield players after two matches so credit to all of them. Now it’s important to relax and enjoy the evening, do a good recovery and prepare for Saturday.

I think it was good. They go down to 10 men and it should be easier for us to win the game, But in fact it makes it more difficult. They get very compact and defend with a lot of players around the box and it’s hard to break them down.

We got that [goal] at the start of the second half which is what we needed. The longer it’s 0-0, it gets harder and harder and harder.

[Where do you place your assist?]  It’s up there for sure. I spoke to Ant at half-time and said if I get into those half-spaces I’m looking to put it in so make sure you get to the back post. I didn’t expect it to work so quickly.

He’s a willing runner, great to play with him. I saw the run and was able to execute the pass,

It’s always a pleasure and an honour to represent my country. It’s been a long time. I’ve always believed that I can play for England and I want to. The manager’s given me the opportunity and I tried to do what he wanted me to do to the best of my ability and I hope he’s happy with how I played.

🦁 #1301Alex Scott reflects on a special night, earning his first senior England cap 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @gabrielclarke05 | @England pic.twitter.com/lC34bAPbbd

It was good, quite dominant. We created a lot of chances but without the quality. When they went a man down, we were too passive at times. We need to be dominant, as I said earlier, go for the throat and put teams away.

I said that to him [Trent, on the quality of the ‘assist’]. I make that run time and time again but only a set number of players have that ability, that technique and the bravery to risk a mistake to play that pass. And that’s why I have been dying to play with him. He’s been on his own journey but has trained really well this week. He should have played more. Sorry, he would have loved to have played more.

I’ve missed playing with Hally. He’s a good lad. We had great chemistry at Newcastle and it’s great to share this stage with him.

It’s my only header. I’d be the worst header of the ball you’ll ever see. Really happy, resally proud to score that because I can’t tell you the number of hours I’ve spent practising headers.

Perfectly competent and signs of promise in the left-back/left-wing axis. England looked too open against 11 men and better teams – hola España – may have capitalised on the sloppiness. But once Sulc was sent off, England gradually turned the screw and created a hatful of chances, running out easy winners.

Another tidy save from Kovar when Bellingham receives a pass from the left, strides towards the D, then drives a daisy-cutter towards the left of goal. The keeper swoops down early to turn it behind with a stiff wrist.

Two minutes of stoppage time are signalled as England try to pen the home side in their own half.

Tuchel has kept the back four on the pitch for the 90 minutes. He was not entirely happy with them in the first half – or his body language suggested that, anyway. But it is a welcomed clean sheet for England after the chaotic defeats to Spain and France.

Ngumoha is enjoying himself and showing off some excellent close control.

Scott and Eze smash shots over the bar from 22 yards within a minute of each other.

Rogers’ diagonal cross is chested down by Eze as he sets up an opportunity to shoot in the area but a defender hacks it away. Ngumoha pounces on the loose ball and plays a neat reverse pass with the outside of his boot to Rogers on the underlap. Rogers goes for power rather than lift to find Eze or Bellingham and the keeper makes another smart save.

Gibbs-White’s pace and direct running have the beating of Chaloupek and he tees up Eze to hammer a left-foot shot that seemed to be arrowing into the net until Kovar stuck up his right hand to paw it over.

Gordon stops, then from a standing start drives past bursts past Chaloupek to the byline and stands up a near-post cross that Rogers flashes wide.

Czech Republic break after England’s attack down the right hits the skids. Hlozek gallops down the middle and lets fly before Scott can catch him. Trafford sees it all the way, dives to his right to save and gathers the loopy effort from the rebound.

Slama hounds Ngumoha into conceding a corner as the Liverpool winger slips under pressure.

Jude Bellingham is wearing the England captain’s armband again. He was also wearing it during the pre-World Cup camp against New Zealand. Thomas Tuchel explained afterwards that the player with the most caps is skipper when Harry Kane is subbed off. Bellingham is also playing centrally, as a False Nine.

Bellingham → KaneNgumoha → SakaScott → Anderson.

England have switched to the Revie Plan with Bellingham as the deep-lying centre-forward.

Czech Republic 0 England 2 (Kane) Eze plays Rogers in down the left of the box. He gets there but falls under the tackle of Krejci, knocking the ball to Kane who thumps it through Hranac’s legs with his left foot from about seven yards.

KANE DOUBLES ENGLAND'S LEAD 🔥Harry Kane in the right place at the right time for the Three Lions 🦁#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/Od9x5kXOsH

Kane stuck around five finishes into that corner in the warm-up. Same finish - accurate and powerful. Finally a first cap for Alex Scott.

As Sam Matterface points out. England having a left-footed left-back has added an extra dimension to their attacking play. I never thought I’d be quoting Sam Matterface but it’s been one of those days. Ambros had taken up a good position in space on the left but the crossfield pass wasn’t good enough and sailed beyond him.

Alexander-Arnold shoots from the right after some slow-slow-slow-quick passing between him and Saka opens up a gap. But he drills it across goal and wide of the left post.

Now Hall does find the target at his third attempt this half but only because Krejci is there to deflect his cross on to the post with the keeper beaten.

Corner on the right for England who procrastinate so long over their positions the referee warns them but does not take it off them. Krejci and Kane have their arms around each other as the ball comes in and the Czech captain pulls Kane to the ground but the referee waves play on.

Saka takes it short and plays a one-two with Alexander-Arnold. Saka cuts it back to Eze to shoot in a pre-cooked move but he is closed down too quickly so he rolls it to Hall 20 yards out and the left-black leans back and launches his shot 20 rows back behind the goal.

England have a corner on the left after a last gasp tackle by Chaloupek on Gordon.

Czech Republic have switched to 3-3-3 in possession and are trying to play. Sadilek is struggling after being kicked by person or persons unknown. Apologies.

Although the goal was built from the right, England have been so dominant down the left. Hall and Gordon, who combined so well for Newcastle, do so again here with the left-back creeping up the inside while the winger goes down the outside and plays it into the box for his former colleague who wafts his shot wide with a lazy air from 15 yards. Should have scored.

Czech Republic 0 England 1 (Gordon) Alexander-Arnold clears Lingr’s cross and runs upfield to join the counter that seems to break down. But a crossfield pass from the home side is picked off by the right-back facing his own goal 30 yards from the Czechs’. He turns and arrows a fine cross to the left of the penalty spot. Gordon lets it bounce and cushions a header back across the keeper and in at the right post. Great finish. High IQ finish as he might say.

TRENT ➡️ GORDON ⚽️🔥Anthony Gordon can't stop scoring for England, 3️⃣ goals in his last 4️⃣ games for England 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/iej0PCW8Ar

That goal was all about Trent. He intercepted in his own penalty area before making a 70-run up the pitch to get on the end of a throughball. That doesn’t work but he wins the ball back and crosses for Gordon to score. The full house from Trent there – showing Tuchel what he brings to the team in just a few seconds of action.

England are attcking from right to left in the second half. England’s trumpeter is in the house and reprises the national anthem.

Eze → Lewis-Skelly who was on a yellow card.

Just before half-time, Krejci, the Wolves centre-half wiped out Saka, watching the man, not the ball, and bodychecking him.

Thomas Tuchel was furious with the fourth official Cihan Aydin, wagging his finger in anger after Bukayo Saka was taken out by Ladislav Krejci. Before that he was quite passive on the touchline, hands in pockets as he watched England trying to break down the Czechs.

Could be another tactical half-time substitution for Myles Lewis-Skelly. Czech players definitely see him as the best chance of a red for England.

The Czech Republic were causing England problems with 11 men but having been reduced to 10 have concentrated on trying to persuade the referee to even up the numbers and also on defending in a low block. Gordon and Hall have the key to unlock the defence but too often when they have sent crosses in, Kane has been in wild rover mode.

Kane takes the ball by the left of the D, spins to wrap his right instep around the ball and try to bend it into the top right corner. Kovar, the PSV goalkeeper, soars to his left to claw it away with his top hand.

Karabec is not going to be able to continue. Good cross from Hall from the left wins the applause of Kane. So near.

Karabec is hurt in a collision with Alexander-Arnold that the referee does not deem a foul.

Every tackle, every collision inspires a Czech demand for a red card. Karabec hits the deck like a bag of hammers when brushed by Rogers’ arm but the referee isn’t buying the implication that he had been elbowed.

Lewis-Skelly ignores Hall’s underlapping run down the inside left and pops it short to Guehi instead. The City defender slips a pass down the outside for Gordon who dribbles into the box and clips an inviting, low cross through the six-yard box. Rogers may have got a touch at the near post and the ball runs across goal. Karabec juts about gets it away,  avoiding the risk of shanking it into his own goal.

Krejci wants a tot-for-tat red card for Lewis-Skelly who slid in and caught Cerv on the foot. He never raised his studs and yellow suffices. The manager Santi is also booked for protesting the colour.

The system seems to be working again. Apologies for the break in updates.

Good work by Kane down the left to get away from Chaloupek and run into the box. He clips a short pass to the near post that Saka tries to finish, improvising a flick, that balloons wide off a defender. The angle made that all but impossible.

That is a big moment in the game, with Pavel Sulc dismissed for a stamp on Elliot Anderson. There was little protest about the foul when it occurred. In fact, even a yellow was a bit surprising. But Umut Meler was sent to the pitchside monitor. Czech Republic looked lively but you would now expect them to sit back and defend.

Czechs are now in a 5-4-0 formation. This will be a test of England to break through the two lines of defence. It will be like the Ghana match at the World Cup.

Pavel Sulc, who was playing so well, has been sent off after the referee was sent to the monitor by VAR. It was a high tackle, catching Anderson’scalf with his studs.

That red card has deprived the Czech Republic of their best player so far. He took it well rather than going off in a Sulc.

Big test for Czech manager Santi Denia, once of Atlético Madrid, who was manager of Spain U17s when they lost the 2017 final to an England team featuring – among other luminaries – Marc Guéhi and Morgan Gibbs-White.

Gordon cuts in from the left on to his right and flashes a shot across goal that flies past the right post.

The ball rebounds to Anderson who flays a shot from 18 yards that Chaloupek throws himself in front of to block only to divert it to Saka and Hranac is there to block that one.

How have England not scored!? 🤯Somehow Czech Republic keep the score at 0-0 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 🇨🇿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/51tmBwgRRf

England are dicing with danger in not picking up Sulc.

What was Thomas Tuchel saying about his England players being a danger to themselves around the box? It was an error there from Elliot Anderson that let Czech Republic through on goal and a better touch from Pavel Sulc would have seen them take the lead. Harry Kane dropped deep to start England’s attack down the right. The flanks will be their route to goal in this game.

Alexander-Arnold loses the ball in the middle of the park. Radosta is sent down the right by a cute pass and he gulls Hall by crossing early after shaping to go down the line. Alexander-Arnold is back to head it away but only as far as Cerv who torpedoes a volley from 25 yards barely a foot wide of the right post.

Kane is given a talking to for tangling with the Czech captain Krejci, giving him a deserved shove hopefully for the heinous crime of wearing the No 7 shirt while playing at centre-half.

Lewis-Skelly mops up at the back after a third rapid Czech Republic break, this one down the right with Chaloupek to the fore. Shielding the ball in the penalty area, he buys a foul and England build again from a free-kick.

Lovely pass by Rogers sends Saka down the right and the Arsenal winger tries to whip over a cross to pick up Kane’s near-post dart but it goes behind the England captain.

The Professional Footballers’ Association has leapt to Cole Palmer’s defence following his withdrawal from the England squad.

The union’s CEO,  Maheta Molango, said the Chelsea forward is a victim of a “sick” system that is demanding too much from players physically.

“When England see five players who need to withdraw when the single most proud moment a player has is to be called up for the national team, you just ask yourself, what’s wrong about the industry?” Molango said at the Fifpro performance summit in London.

“You see people like Cole Palmer, someone who would have played four consecutive summers in a row had he gone to the World Cup, and you wonder why is he missing?”He’s missing because he’s a victim of the calendar and that’s something that needs to absolutely trigger the alarm bells.”

Trevoh Chalobah will earn his third England cap in tonight’s Nations League match against Czech Republic. The Como centre-back, 27, played in the 6-4 defeat of France in the Bronze final at the World Cup and his other appearance for the Three Lions was in the defeat by Senegal last year.

Trent Alexander-Arnold will make his first England appearance in 15 months after being given a start. The Real Madrid full-back, who was not selected for the World Cup in the summer, earned his last cap against Andorra in 2025.

He replaces Jarell Quansah in Thomas Tuchel’s line-up that lost to Spain at the weekend.

“Trent had a very good training week and the excellent training in Wembley after the match, where he showed that he absolutely wants to play and wants to be with us,” said Tuchel on the eve of the game at Fortuna Arena.

“We’re good. Everything is fine. He’s ready to go. He has qualities that you all know, like he’s strong on the ball, excellent crossing, good finishing. And very, very good on the ball. That’s basically what he brings.”

Ezri Konsa, who missed team training on the day before this game, is out. Morgan Rogers, meanwhile, steps in for Jude Bellingham in the No10 role as Tuchel looks to juggle four matches in 11 days during this extended international break.

Trent Alexander-Arnold is in line to make his first England start under head coach Thomas Tuchel for tonight’s Nations League game against Czech Republic.

Injuries to Nico O’Reilly and Ezri Konsa have forced Tuchel into changes at the back, with Alexander-Arnold expected to come in at right-back, Trevoh Chalobah to replace Konsa and Lewis Hall to step in for O’Reilly.

Alexander-Arnold has made only one appearance under Tuchel, as a substitute in a World Cup qualifying win against Andorra in June 2025. His last start for England came under interim head coach Lee Carsley, when he scored in a victory over Finland.

Jude Belllingham could be given a rest after playing the full 90 minutes in the defeat by Spain, which would give Morgan Rogers an opportunity in the No 10 position.

Man City used ‘sham’ sponsorships in £830m cheating scheme

Manchester City arranged “sham” sponsorships in a near-£1bn plot to flout Premier League rules, an independent commission has found.

It was confirmed on Tuesday that City had been found guilty of all charges related to “serious breaches” of the league’s financial rules, with the commission also upholding all but one in relation to their failure to co-operate with an investigation spanning over three years.

The commission found that, of £949.94m City claimed in commercial income over a nine-year period, only £119.25m was legitimate, with the remaining £830.69m illicitly paid by their Abu Dhabi owners.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Uefa Nations League match between Czech Republic and England from Slavia Prague’s Eden Stadium. The home side, 49th in the Fifa rankings, scrambled their way to World Cup qualification with victories in the play-offs in penalty shoot-outs over Ireland and Denmark, promptly stank Group A out in Mexico/Canada/United States, drawing with South Africa but losing to South Korea and Mexico to finish last.

Miroslav Koubek, their 74-year-old manager, the oldest in the competition’s history, promptly stood down and has been replaced by their first foreign head coach, Santi, the former Atlético Madrid centre-half, who spent 15 years moving from managing Spain’s U17s, to the U19s and then the U21s. Little wonder, given his CV, that he is looking to refresh his squad with a transfusion of young players, a requirement made all the more urgent by the international retirement of stalwart centre-forward Patrick Schick and the absence of West Ham’s Tomas Soucek who damaged his ankle in that 3-0 defeat by Mexico on June 25 and has not kicked a ball since.

Santi started his stint in charge and this campaign in Group A3 with a 2-1 defeat by Croatia but there were some very positive signs – they set up as a 4-3-3 in classic Spanish/Cruyff style and pressed like dervishes. England, who conceded three goals when players made mistakes when subjected to aggressive pressing in their opening 3-2 defeat by world champions Spain, will have to find better solutions tonight, either by holding their nerve or counterpressing with fewer mistakes.

Given England are ranked 45 places higher, their results, if not all performances, at the World Cup were commendable and the way in which they rattled Spain and should really have given themselves a bulwark against the comeback by converting their penalty at 2-1 up,  an away win should be relatively straightforward. But they did lose on their last visit to Prague in a Euro 2020 qualifier having won 5-0 in the home leg.

#1370. Russell must do something wacky now after disappointing Bahrain GP qualifying

Never mind the lack of an ice vest, George Russell is somehow going to need to be the coolest man in Malaysia if he is to turn seventh on the grid into a positive result in Sunday’s Bahrain Grand Prix.The first race in Sepang in nearly a decade – a late addition to the calendar because of the conflict in the Middle East – promises to be an absolute scorcher. It might even be worth setting your alarm for the 8am UK start time. Red Bull’s Max Verstappen will start in pole position for the first time this year. He will have Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton alongside him.

It will be the first time since Hungary 2023 that those two gladiators have started on a front row together. Throw in sweltering temperatures, low grip, high tyre degradation, and the ever-present threat of a Malaysian monsoon sweeping through Sepang, and you have the potential for fireworks.

Russell might need something wacky if he is to do anything from that far back. This was a desperately disappointing result for the British driver. After his victory in Baku last weekend, Russell was hopeful he had finally found the winning formula and that he could continue to take the fight to his team-mate Kimi Antonelli, whom he trails in the drivers’ championship by 66pts.

Eighth, four places behind, and 0.24sec slower than the Italian, was not what Russell would have had in mind, although both Mercedes drivers will rise a spot because of the five-place grid penalty meted out to Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar for exceeding his engine allowance for the season.Russell will have felt particularly disappointed as Antonelli only got one run in Q3 after using up a set of soft tyres when he made a mistake and went off track in Q2. He now trails his team mate nine-seven in qualifying head-to-head this year.“No to be honest,” Russell admitted when asked whether he knew why he was so slow. “This circuit is an outlier in terms of the abrasiveness of the tarmac.“The lap times seven years ago were six or seven seconds faster and at certain points on the track it feels like you are driving on gravel, which is the same for everyone, but it is clearly affecting us more than others.”Mercedes’ lack of performance was doubly unexpected because not only did they arrive here with a massive upgrade package, but Russell revealed this week that he and Antonelli were foregoing the cooling vests you see some drivers sporting on the grid, in favour of car performance.

Toto Wolff, the Mercedes team principal, admitted it was a head-scratcher. “Very difficult to understand,” the Austrian said. “We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we did not see all year, but then you can say it is very hot and the tarmac is different to all the [other] tracks. It looked really good this morning. We seemed to have, at least with Kimi, made a step in understanding. And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”

Still, both titles are in the bag so Wolff cannot be too unhappy. Russell is the one who will be really miffed. He really needs to be beating his team-mate pretty much every race weekend if he is to get his title hopes back on track.

At the front, the mood was somewhat different. Verstappen became the first non-Mercedes-powered pilot to take a pole position this year. It was a first pole position for Red Bull Powertrains, too. And with his long run pace looking more than decent, Verstappen should really hold on for his first win of 2026. Hamilton will do his best to hang on to the Dutchman’s coattails. The seven-time champion was delighted when told he had taken P2. “Let’s go guys! Finally! Great job guys, really great job. Car felt great.”

This was indeed an excellent performance from the Ferrari man – and just the tonic for the Scuderia after weeks of gossip and speculation. Hamilton was admittedly three tenths slower than his rival, which he put purely down to a power deficit on the straights, but he said he was hopeful his long run pace was more competitive. The last time a F1 held a race was held here back in 2017, the British driver claimed pole only to be overhauled by a youthful Verstappen. He will be desperate to turn the tables this time.

“It was really hard to find a good balance, and we made one change before qualifying and we hit the sweet spot,” he reflected afterwards. “I am so, so grateful. I will try my best to hold on to Max tomorrow, and if we are in the fight that would be awesome. I’ve been talking too much, but I guess you talk more when you are happy. It was my best lap of the year. It feels like I won, and I will give it everything tomorrow.”

It is Russell, though, who needs a result even more badly if he is to remain a factor in the championship. “As a team, we have yet to have a bad race this whole season and this was clearly a very bad qualifying for us,” he admitted, adding that “all the numbers” from the upgrade package suggested it was an improvement on the old car. “But I think there is going to be a lot happening tomorrow. The tyre deg is huge and race pace will be king. So even though today was a real disappointment it is not the be all and end all.”

No. 1 ☝️#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/01PqrckQS9

Tomorrow’s race will be the first time since Hungary 2023 that Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton will start on the front row together. It is a reasonable run down to turn one and there are overtaking opportunities through the first few corners at Sepang, with it being similar to the configuration in China, with plenty of lines and moves on offer.

Respect between two great champions 🤩#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/fbZ6aoKRyw

“Very difficult to understand. It looked really good this morning. We seemed to have, at least with Kimi [Antonelli], made a step in understanding. And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”

On Kimi Antonelli’s track limits breach in Q2:

“Not good, because Q2 you know you are going to get through. You lose a set [of softs] in a qualifying that is so tight, where we are on the back foot. That is not good.”

Lewis Hamilton says this is the biggest crowd he has ever seen at Sepang, thanking the fans for making it here today. That is actually a bigger compliment than many watching at home may realise. The traffic this weekend has been horrendous. After 10 years without a race in Malaysia, during which time F1 has grown massively, I think they have forgotten how to do traffic management. Shuttles are inconsistent, taxis can’t get in/out, it’s taking forever just to reach the airport a few kilometres away - some fans have been braving the heat and walking. It took over two hours to get back into Kuala Lumpur last night (48km). “The car has been very good since last week. It is good to come back [from his wrist injury] at such a time and I am enjoying it, fighting for the top three. Even though it was not my finest qualifying session it is a good feeling.

“It is a bit unfortunate we take a penalty on a track where we are that fast but, from eighth, I am confident we can come through the field and come back for a good result.”

“I love this energy [from the crowd]. Big, big thank you to Malaysia for welcoming us. It is so hot here. I keep saying it, but that has made it a massive challenge for the tyres, the car, the mechanics in the garage. I am really, really thankful to my team. We made so many changes through all these practice sessions. Because the cars are sliding, the tyres are overheating, it was really hard to find a good balance, and we made one last change going into qualifying and I think we hit the sweet spot. To be able to close the gap to two or three tenths to Max [Verstappen], who has been so quick all weekend, is great, and I am so grateful.

“I am much happier with where the car is, but tomorrow is a completely different ballgame. Making these tyres last around this track, they are overheating from the get-go. Every little bit of wheelspin you have, every little snap you have makes a difference of how far you are going to go. I like to think we have got a good balance. Max was really quick on his long runs, so I will just try my best to hold onto him tomorrow.”

The screens in the media centre here in Sepang tell me that the air temp right now is 32.8C and the track temp is 58C. It feels even hotter. Lots of chat about cooling vests this week, which are optional. George Russell is among the drivers who isn’t using one, which is interesting a) because Russell has suffered badly from heat in the past (Qatar, Singapore) and b) because he says Mercedes chose to put the development money into car upgrades instead.

It’s an interesting admission. Not everyone is sold on the idea of cooling vests. Ferrari and McLaren will definitely be using them this weekend, for instance. Max Verstappen won’t as he doesn’t like them. Russell thinks the FIA should just develop the tech themselves and it shouldn’t be part of the budget cap.

“Our team have put a lot of emphasis this year on the cockpit temperature,” he said. “We won’t be running the cooling vest because we haven’t put the resource into making it robust enough. I feel we need the FIA just to step in and say ‘Here’s some money extra in the cost cap or there’s an external company who’s going to develop it for everybody’. Because we should all be wearing it. When it works, it works great. So, I would like to wear it this week, and I would like to wear it next week. But the team asked me...look, we can develop it, and we can put the money towards it...[but at a cost].

He added: “The top itself is not expensive ..you’ve got to effectively make a system where you can fit a block of dry ice or actual ice, and then has the airflow to circulate the cool water throughout. If that system isn’t robust enough, then suddenly you have no circulation, and then you get hot. You get ambient temperature circulating. The vest is one-design, but the system that circulates the water is different [at different teams].”

Hadjar has looked good since returning from his wrist injury so could be fighting it out near the front of the grid, although his five-place penalty will drop him down. We know Lindblad will be at the back and is very likely to be joined there by Colapinto, who is not going to be qualifying high up in the top ten in his Alpine.

Haas have announced that Frenchman Esteban Ocon will leave at the end of this season. Ocon now faces an uncertain future, with it difficult to see a spot for him on the F1 grid next season. There are suggestions that the 30-year-old’s replacement will be Brazilian Ferrari junior Rafael Camara, although nothing has been confirmed on that front. 21-year-old Camara currently leads the Formula 2 championship.

TGR Haas F1 Team and Esteban Ocon will part ways at the conclusion of the 2026 season. With plenty of racing ahead, our focus remains on working together to maximize every opportunity through to the final race of the year.#HaasF1 #F1 pic.twitter.com/4iQAuqnSyA

Aston Martin have now confirmed their driver line-up for next season, retaining both Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll. There had been reports that Alonso had been contemplating retirement but the 45-year-old will continue into another season.

Aston Martin Aramco confirms Lance and Fernando will continue as the team's drivers in 2027. Read more: ​https://t.co/ePyjJdyAIB pic.twitter.com/VogFUEbNxy

Other than the second seat alongside Ollie Bearman at Haas, the only other team to keep an eye on is Racing Bulls, with no definite confirmation on their exact driver line-up for next season.

Ferrari this week have publicly backed their team principal Frederic Vasseur, amid speculation over the Frenchman’s position and comments made by former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner, who said the job at Ferrari would be a “dream job”. Ferrari, who sit second in the constructors’ standings, have not won the drivers’ championship since 2007 (Kimi Raikkonen) and the constructors’ since 2008. Here is a snippet from Tom Cary’s piece on the matter:

In a hastily convened media call on Tuesday morning, Maria Conti, Ferrari’s chief communication officer, said the Scuderia had decided to issue a vote of confidence in Vasseur in response “not just to the story of Mr Horner, but in general, the speculation about Fred”.

“Ferrari has made its choices,” Conti said. “We have confidence – full confidence – in Fred Vasseur and in his team, and we continue to do so.

“At this time, it’s really important that the team remains united and cohesive, and we are focused with all the energy on the work ahead.”

“It is great to be back [in Malaysia]. I am really enjoying the track. We have had some wonderful races here over time. It is actually the 20th time we have been here, it started in 1999, and it is really exciting to be back. I really enjoyed getting out on the track and watching the cars closely.

“The drivers are super fit and they have some cooling but it is not easy. But you almost cannot get enough fluid through your body before your stomach gives up. Having this race and Singapore back-to-back increases that challenge.”

Especially with the big upgrade they have brought this weekend, Mercedes’ lead at the summit is looking unassailable right now.

Almost nine years ago to the day, Max Verstappen took just his second race victory in Formula 1. Lewis Hamilton, who took pole position, and Daniel Ricciardo joined Verstappen on the podium. Despite being nine years ago, plenty of drivers still on the grid were racing that weekend. Here they are and who they were racing for:

Max Verstappen (Red Bull) Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes) Valtteri Bottas (Mercedes) Esteban Ocon (Force India)Nico Hulkenberg (Renault)Sergio Perez (Force India)Fernando Alonso (McLaren)Lance Stroll (Williams)Carlos Sainz (Toro Rosso)Pierre Gasly (Toro Rosso)

With Russell winning in Baku and Antonelli finishing fifth, the latter’s championship lead was cut to 66 points. If Russell is going to usurp his teammate, he is going to need a few more similar results to last weekend due to the size of Antonelli’s lead. If Antonelli were to suffer a retirement, then that completely changes the outlook.

Formula One returns to Malaysia for round 16 of the season for the Bahrain Grand Prix. That probably sounds strange but after the Bahrain Grand Prix was originally postponed in March, F1 reinstated it to the calendar with Malaysia hosting it because of the ongoing war in the Middle East. Despite being held in Malaysia, Bahrain have retained the naming rights for the event, which is officially known as the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. The last time Formula One was in Malaysia was nine years ago back in 2017, when a young whippersnapper named Max Verstappen, still four years away from winning his first world championship, claimed just his second victory.

Last time out around the streets of Baku, Mercedes’ George Russell claimed victory at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, pipping Verstappen by just a tenth of a second. That was Russell’s first grand prix win since June and cuts his team-mate Kimi Antonelli’s lead in the drivers’ standings to 66 points. Antonelli had a challenging weekend in Baku, starting 16th after a crash in qualifying and coming home in fifth to see his championship lead to Russell cut by 15 points.

Verstappen was quickest in first practice yesterday, with the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc fastest in second practice. Earlier today, championship leader Antonelli was nearly three tenths clear of the field in third practice. Mercedes, 160 points clear at the top of the constructors’ standings, have brought significant upgrades this weekend, which includes a new floor, rear suspension and rear corner. It is the team’s first significant car update since the Canadian Grand at the end of May.

This race in Malaysia represents the second leg of the season’s first flyaway triple header, with the Singapore Grand Prix to come next weekend, so the demands on the teams and the drivers are incredibly high. Qualifying from Sepang gets under way at 9am (GMT).

#1369. Observation of prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The dynamics of isolated quantum systems following a sudden quench has a central role in many areas of material science, high-energy physics and quantum chemistry1,2,3,4. Such far-from-equilibrium quantum dynamics—which features complex phenomena with implications for thermalization, non-equilibrium phase transitions and Floquet phase engineering5,6,7,8—is challenging to study numerically, in particular, in high-dimensional systems9,10. Here we use a programmable neutral-atom quantum simulator11 to systematically explore quench dynamics in spin models with up to 180 qubits. By initializing the system in a product state and performing quenches across a broad parameter space, we discover several stable, qualitatively distinct dynamical regimes. We trace their robustness to Floquet-like prethermal steady states8 that are stabilized over exponentially long emergent timescales by strong dynamical constraints. We further observe sharp peaks in the dynamical response that are quantitatively explained by the structured melting of prethermalization through resonances. In two dimensions, we uncover a prethermally driven, first-order dynamical phase transition linked to the proliferation of Néel-order defects6,12, and probe it quantitatively using a generalized Clausius–Clapeyron test. Together, these results establish a programmable route to high-energy prethermal phase structure: long-lived dynamical phases, their resonant breakdown and a first-order dynamical phase transition that is not inherited from the equilibrium phase boundaries.
