#1323. Replacing the neurons that Parkinson’s destroys

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Laura Dattaro is a science journalist in Maplewood, New Jersey.

In people with Parkinson’s disease, neurons in the brain that produce dopamine are continuously lost. Without the neurotransmitter, which is crucial for movement, control of motor function begins to break down, resulting in symptoms such as tremors — one of the hallmarks of Parkinson’s.

Replacing dopamine is the goal of many treatments. Since the 1960s, that’s been done with a drug called levodopa, an amino acid that the brain converts to dopamine. But that conversion is carried out by the dopamine neurons that Parkinson’s eats away at. Lose too many, and the medication can no longer reliably control symptoms.

Some researchers have therefore long been eyeing the possibility of restoring those neurons. That entails growing them outside the brain and then injecting them through holes drilled into each side of the skull. The hope is that the cells will take root and begin to replenish the dwindling supply of dopamine.

Nearly four decades after such a transplant was first attempted, the work is beginning to pay off. Since early 2025, four phase I and II clinical trials have reported early results showing that the treatment is largely safe, with some people reporting improved motor skills and less ‘off’ time, during which their medication is ineffective. Off time can result from small daily changes, such as to diet, as well as the loss of dopamine neurons over time. Some of those treatments are moving into phase III trials for efficacy. More trials are in the works, raising cautious hopes that a new treatment for the disease is on the horizon. One of the first trials to test the cells in people with Parkinson’s was successful enough that the treatment is already available in Japan, albeit under strict regulatory oversight.

“This is such an exciting place to be,” says Claire Henchcliffe, a neurologist at the University of California, Irvine. “These are first-in-human trials. We’ve never had any products like these before.”

Despite the momentum, no one thinks that the treatment is ready for large-scale use. The trials so far have been small, with no control groups, and were designed to measure safety, not effectiveness. They’ve opened up a host of questions for researchers to investigate, including which type of cell to transplant, how many to deliver and where to inject them. There’s also work to be done to understand how the brain responds to its new members.

Transplanting foreign cells requires around one year of immunosuppression, and the brain surgery itself carries risks, including haemorrhage and infection. But the trials move cell transplants from a theory requiring proof to an early-stage treatment needing development, says molecular neurobiologist Kwang-Soo Kim at McLean Hospital in Belmont, Massachusetts, who completed the first transplant of neurons derived from the cells of a person with Parkinson’s in 20171. The question now, Kim says, is, “How can we optimize them?”

To begin down the road to approval, researchers led by Jun Takahashi at Kyoto University, Japan, injected cells grown from donor tissue — known as allogenic cells — into the brains of seven people with Parkinson’s. The procedure seemed to be safe: none developed tumours, a concern of transferring immature cells into the body2.

Positron emission tomography (PET) scans showed that, two years after surgery and around 9 months after immunosuppression was stopped, on average, participants had more dopamine in the putamen — the part of the brain into which the neurons are injected — than they did before the procedure. This showed that the transplanted cells remained biologically active, even after immunosuppression was stopped. The movement symptoms of some of the participants also showed signs of improvement.

On the basis of the results, the Japanese government gave the team conditional approval for the cell transplantations. This regulatory stage gives people access to the therapy, and the costs are covered by the national health insurance system, while researchers closely observe and document their progress — similar to being in a phase III clinical trial in the United States. Full approval will take seven years, Takahashi says, during which his team will monitor safety and efficacy.

The concept behind stem-cell therapy for Parkinson’s was first tested in people in the 1980s, when researchers transplanted dopaminergic neurons taken from 8–10-week-old aborted fetuses into the brains of people with Parkinson’s. The participants showed improvements in their motor symptoms. After three years, one participant had improved enough to stop taking levodopa. Nearly two decades after treatment, two individuals still had the motor improvements seen in the years immediately after surgery and had stopped taking medication more than a decade earlier.

Dopamine neurons are lost in Parkinson’s.Credit: Janko Kajtez/Parmar lab

But this approach has a major flaw: fetal tissue is rare and difficult to obtain, and using cells derived from it in research is legally and ethically complex, says Malin Parmar, a neurobiologist at Lund University in Sweden. Parmar has worked on the TransEuro study, which used fetal tissue for the treatment of Parkinson’s3. “You can never upscale them into reliable therapies,” Parmar says.

But a 2006 discovery4 of how to revert any mature tissue into stem cells — dubbed induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) — and then coax them into becoming any other cell was a game-changer. Suddenly it was possible to imagine creating vast amounts of cells for research and medicine, and it didn’t take long for researchers to start probing the best ways to turn iPSCs into dopaminergic neurons — work that is now making its way to people. “It has turned from, ‘This has been done before, it won’t work,” to suddenly, ‘Oh boy, I can’t keep up with all the clinical trials,” Henchcliffe says.

In 2023, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared the way for Sumitomo Pharma in Osaka, Japan, which makes the cell product used by Takahashi, to conduct trials in the United States. Three people have already received transplants, says Joseph Ciacci, a neurosurgeon at the University of California, San Diego, who is leading the trial. His team aims to treat eight people.

Ciacci is hopeful that the brains of people he has treated can recover lost function after the transplants. The new neurons could be a buffer against treatments such as levodopa becoming less effective over time. “I feel very excited about it,” he says.

Sumitomo says it has also begun a larger trial that will enrol dozens of people, including a control group that will receive sham surgery. The company aims to compare the cells used in both trials and launch its therapy in the United States by 2032.

Three other trials have reported results so far, using a mix of cell types. All have a small sample size — fewer than 15 people — and none of them has a control group. The results should therefore be interpreted cautiously, researchers say. Still, all of the studies that have reported data met their safety endpoints and showed early signs of clinical benefit.

A trial involving 12 people, co-led by Henchcliffe, reported similar results to those of Takahashi’s team, including increased dopamine uptake at 18 months measured using PET and improvements in motor scores5. The trial was sponsored by stem-cell specialist BlueRock Therapeutics in Cambridge, Massachusetts, which is a subsidiary of multinational pharmaceutical company Bayer.

Blue Rock’s cell product, called bemdaneprocel, received the FDA’s Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapy (RMAT) designation in 2024 and the Japanese health ministry’s Pioneering Regenerative Medical Product designation in December 2025. The team is currently enrolling participants in a phase III trial that will include a sham-surgery control group; it aims to transplant cells into 102 people in the United States, Canada and Australia and monitor their motor function for 18 months.

A third trial in eight individuals, run by the biotech company Aspen Neuroscience in San Diego, California, used dopaminergic neurons generated from the participants’ own cells, known as autologous cells. The cell recipients showed motor improvements, and several were able to reduce their dose of levodopa, according to results presented at the International Conference on Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s Diseases in March.

Dopaminergic progenitor cells are injected into the brain of a person with Parkinson’s.Credit: Kyoto University Hospital

The company has now completed transplants in another seven people with its cell product, called sasineprocel, and received RMAT designation in July. It plans to begin a phase III trial of the treatment this year.

In the same month, Parmar and her colleagues reported the first results of a trial, called STEM-PD, in which they transplanted neurons derived from embryonic stem cells into eight patients. The participants showed “good early signs” of symptom improvement, Parmar says. Six of the seven people who completed the follow-up period opted to reduce their dose of levodopa as a result. Similar to the other trials, none grew tumours or had other serious reactions to the cells, but one participant died ten weeks after the transplant owing to an infection they developed while taking immunosuppressive drugs6.

Taken together, Parmar says, the trial results show that the transplanted cells survive and don’t generate tumours. But more people need to be followed up for longer periods before the treatment can truly be called effective, especially given that treatments such as levodopa already exist, she says. She recommends that researchers adopt an approach of skynda långsamt, a Swedish phrase meaning to rush slowly. “What we have is really hopeful and very promising,” Parmar says. “But the expectations are super high.”

While trials seek evidence that the approach works, researchers are also trying to get a better understanding of how the brain responds to allogeneic and autologous transplants, with an eye to further boosting safety and efficacy.

Allogenic transplants require that people undergo immunosuppression, generally for one year, to prevent the brain from attacking or rejecting the cells. But some researchers are working on a way to do away with that need by genetically ‘cloaking’ allogenic cells — editing certain genes to hide the cells from the immune system7.

Last year, a team led by researchers at the Florey Institute in Melbourne, Australia, coaxed human stem cells into overexpressing genes that modulate the immune system. They then grew the cells into neurons and implanted them into a rat model of Parkinson’s. The rats that received the edited cells mounted less of an immune response than did those that received unedited neurons, and showed greater improvement in motor symptoms8.

Autologous cells don’t require such immunosuppression. But they do have their own drawbacks. Because they need to be generated for each person, individuals need to wait months before the cells can be implanted — a particular problem for people with Parkinson’s, whose neurons are continuously being destroyed. Using individualized cells for each transplant also introduces variation that makes measuring outcomes in clinical trials difficult, Parmar says. It’s more expensive than a treatment using allogenic cells, too, which researchers hope will eventually be available in large, off-the-shelf batches.

It’s even possible, says Parmar, that autologous cells from a person with Parkinson’s might be innately susceptible to developing the disease after transplantation, meaning that the treatment’s success could be shorter-lived. In 2020, Parmar and her team transplanted neurons derived from either an embryonic stem-cell line or a person with a gene mutation linked to Parkinson’s into a rat model of the disease. Both types of cell survived and rats receiving either type had improved symptoms. But in the rats that received the cells with the Parkinson’s gene, the transplanted grafts showed early signs of disease development9. Regardless of the source, turning immature brain cells into a viable, accessible treatment will require improvements to the processes for generating them en masse. Researchers are hoping that automation and standardization will bring down both the cost and the time needed to produce them. Some draw comparisons to full-genome sequencing: the first full human genome cost hundreds of millions of dollars to sequence, but today it can be done for about US$1,000.

Work is also needed to improve the survival of implanted cells. Although the trials — which are testing both high and low cell doses — show that some cells do take root in the brain and become productive dopamine-producing neurons, many more do not. In the BlueRock trial, for example, researchers delivered 900,000 cells to each side of the brain of people in the low-dose group, but they expected that only 150,000 cells per side would survive. In the high-dose group, participants received 2.7 million cells on each side of the brain in an attempt to have 300,000 survive5.

“After the cells are put into brain, you have no more control,” says Su-Chun Zhang, director of the Center for Neurologic Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys, a non-profit research institute in La Jolla, California. “They are on their own.”

Some researchers who are trying to improve cell survival think that the environment into which cells are transplanted might matter — just as the quality of a plot of land can affect a gardener’s outcomes. “We have spent many, many years to improve the seed,” Kim says. “But we didn’t pay attention to the soil.”

Like fertilizing soil, preparing the brain before the transplant could help. Some groups, for example, are exploring whether injecting specific growth factors along with the cells might coax them into becoming mature dopamine neurons. And in 2023, Kim and his team discovered a phenomenon they called ‘needle trauma’ in mice, in which the brain responds to placebo injections with an immune response that causes inflammation and kills brain cells. Transplanting immune cells called T cells along with the placebo injection suppressed the response10.

Kim is also concerned about the potential for cells to acquire mutations during the reprogramming and manufacturing process — and the potential long-term effects of such genetic changes, given that the cells might remain in a person’s brain for decades. “Stem-cell therapies are living products,” Kim says. Questions about such genomic integrity highlight the careful balance researchers must strike when pursuing a desperately sought after and potentially life-changing treatment but one that researchers still know so little about. That was obvious to Kim in 2020, when he was inundated with calls, e-mails and letters from people with Parkinson’s and their families after the publication of preliminary results for the first person to receive his transplant.

“We have to keep optimistic, and we have to give them hope,” Kim says. “But very informed hope.”

#1322. Gasperini: ‘Roma in the mix for Scudetto race, great performance in Manchester’

Gian Piero Gasperini admits Roma ‘are in the mix’ for the Scudetto race after thumping Sassuolo 3-0, and ‘even when we lost, we still scored lots of goals’ against Manchester United and Real Madrid.

The Giallorossi needed something to boost their confidence after fumbling a 2-0 lead to lose 3-2 at Manchester United in the Champions League midweek.

This was certainly convincing, as they never looked in danger when sweeping Sassuolo aside 3-0 thanks to Mario Hermoso, a deflected Donyell Malen effort and Rodrigo Mora’s angled drive through the legs of Duje Caleta-Car.

However, considering they had 28 shots against a side that has now lost five on the bounce, the 3-0 result seems limited.

“There were some very strong performances this evening, including a great Hermoso goal to break the deadlock, and it was not easy against a side that clammed up, but we played with quality,” Gasperini told Sky Sport Italia.

The last time they lost in the Champions League to Real Madrid when leading 3-1, it was also followed up immediately by a Serie A victory.

“There are defeats and defeats, though. It was an incredible run of games, we lost only to Real Madrid and Manchester United, but also had a run of victories, drew with Como and Napoli. Those two defeats hurt because they were late and we were leading, but they did come at the end of strong performances and against top level opponents.”

All three goals this evening were from battering through the Sassuolo defence, even when Alberto Aquilani changed tactics to smother them.

“Undoubtedly, this season we improved a lot in attack, so now we score lots of goals in different ways and with different players,” noted Gasperini.

“We are sharper too as well as having confidence, because Hermoso scored like a striker. I also saw an extraordinary Matias Soulé performance. Even when we lost, we scored lots of goals.

“In fact, I don’t believe this is a response to a defeat, it’s just more confirmation from this team of the track they are on. Let us not forget Balerdi had a great performance in Manchester until that unlucky moment, and that United only started the comeback thanks to an absurd penalty.”

Gasperini has always denied they are even in the conversation for the Scudetto, so he was asked if he’d take second place right now.

“I don’t know, it’s fun to play this season. We must not delude ourselves or disappoint ourselves, so there’s no harm in dreaming, especially with the journey that we are on. I don’t know what we could be capable of achieving,” he replied.

“As everyone says, quite rightly, Inter are the best placed to win. For the rest, all of us are in the mix, including us, and can have our chances. Lazio won nine of their last 10 games, so of course they are up there.

“If Inter slip up a bit, then everyone can dream and try to challenge.”

This result puts Roma in a strong position, because Inter and Como face each other on Sunday, while Lazio have a difficult trip to Napoli, so it should see them at least go into third place.

“We’re not interested in those games, we’re just sitting perched on the fence peering at them,” joked Gasperini.

#1321. Pierre Sage’s Lyon return ends in disappointment for Crystal Palace

Pierre Sage felt Crystal Palace were “really far off” his expectations after suffering a 3-2 away Europa League defeat by his former side Lyon.

Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.

Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break, before Pavel Sulc restored the two-goal lead, and substitute Daichi Kamada’s late goal proved a mere consolation.

“At the end, we were frustrated by the result, but in the first half we have to be frustrated in the way we play,” said Sage, speaking to PalaceTV.

“I think we didn’t play this first half. We are really far off our standards in the mental side of the play, in the tactical side of the play, because the players are too high between our lines and we really struggled a lot with that.

“When you give back the ball to your opponent, you suffer a lot and we were better in the second half. You cannot win this kind of game by playing only one half.”

Sage’s side got the better of his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, after they bounced back to beat Nottingham Forest 3-1 at Selhurst Park on Sunday.

After that victory, the Frenchman called for more consistency from his team, but on Thursday night was left ruing missed opportunities and goals conceded too easily by last season’s Conference League winners.

Sage was sacked by Lyon in January 2025 after a 14-month spell with the Ligue 1 outfit. Like Glasner’s, his own reunion ended in disappointment.

He told Uefa: “It’s a very disappointing return because we lost. I can’t take satisfaction from coming back home or seeing familiar faces when the result isn’t there.

“The scoreline may have been close, but there was a big difference in the way the two teams played.

“We improved considerably after the break and gave ourselves a chance, but conceding that third goal made things difficult.

“I think our second-half efforts deserved an equaliser, although winning would have been a generous reward given that we only really played [to our level] for one half.”

The veteran captain said: “It has been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it so we’re very happy with the performance.”

When asked about Evanilson’s header, which Smith supplied the assist for, he replied: “It wasn’t my best cross but I put it in an area, what a finish from him and I think we deserved that little bit of luck.

“From there on we went on to win the game but in the second half we got a little bit tired but the quality that came off the bench is great and we look forward to Sunday now.

“It’s a great header, he deserved it because he has worked very hard this season and many more to come from him.”

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Thursday night’s European football with Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Bournemouth in Europa League action, and Brighton hosting Kauno Zalgiris in the Uefa Conference League.

Palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. The former Palace shareholder was the reason the club missed out on Europa League participation last season because Lyon were in the same competition and thus Palace were considered in breach of multi-club ownership rules. Textor sold his stake in Palace, but despite the club’s best efforts they had to settle for the Conference League, a competition they subsequently won.

Palace could have been three or four down against Nottingham Forest at the weekend but fought back for a much-needed Premier League victory. They made a winning start in Europe, beating Lech Poznan 4-0 at Selhurst Park in their opening Europa League game.

Bournemouth and Sunderland also made winning starts, despite both teams’ poor form domestically. Sunderland travel to Portuguese side Torreense, while Sturm Graz are the opposition for Bournemouth’s first ever European game at the Vitality Stadium (or Dean Court if you prefer). Bournemouth continue to be without Justin Kluivert, Eli Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott because of injury.

Brighton are favourites to win the Conference League and play their first game in the competition against Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris. Lifting the trophy in Istanbul at the end of the season would assure Brighton of a place in next season’s Europa League, though given their Premier League form and Manchester City’s predicament, Champions League qualification could be a realistic aspiration. Brighton won with 10 men at Sunderland on Saturday, and were successful in their appeal against Pascal Struijk’s red card.

Mikel Arteta has praised Noni Madueke’s response to a difficult start to the season after the winger played another decisive role in Arsenal’s 1-0 victory over Hull City.

Martin Odegaard scored the only goal at the Emirates Stadium after 72 minutes, reacting quickest when Kostas Tzolakis saved Madueke’s effort.

Arsenal were far from their fluent best, but the victory moved the defending champions six points clear at the top of the Premier League.

As reported by Arsenal News, Arteta believes Madueke has transformed his performances after responding positively to limited playing time earlier in the campaign.

Arteta said of Madueke: “That’s the second part of the story – the first is that you need to earn the right to be able to do that.

“Noni did that, he reacted to not playing often, went away, started to train and was a different Noni.

“He wasn’t going to accept that situation, he meant business, and since then he has been incredible.

“Now you are in that position, he needs to hone and improve it, so let’s see if he can do that.”

Madueke was Arsenal’s most dangerous attacker against Hull, registering five successful dribbles and creating several opportunities.

Sky Sports also reports that he is now averaging 3.57 chances created per 90 minutes, the highest rate of any Premier League player this season.

Madueke’s improvement could be particularly important while Bukayo Saka is unavailable.

Earlier in the season, a January exit was even being discussed. CaughtOffside reported in September that Atletico Madrid and Juventus were monitoring his situation after his limited Premier League involvement.

That possibility now feels considerably less likely.

Madueke has responded exactly how Arteta would have wanted: rather than becoming frustrated, he worked independently during the international break and returned sharper. His passing accuracy, crossing and dribble success have all improved compared with last season.

There is still one obvious area to improve. Madueke had chances to score against Hull and could have made the victory far more comfortable.

But Arsenal now have a winger who is creating chances at an elite rate and increasingly influencing important matches. If he can add more ruthless finishing, Arteta may soon face a genuine selection dilemma when Saka returns.

#1319. Inside the insane trophy room of Chelsea legend Branislav Ivanovic: Framed pictures of his 42 goals, a ring from Didier Drogba... and an LED football pitch

Published: 04:50 EDT, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 04:50 EDT, 7 November 2026

Legendary Chelsea defender Branislav Ivanovic's insane private trophy room has gone viral after a fan posted a tour of the museum online.

The now 42-year-old made 377 appearances for the Blues during a nine-year stint at the club from 2008 to 2017.

He enjoyed a hugely successful time with the west London side, winning ten trophies and becoming one of the club's most decorated defenders.

As well as winning three Premier League titles he landed three FA Cups,  the League Cup, the Community Shield and the Europa League. He also has a Champions League winners' medal with the Blues, though the Serb did miss out on playing in the 2012 final after famously being told by Geoff Shreeves live on Sky Sports that he was suspended following their win over Barcelona in the semi-final.

Branislav Ivanovic won 10 trophies with Chelsea across nine years with the Blues

The Chelsea legend has built a private trophy room in his hometown of Sremska Mitrovica to rival any other

In a video posted to Instagram a fan from Ivanovic's hometown Sremska Mitrovica explained he was allowed access to the private showroom and documented the breadth of trophies, personal honours and shirts he has collected throughout his illustrious career.

Many of the souvenirs are from his time in Russia with Lokomotiv Moscow and Zenit St Petersburg, as well as those he got at Chelsea.

The private museum holds over hundreds of shirts alone and has an entire wall adorned with shirts just given to him and signed by someone he either played with or played against including the likes of Zlatan Ibrahimovic, Neymar and Javier Zanetti.

Most Chelsea fans will remember Ivanovic's most crucial goals such as his winners in the Champions League round of 16 against Napoli and the 2013 Europa League final against Benfica.

And the Serbian appears to have made an effort to immortalise every single one of his club goals by framing and displaying a photo of all 42 from throughout his career.

Amongst other quirky designs, the room has a set of football leg stools for guests to sit on at the bar

Mourinho gets a mention having won the Premier League, Fa Cup and League cup with the Serbian in the 2014-15 season

There is also a replica of every trophy he has won in his career as well and a specialty ring he received as a gift from Didier Drogba after Chelsea's 2012 Champions League triumph.

Ivanovic didn't forget to add some style to the room by installing an LED football pitch to light the room and putting swanky football leg chairs at a fully stocked bar.

He even has a slide solely dedicated to displaying quotes from his former manager Jose Mourinho about him including the Special One's description of Ivanovic as 'The Perfect One'.

Since leaving Chelsea in 2017 the Serb moved back to Zenit St Petersburg before ending his career back in England with West Brom in 2021.

#1318. Rodrigo Mora: ‘Football is crazy sometimes, Cristiano Ronaldo my idol’

Rodrigo Mora concedes ‘football is crazy’ after scoring his third consecutive Serie A goal for Roma and looks forward to a senior Portugal debut even without ‘idol’ Cristiano Ronaldo.

The 19-year-old talent was a big investment this summer from FC Porto, secured for €25m for effectively only half his contract.

It took a while for him to make his mark in the Giallorossi jersey, but this evening he scored in the 3-0 win over Sassuolo, his third consecutive Serie A match on target.

“It was a very good pass from Malen, I tried my luck, and I was happy to score another important goal, so Roma keep pushing with another win,” Mora told Sky Sport Italia.

He now has four goals in nine Serie A games, plus two assists in four Champions League appearances under Gian Piero Gasperini.

“When I arrived here, I thought we were strong. Every time I training I thought we were a very good team, we are proving that in the match and need to keep this momentum going.”

Mora seems to have really hit his stride in the last month, as after struggling to even get into the starting XI, he has flourished in recent weeks.

“Football is crazy, because one day you don’t play, the next you play. I was ready, now it’s my third goal in a row, so it’s important to always be ready when the moment comes.”

Rodrigo Mora has also received a call-up for the senior Portugal squad, which will be a very different team now that Cristiano Ronaldo has retired from international duty.

“It’s a very proud moment for me and my family, it is always a pleasure to play for Portugal. Now Cristiano is not there, but is an idol for everyone in Portugal, including me. I learned a lot when I came to the national team, I am very happy to be there.”

#1317. Steely Chelsea triumph despite losing Martinez to head injury

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

“Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso said: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

“We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding new ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

How different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

Neto fires past Pickford to double Chelsea's lead! 🔥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SOJeBP5mq0

It cannot be overlooked how this win owed a debt to the erratic refereeing of Paul Tierney, especially the amnesty he offered to Morgan Rogers on the stroke of half-time.

Already booked, Rogers was fortunate not to receive a second caution for a lunge on James Garner which took the man after the ball. A replica challenge by Everton’s Harrison Armstrong had warranted a yellow card in Tierney’s world just 21 minutes earlier.

The home team’s argument that this was a potential game changer was supported when the England midfielder was inevitably involved in the move which led to Neto breaking through 44 seconds into the second half – a lead Chelsea never looked like surrendering as Everton’s attacking limitations were exposed.

Chelsea break the deadlock inside a minute of the second half! ⚡ Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/E63rtGQnbv

That should not disguise how this is a different Chelsea, contrasting not just with the characterless and rudderless team of last season, but also the defensively flawed version that began this one. Mike Penders deputised for the stricken Martínez – conscious but taken to hospital as a precaution – and was well-protected.

As much as Alonso’s artistry as a midfield maestro is presumed to define him as a coach, one cannot help but believe there are many who underestimate him as a football student. He was never going to return to England clinging to one idea given his previous Premier League experience, and he intuitively knew an away game at Everton was one for foot soldiers.

He signed Jordan Henderson for such a task. Just like his manager, the former Liverpool captain was primed for enemy territory.

Alonso’s anticipation of a fixture in which a battle had to be fought before there was an outbreak of football proved correct, aided by the fussy and generally terrible first-half officiating of Tierney.

Bizarrely, Alonso had as much cause to curse Tierney for the first of several contentious decisions, booking Armstrong for an aggressive but ultimately fair lunging challenge on Josh Acheampong. That enraged the home supporters to inspire Everton to their most dangerous spell, Thierno Barry coming closest to troubling Martínez before half-time.

Although Moisés Caicedo was denied a goal-of-the-season contender when a vicious 20-yard volley struck the crossbar, the scrappy, stop-start flavour of the occasion initially suited the hosts.

Caicedo rattles the woodwork with a stunning effort! 💥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/CSIM9ogtSp

Rogers’s reprieve changed all that. Inexplicably inconsistent as Tierney was, Chelsea exhibited a steel which thrilled Alonso as much as those games when Cole Palmer, Rogers and João Pedro are in full flow.

“They didn’t score, but did a fantastic job for the team,” Alonso pointedly said of his attackers.

Alonso’s name has not echoed so loudly across the Mersey since he played a few miles down the road from Everton’s new home. After several calamitous appointments, those fans can believe their team are in safe hands again.

A good win for Chelsea at Everton, but above all, let’s hope Martinez is back to full health soon.

Moyes accepted that his side had were not good enough.

He told TNT Sports: “We were a little bit unlucky with the goals. It wasn’t good defending, but it takes a couple of deflections before it gets to Neto. It makes it a relatively easy finish for him.

“The second one was a free-kick which obviously ricochets around, so I think there were parts of the game we did OK, but we didn’t offer enough to create enough, to make enough chances. I can’t think of many, so that is probably the biggest indictment.”

He had a minor gripe over a first-half tackle that was reviewed, saying, “I think the Morgan Rogers tackle on Jimmy [Garner] could have been questioned.”

However, given the good start to the season for Everton so far, he does not have too much rancour.

"Not as good as we wanted." 💬 David Moyes reflects on Everton's defeat to Chelsea 🔵 🎙️ @jules_breach | Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/qPU64VjHYC

He describes the planned tests as “precautionary” and says, “as far as I know, he left the stadium conscious.”

Neto added more detail to his thoughts on the game.

On his first goal, he explained how Everton’s defensive approach allowed them to react: “We know that they came man-to man. In the second half we adjusted some stuff. We tried to get the best of the man-to-man press and we got away. We got the cross and I could finish well, so really happy.”

He credited his Portugal coach, Jorge Jesus, with his calmness in front of goal, adding: “This comes a little bit from the new coach of the national team that says when you are near to the area you need to pass to the goal, so really happy with that.”

With Chelsea now in the Champions League places, Neto was keen to keep up the momentum. He said: “It’s really important. We know it’s tough to play away, even at home there are no easy games. We came here with personality, with good intentions to win the match and really happy with the result.”

Chelsea captain Reece James’ surgery could be out for a couple of months, Xabi Alonso explained.

He told the  press: “I wish him the best recovery. We won’t set timelines, but we expect him to be out for several weeks. It’s not going to be short. Whether it’s before or after Christmas then time will tell. It needs to be done properly.”

He is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is important and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

In his press conference ahead of the weekend, Everton boss David Moyes was not too concerned by his relatively small squad.He said:  “Leicester City won the league with not too many players. We have not got too many players. I am not saying we’re going to win the league, but we want to try to challenge and be around the top teams.”

That might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

David Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

#1316. 'I want to win the Ballon d'Or': JJ Gabriel sets out his lofty ambitions as Man United wonderkid, 16, closes in on move to Real Madrid after quitting Red Devils

By BEN WILLCOCKS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 06:08 EDT, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 06:09 EDT, 7 November 2026

Manchester United wonderkid JJ Gabriel has revealed his ambition to win the Ballon d'Or as he dropped the clearest hint yet that he is heading to Real Madrid in an interview with Spanish media.

The 16-year-old sensation stunned Manchester United with a formal transfer request in September and is now on the verge of finalising his move to the Spanish capital.

Daily Mail Sport exclusively revealed Madrid's growing confidence in securing the free-scoring starlet last month, with Gabriel now having secured a European Union passport through his mother's Cypriot heritage.

The youngster, who is currently working with a personal trainer in Madrid, practically confirmed the transfer in an interview with Spanish newspaper Marca on Friday night, admitting he had a clear preference to Real over archrivals Barcelona.

'Obviously Madrid,' Gabriel told the outlet when asked which LaLiga giant he preferred.

According to the newspaper, who expects his move to be finalised in January, Gabriel's response prompted a laugh from his father and mentor Joe O'Cearuill.

Manchester United prodigy JJ Gabriel poses for his interview with Spanish newspaper Marca

Gabriel is set to complete a move to Real Madrid after formally requesting to leave Old Trafford

'My dream is to win the Ballon d'Or,' explained the talented youngster, who scored a hat-trick for Manchester United in the UEFA Youth League just days before submitting his transfer request.

Although Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe and Barcelona's Lamine Yamal narrowly missed out on winning the 2026 Ballon d'Or - which was held aloft by England captain and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane - the two LaLiga giants have long had a rich association with the award, regularly producing the world's best footballer.

While sources at United insist there has been no club-to-club contact, it appears only a matter of time before Gabriel is sporting Real Madrid's iconic all-white jersey.

It is understood Gabriel will play for Madrid's Castilla team, which plays in Spain's third division, as well as in the Youth League.

Gabriel broke a series of records playing for United youth teams, including becoming the youngest player to feature in the Under-18s.

The prodigy, who was 14 when he netted twice on his debut, has also played - and scored - for Manchester United's Under-21 side.

The Red Devils were rocked in September when Gabriel and his representatives made a bombshell request to have his academy contract torn up. That request was immediately refused by United and, while there was faint hope that a compromise could have been found to keep him at Old Trafford, he has stayed away ever since.

Gabriel's dream is to win the Ballon d'Or, which was awarded this year to England's Harry Kane

As Daily Mail Sport previously reported, United's decline since the days of Sir Alex Ferguson has been the driving force behind Gabriel's family seeking an exit. United have not won a Premier League title since 2013.

A source close to the family explained that United are 'far away' from the likes of Barcelona, Real Madrid, Bayern Munich, as well as domestic rivals Arsenal and Manchester City, and that they want him to 'learn from the best' to maximise his talents.

His father has been described as a fiercely ambitious, pushy parent and is credited with the decision to get JJ out of United in an attempt to fast-track his career.

#1315. Could chemicals contribute to Parkinson’s?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Tammy Worth is a freelance health-care reporter in Kansas City, Missouri.

Potential links between pesticide exposure and health problems are hard to tease out.Credit: brt COMM/Alamy

In May, Vermont became the first US state to pass legislation that bans most uses of paraquat, a chemical herbicide linked to an increased risk of Parkinson’s disease. Other states have also examined paraquat’s safety. California’s Department of Pesticide Regulation studied the chemical in 2024, but chose not to ban it. However, in August, after persistent advocacy from farm workers and environmental groups, the state announced plans to phase out paraquat over a two-year period.

Paraquat is already banned in 70 countries, including China, Brazil, Turkey and member states of the European Union (where it’s been prohibited for nearly 20 years). And paraquat isn’t the only chemical under scrutiny. Other pesticides have been identified as potential triggers of Parkinson’s disease, including the heavy metals; the fish poison rotenone and the solvent trichloroethylene (TCE), which used in dry cleaning.

Although many researchers are certain that environmental factors play a fundamental part in Parkinson’s risk, they have struggled to convince regulators, particularly at the US federal level. Population studies take decades to complete, and the interplay between environmental toxicants and individuals’ genetic risk is difficult to tease out. But many neurologists and Parkinson’s advocates think that the science is sufficient to link some chemicals to the condition.

The delay in regulatory action is not caused by a lack of research, says Beate Ritz, an epidemiologist at the Fielding School of Public Health at the University of California, Los Angeles. “You can pile on as much science as you want to; it won’t change a thing until there is political will.”

It’s widely accepted that Parkinson’s disease is linked to a combination of factors, including genetics, changes to the brain as it ages and environmental triggers.

Genetics might be the most well-understood factor. About 20 gene variants have been linked to Parkinson’s. These variants are thought to cause the accumulation of proteins that clump to form Lewy bodies — aggregations that damage dopamine-producing nerve cells and deplete the brain’s supply of this ‘feel-good’ neurotransmitter. The loss of dopamine affects the brain’s ability to control movement.

But genetics accounts for only about 5–15% of cases of Parkinson’s disease. Other causes include behavioural factors such as physical activity, diet and smoking. Head trauma, some medications and even having red hair (because of a mutation in the MC1R gene) could also increase risk.

The potential link between chemicals and Parkinson’s was discovered in the early 1980s. Neurologist William Langston and his colleagues at the Santa Clara Valley Medical Center in San José, California, found that a small number of people who had taken a synthetic opioid called MPTP exhibited Parkinson’s-like symptoms1. Langston noted that when MPTP entered the brain, it was quickly converted to the toxic metabolite MPP+, which damages dopamine-producing neurons and is structurally similar to chemicals such as paraquat.

There’s seldom a one-to-one correlation between a toxicant and the development of Parkinson’s, says Rebecca Gilbert, a neurologist specializing in Parkinson’s disease and chief mission officer of the New York City-based American Parkinson Disease Association. She says it’s rare that someone’s Parkinson’s can be traced directly to them playing on their grandfather’s farm that was sprayed with paraquat when they were seven years old. Instead, it’s typically an amalgam of several risk factors. “I picture it like a glass of water,” Gilbert says. “You pour in that exposure to the spraying when you were seven, and then you pour in genetics, and then you pour in a little TCE.”

Part of the challenge of deciphering how different chemicals contribute to Parkinson’s disease is that much of the damage occurs slowly, long before a person is diagnosed. And during those years, other factors can modify disease progression — making it difficult to pinpoint which exposures matter.

Study participants can’t be exposed to pollutants deliberately, so scientists seeking to establish that association are left with epidemiological and animal studies. But epidemiological studies take decades, and no country has an official registry of people with Parkinson’s disease for researchers to contact. And animal studies can’t completely mimic either the age-related loss of dopamine-producing brain cells or the full range of Parkinson’s symptoms.

Ray Dorsey, a neurologist at the Atria Health and Research Institute in New York City, studies environmental triggers of Parkinson’s. In work published in 2023, he highlighted a handful of case studies of people who developed Parkinson’s after TCE exposure2. One of these looked at 99 pairs of twins and found that exposure to TCE increased the risk of Parkinson’s by more than 500%. “We’re paying a really high price for dry-cleaning things,” Dorsey says.

One of the most well-known epidemiological studies of Parkinson’s involved military personnel stationed at Camp Lejeune, North Carolina. In 1982, the US Marine Corps found that water on the base was contaminated with volatile organic compounds, most notably TCE. A study3 published in 2023 focused on the health conditions of people who had been at Camp Lejeune for at least three months between 1975 and 1985. When researchers followed up these individuals between 1997 and 2021, they found that their rate of Parkinson’s disease was 70% higher than it was among personnel who had been living at Camp Pendelton, California — where the water was not contaminated — for at least three months during that same ten-year period3. Even among the Camp Lejeune veterans who did not have Parkinson’s, there was a higher prevalence of symptoms that might pre-date a Parkinson’s diagnosis, such as constipation, tremors and loss of sense of smell.

Use of the weedkiller paraquat has been linked to Parkinson’s disease.Credit: Romeo Gacad/AFP via Getty

Ritz uses geographical information system modelling to track environmental exposures and their link to conditions such as Parkinson’s. One of her focuses is farming communities. In a study published in 2024, she and her colleagues analysed people living or working near three agricultural counties in central California where farms were treated with paraquat4. The data went back to 1974, and peoples’ exposure times ranged from about 8 to 30 years. The researchers found that having higher exposure at work or at home increased the chance of getting Parkinson’s by 91%.

It’s intuitive to study people living and working in farming communities because of their direct contact with chemicals and the ability to track which products are used. But Dorsey co-authored a 2025 paper that found that the risk could extend to a wider population5. The study tracked people living near golf courses in Minnesota and Wisconsin. The researchers compared a 5,113-person control group and 419 people with Parkinson’s and found that living within 1.6 kilometres of a golf course raised the chance of getting Parkinson’s by 126%, compared with the risk for people who lived at least 9.6 kilometres away. The researchers also observed that this risk dropped the farther away people lived. The authors posited that the increased risk close by could be due to exposure to pesticides through inhalation and groundwater. Researchers didn’t measure the types or levels of pesticides, but noted that they are frequently used on golf courses, particularly in the United States, which uses as much as 15 times more pesticides on golf courses than do European countries.

“It shouldn’t be terribly surprising,” Dorsey says, “that chemicals designed to damage the nervous system of insects might have similar consequences on the nervous system of humans.”

Rotenone is another pesticide that could contribute to Parkinson’s. But there are few human studies that link it to the condition. One commonly cited study from 2011 compared 110 people with Parkinson’s (mostly farmers) who had formerly applied restricted-use pesticides on private property and a control group of 358 people from Iowa and North Carolina who regularly used chemicals at work in the 1990s, but were not cognitively impaired or diagnosed with Parkinson’s. Researchers found that people who had worked with rotenone — which degrades the function of mitochondria — had a 2.5 times higher risk of developing Parkinson’s than did people in the control group6. More-recent animal studies lend credence to this link. A 2025 study found that rats exposed to rotenone for 21 days had dysfunction in motor cortex synapses and upregulation of C1q (a glycoprotein) in the substantia nigra, a part of the brain that is affected in Parkinson’s7. This increased activity suggests an inflammatory response in that region of the brain.

For Parkinson’s researchers, chemicals linked to the condition can’t be banned quickly enough. But regulators in the United States seem more hesitant than their counterparts in many other countries.

The European Union banned TCE a decade ago. The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) released a review of TCE in 2024 that prohibited its use in consumer products and many industrial and commercial products as of 15 September 2025. There are exceptions for some applications, however, including one lasting 50 years for what the EPA calls “essential laboratory use”.

Paraquat is undergoing review by the EPA, in a process conducted on regulated pesticides at least every 15 years. The agency has requested more data from manufacturers, and has said that it will host a roundtable to solicit public input.

Rotenone is banned in the European Union and the United Kingdom, but continues to be used in the United States and Canada to control invasive fish populations.

“The EPA demands an absurd level of proof that something is dangerous,” says Tim Greenamyre, a neurologist at the University of Pittsburgh in Pennsylvania. “They don’t like epidemiological studies,” he says, but they also “throw out animal studies because they say toxicants aren’t given at the exact dose that humans get”.

Greenamyre has a personal stake in this issue. He studied rotenone in his lab for decades and was himself diagnosed with Parkinson’s in 2021. Because of the lack of research on chemical causes of the disease, he says, any connection between his exposure and his diagnosis would only be speculative. But he hopes to help fill that gap in knowledge: he has received funding to study the mechanism by which rotenone, TCE and paraquat might trigger Parkinson’s.

Another open question is how many other chemicals might cause damage to the brain similar to that in Parkinson’s. Ritz’s current research is focusing on organophosphates and organochlorides, but she says there are many other potential offenders, including carbamates, pyrethroids and neonicotinoids — all pesticides.

Researchers such as Ritz have access to pesticide report systems that record who is spraying which chemical, where and when. But by the time they finish studying one pesticide, it has been replaced with a different one, which is later replaced by yet another.

“We are basically 20–30 years behind what’s happening in the fields,” Ritz says. And with every new contaminant that enters the scene, the potential that one might trigger Parkinson’s ticks up a notch.

#1314. Robbie Savage’s Reaction After Son, Charlie, Scores Against His Peterborough Team

Most FA Cup first-round ties come down to the usual storylines: giant-killings, rare TV coverage and a big pay day for the lower-league clubs.

Peterborough United against Reading had something far more personal going on. On the touchline was Posh boss Robbie Savage, and on the pitch was his son, as they came face-to-face in a professional setting.

Reading’s midfield boasted Charlie Savage, who has followed in his father's footsteps, having become a professional footballer in 2021, and he enjoyed a unique afternoon at the Weston Homes stadium in what was a rare start for the midfielder.

Before half-time, the plot had already taken a cruel turn for Savage senior, the former Wales international, as one side dominated on a cool and cloudy afternoon in the FA Cup First Round.

Savage was only appointed at Peterborough in October, and within weeks the draw had pitted him against the club where Charlie has played since leaving Manchester United in 2023.

The 52-year-old was open about how strange the build-up felt. He admitted that facing his son could be “horrible” and put their usual phone calls on hold, ensuring that Charlie wouldn’t accidentally let slip anything about Reading’s preparations.

“I will be consoling him or congratulating him,” Savage said of what would come after the final whistle.

The form guide only pointed one way, with Reading sixth in League One and Peterborough 22nd going into the tie, as one of the best stories of the round played out on Saturday afternoon.

Reading were already 2-0 up when Charlie struck in first-half stoppage time. His deflected effort found its way in for 3-0, in what was his first goal of the season, and he wheeled away to celebrate in front of the travelling Reading fans.

TNT Sports’ cameras quickly cut to the Peterborough dugout, where Savage was clearly torn between pride and the pain of watching his side go further behind.

Reaction on social media was interesting to say the least, with one fan saying: ‘He actually just looks like he’s buzzing his lad has scored but is pretending he’s p***** off.’ Another agreed: ‘He’s deffo pretending to be p***** off, he’s buzzing.’

Whilst others focused on how hard Savage was working to keep a straight face: ‘Trying his best not to be proud on the sidelines,’ wrote one. ‘He’s holding back everything he has not to smile,’ said another.

Another angle saw fans question the Peterborough boss’s acting skills, with one posting: ‘Look at manager pretending to be p***** lmfao.’

A second was even more blunt: ‘That's the worst bit of acting from Robbie trying to look angry.’

Reading added two more after the break to complete a 5-0 win at London Road, sending Charlie through to the second round and his father out of the competition.

Any pride Savage felt for his son was quickly overshadowed by his side’s display. Speaking afterwards, he called the defeat “embarrassing” and took the blame himself.

“I’m devastated. It’s not acceptable, it’s embarrassing,” he said. “It’s on me, I pick the players and I pick the tactics.”

The Supercomputer has crunched the numbers and predicted the entire 2026-27 Premier League table in full

It is a tough start to life in the dugout at Peterborough. Savage won his first game in charge against Leicester City, but Posh have now gone six matches without a win since.

For the Savage family, though, this is one afternoon that won’t be forgotten in a hurry, as this father-son duo have a professional moment in time to look back on, even if one will be happier than the other.

#1313. Report Cagliari fan in hospital after fall from stands

There was an unfortunate incident after Cagliari’s 1-0 victory over Frosinone, as a supporter fell from the stands trying to salute the players, who rushed to his aid.

According to Sky Sport Italia, the fall occurred as the squad was walking over to thank the fans for their support several minutes after the final whistle of today’s Serie A encounter.

Captain Alessandro Deiola and goalkeeper Elia Caprile were the first to realise what had happened, and rushed over to help him.

An ambulance is always ready on the sidelines in top flight matches, and was called in take the supporter to the local hospital.

It’s reported the fan has been diagnosed with a fractured clavicle, but there are no more serious complications.

If all goes well, he should be released on Sunday to continue his recovery at home.

The Unipol Domus where the Sardinians play their home matches is a temporary structure, and was put in place while plans to reconstruct the Stadio Sant’Elia were worked through.

That arena now lies in ruins and is overgrown with vegetation just yards away from the current stadium.

#1312. Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card

Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

For Andoni Iraola, who had failed to beat Brentford in six attempts as manager of Bournemouth, it would have made for an immensely pleasing sight. After last weekend’s thrashing by Manchester City, Liverpool have responded with a 6-3 Champions League win over LASK and this victory against a previously unbeaten Brentford. Iraola will know, however, that his team’s numerical advantage was the fundamental reason for the dramatic shift in the flow of this game.

The Gtech Community Stadium simmered with outrage following Yarmoliuk’s red card, which came in the eighth minute of first-half stoppage time, and the home fans probably had a point. Yes, there was a movement of the midfielder’s head towards Jacquet, but it was hardly an act of violence. Jacquet’s reaction, collapsing to the turf in mock agony, was embarrassing but predictably effective. Cynics would say the Frenchman changed the game for his team. Purists would argue this is no way in which to influence a match.

Keith Andrews, the Brentford head coach, chose against complaining too aggressively. But he did make it clear what he thought of Jacquet’s behaviour. “I do think they were cute and clever,” Andrews said. “He is walking into Yarmo. But we need to look at ourselves and I understand why it was a red. Yarmo is an amazing young man and he will learn from this.”

Brentford had been the better team before this decisive incident and they deserved their lead, given to them by a majestic header by Keane Lewis-Potter, from Igor Thiago’s cross. It was a moment of attacking quality that Iraola’s glitzy attackers had looked unlikely to replicate, especially when Barcola fluffed a one-versus-one showdown with Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

To play an entire half of Premier League football with only 10 men is a brutal examination, though, and Brentford were unable to pass the test. Wirtz unleashed Muñoz after an hour, allowing the Spaniard to fire home with his left foot, before Barcola’s header found Isak in the box with 20 minutes remaining.

It was Isak’s fifth goal of the campaign, which means he has now beaten last season’s tally of four. He has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford. “I didn’t have too many chances,” Isak said. “I was waiting for my moment.”

Any hopes of a Brentford comeback evaporated in stoppage time, when the home side lost another man to a red card. This time it was Vitaly Janelt, who received his second yellow for fouling Rio Ngumoha, Liverpool’s sparkling teenage winger. From there, Liverpool’s attempts to score a third were comically poor. “We lacked some composure,” admitted Iraola. “But it was a good battle today, and very important points for us. To take three points here is very valuable.”

An encouraging result for Liverpool, then, but this was not an afternoon without concerns. The first-half showing was worrying, and there were also injuries to Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong. Both players limped off, and Iraola said they will now be out “for some time”.

The loss of Szoboszlai will be a particular concern, as he was rushed back from a hamstring injury for this game but then felt the same muscle again after only 32 minutes of action. “It’s a very delicate situation,” said Iraola.

The injury to Frimpong meant that Muñoz, a winger, played most of the second half as an attack-minded right-back. He did so excellently, and took his goal with impressive composure after Wirtz had pushed the ball into his path. Liverpool’s second was similarly clinical, as Isak pounced on Barcola’s knock-down in a congested penalty area. These, clearly, are the moments of game-changing quality that Liverpool expect from their big-money forwards. Iraola will hope it was a sign of things to come.

Speaking to Sky Sports after his first Premier League win as Fulham head coach, Arbeloa said: “I’m so happy, happy for my players, happy for my supporters, happy for everyone at the club that they deserve this victory. We [waited] a lot of time and some many games that I think we deserved this victory before, but today we did a very good game and yes, I can’t believe that the game finished just 1-0.”

9 - Florian Wirtz's nine chances created from open play against Brentford is the most by a player in a Premier League game since Sadio Mané v Burnley in January 2021 (9) and the most by a player in an away game since Samir Nasri v Spurs in August 2011 (10). Progress. https://t.co/xyMIQP9y5p

A huge moment for Alvaro Arbeloa and Fulham 💪 A 1-0 win over Hull takes them out of the relegation zone for now ⬆️ #FFC #BBCFootball https://t.co/cQaDybcESl

Erling Haaland straight down the tunnel at full-time here. He was limping for the last minute of the match after a block from Jack Clarke caught his ankle/shin area.

Liverpool turn things around, but you wonder whether this match would have ended differently had Yarmoliuk kept his head on the stroke of half-time.

Haaland’s double is enough for City today, but the Norwegian hobbles down the tunnel immediately having taken a knock in the dying minutes of the game. It is to be seen if that’s anything to be worried about... City maintain their perfect record, anyhow.

FULL-TIME: Erling Haaland grabs a brace as Man City beat Ipswich at the Etihad 🔵 https://t.co/WGp2lzpFjs

Brentford have not given up, but Liverpool are hanging on. Barcola the latest player to make a meaningful defensive intervention.

Fatawu is presented with an opening but the Ghana winger loses his footing and the chance passes Ipswich by.

A second Brentford red card! Janelt pushes Ngumoha with the youngster bearing down on goal and is given his marching orders. The hosts will finish this match with nine men.

Could have been 4-2. Ndiaye tries to shape an effort around Walton instead of squaring to Haaland and the chance to put the game to bed goes begging.

Twelve minutes of time added on have been indicated.

Fulham have won a Premier League football match! Arbeloa will breathe a sigh of relief after that. The hosts were by far the better side but almost undid their own good work at the end.

Sessegnon is off deep into stoppage time for a poor challenge on Hull’s Vaz.

Fulham are making themselves work for what would be their first three points of the season. All self-inflicted, of course.

Manchester City 3 Ipswich Town 2 (Flemming) It could have been 4-1 moments ago, but instead City are in for a nervy finish. Flemming goes straight down the middle.

The referee goes to the monitor after Guehi fells Fatawu inside the City box... and the penalty is awarded!

Barcola hits the woodwork! The Frenchman attempts to lob Kelleher off the second phase of a corner but his effort comes off the crossbar.

Manchester City 4 Ipswich Town 1 (Haaland) Ndiaye’s effort crashes off the crossbar and the ball falls to the feet of Enzo, who picks out Haaland and the Norwegian does the rest. What a finish. That’s his 13th City hat-trick.

Huge chance for Brentford! Anthony flashes a threatening ball across the face of goal and there Thiago is waiting and surely should score! He cannot arrange his feet quickly enough and Alisson is able to gather the ball with ease.

Liverpool’s front four have taken some criticism this season, and rightly so, but they have turned up in this second half. Wirtz assisted Munoz for the equaliser, and now Barcola has assisted Isak for the second.

The red card was the turning point in this game but the £400m frontline have delivered what was expected of them since the break.

Brentford 1 Liverpool 2 (Isak) The Swede is only just back from injury, and in all fairness has not looked great for much of this afternoon, but he’s put Liverpool infront here. Mac Allister plays a one-two with Wirtz down the right and the ball is worked to Barcola at the far post. The France winger nods it into the path of Isak who composes himself before spearing the ball beyond Kelleher.

Hull haven’t given up the ghost at Craven Cottage, knowing how easily Fulham crumbled last time out. Belloumi tries his luck from distance but cannot find the target.

Superb finish by Victor Munoz to level the scores here. Brentford were caught upfield and they were in trouble from the moment Florian Wirtz was able to slide the ball in behind for the Spanish winger. It comes as Liverpool were just starting to make their numerical advantage count.

Manchester City 3 Ipswich Town 1 (Haaland) Ndiaye does well to play in Haaland who breezes past Outtara before lacing the ball into the bottom corner.

Brentford 1 Liverpool 1 (Munoz) Ngumoha plays the ball infield to Wirtz on the half-way line, and the German threads a ball in behind for the rapid Munoz to gallop on to, he cuts inside Lewis-Potter and fires the ball beyond Kelleher with his left foot.

Iwobi goes close. His curled effort has Tzolakis scrambling but zips just wide of the mark.

Fernandez, on as a second-half substitute, tries his luck with a free-kick from 25 yards out, but he cannot get the requisite dip on the ball to bring it down and it flies over.

Fulham are still dominating the ball and have been by far the better side. Their possession share remains in the high seventies. They’ve completed 476 passes to Hull’s 94.

A second goal would surely put this one to bed.

Liverpool brought on Jeremie Frimpong as a half-time substitute but he’s already limped off. That’s the second injury they have picked up today, after Dominik Szoboszlai.

This is a proper test of Liverpool’s creative ability now. Ten-man Brentford are going to sit deep for most of this second half, I am sure. Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak, Bradley Barcola... time to deliver some game-changing quality.

Jacquet goes into the book. A loose pass out from the back is picked off my Brentford substitute Schade and Jacquet snaps in too enthusiastically and receives a yellow.

Chance! Will Fulham rue all these missed chances? King is involved once more, standing up a cross to the back post where Garcia nods down for Iwobi to stroke goalwards near the penalty spot, but Tzolakis does well to get down low to his left and keep Fulham’s advantage to just one goal.

Mateo Kovacic comes off injured for City. It is probably just a knock as he’s sat on the bench rather than heading down the tunnel. Was a standout player in the first half.

Close! Ajayi’s clearance comes straight back and Charles works the ball to King on the right, but with just the keeper to beat, the midfielder’s effort is saved by Tzolakis with his feet. King really should be scoring there.

Still some time before the Liverpool game resumes given the time added on at the end of the first half.

Following his clash of heads with Jarrad Branthwaite in the lunchtime kick-off at the Hill Dickinson Stadium, the Chelsea goalkeeper has now been taken to hospital to undergo precautionary tests.

Brentford lead Liverpool thanks to Keane Lewis-Potter's header, but the second half could be tricky for the Bees after Yehor Yarmoliuk was sent off just before half-time. Liverpool are yet to have a shot on target despite having seven shots in the first half. #BRELIV https://t.co/o9HE2Fh8qb

Andrews will be furious with how that first half ended. His side had done brilliantly to establish a lead, but will have their work cut out keeping Liverpool out after the break with the visitors a man to the good.

With half-time fast approaching and Brentford in front, this is absolute madness. Yarmoliuk looks to have butted Jacquet in an incident that reminds of Bentacur’s red card at Old Trafford last weekend.

The referee is sent to the pitchside monitor after a lengthy delay and Yarmoliuk is off!

We’ve had the second VAR review in just a few minutes here, and this one has resulted in a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk for a “headbutting action”. I have to say, this feels harsh. It’s pretty tame. There is a tiny movement towards Jacquet, who collapsed to the turf in dramatic fashion, but he’s hardly caused the Liverpool defender any damage. That will change the dynamic of this game.

Haaland restores City’s lead after Maeda had cancelled out Foden’s opener.

Arbeloa’s side are in front and could have been ahead by a wider margin, but we’ve been here before...

Gary Neville is a w-----, is a w-----.....is quite a loud chant here at City. Fans in a good mood here after Erling Haaland scored in his eighth game in a row.

Brentford 1 Liverpool 0 (Lewis-Potter) Outtara curls in a wonderful cross and Lewis-Potter steals in to head the ball beyond Alisson from 10 yards out.

Brentford take the lead, and it’s a lead they probably just about deserve on the run of play. It’s an absolutely superb header by Keane Lewis-Potter, up from left-back, as he thumps Igor Thiago’s cross into the top corner of Liverpool’s net. Textbook technique.

Just after Wirtz was denied a penalty of his own, Mac Allister looks to have won a spot-kick for real off a challenge from Outtara. The referee gives it, but is then sent to the monitor and the decision is reversed. Correct decision. Outtara clearly got a piece of the ball first.

Liverpool have been awarded a penalty but I don’t think this will stand. It shouldn’t stand. Dango Ouattara got a touch on the ball when he lunged in on Alexis Mac Allister.

Yep, the penalty has been overturned. Referee John Brooks missed Outtara’s touch on first viewing but the replays were pretty conclusive.

Manchester City 2 Ipswich Town 1 (Haaland) Kovacic wriggles free of his markers and darts to the by-line.
